openQuestions.question: How is a contradiction presented to a member, and what does resolving one look like (both sides in the record's words; a resolution that records its kind and may promote double-speak into a finding)?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Contradictions are 'golden nuggets' the system exists to find; in our own record they carry a duty to resolve. PRESENT and RESOLVE are undesigned and nothing shows a candidate to a member.
openQuestions.context: A contradiction is two things the record holds that cannot both be true. The system already pairs statements worth comparing and lets an AI run label each pair (in the world, in our own record, a difference of precision, unrelated, undetermined), but these 'candidates' are stored out of sight; no member sees them yet.

canonSays.says: Three cases: in the WORLD a finding, 'drawn attention to' and never fixed; in our RECORD a defect with a duty to identify, present and resolve; a difference of precision is no contradiction.
PRESENT: a member sees both sides in the record's own words, never a machine verdict. RESOLVE: a member's attributed act that never deletes either side.
At least one resolution kind must be able to promote the conflict into a finding: double-speak found while cleaning our record becomes a finding about the subject.
Labels are world, record, precision, unrelated, undetermined; a candidate is 'proposed machine work and no finding'; no read shows one to a member.

openQuestions.whyOpen: Only detection is designed and built. Nothing says where a candidate appears, what 'both sides with enough context' contains, which resolution kinds exist (misquote, our capture error, genuine double-speak, difference of opinion), or what promotion to a finding does. The irreconcilable pair (two well-supported findings the group keeps both of) needs a claim object Bob has not ruled on. Detection passed its gate (0/17 false conflicts, M-162) only on a test fixture, not real documents.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Nothing: the old interface never shows a contradiction candidate.

options.option: Show candidates as 'Noticed' queue items opening a side-by-side page (side A, side B, each with document, date and surrounding passage), with resolve acts named by kind
options.tradeoffs: Uses the one queue members already learn; could flood it if real false conflicts exceed the fixture's.

options.option: Show them only in place, as a mark on the question or document where a side sits
options.tradeoffs: Quieter and in context; a conflict between two projects' work may never be seen by anyone.

options.option: Design 'record' conflicts first (the duty) and treat 'world' candidates as a prompt to open a question whose conclusion is the discrepancy
options.tradeoffs: Matches the doctrine's priorities and reuses built question acts; the irreconcilable pair still waits for Bob.

openQuestions.recommendation: The third option, delivered through the first (a Noticed item opening a side-by-side page), with a resolution vocabulary Bob approves; measure false conflicts on real documents before anything reaches members.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob for the resolution kinds, the promotion to a finding and the irreconcilable pair (doctrine); Design for the side-by-side layout within them.

ruled.decided: A contradiction is conditional: two assertions that cannot both hold in the same respect. Resolving one means finding the respect in which they differ, finding the side that is wrong, or recording that the conflict is genuine. A candidate a member takes up becomes an inquiry whose conclusion records its kind (dissolved, corrected, or genuine; double-speak becomes a finding, and an obligation set against an act goes to conformance). It is shown inline wherever the two points already sit, through a tension mark and a short 'how do these differ' clarifier, with a dedicated contradiction screen only as the escalation; context may fill in facts and recommend judgements, labelled, but never silently decides. An undetermined candidate is a lead, never a duty; a record duty binds the joined members of every project drawing on either side until it is resolved; two projects' different conclusions are plurality unless they cannot both hold in the same respect, when a tension mark asks how they differ; the machine recommends only which respects may differ; a hypothesised cause is published as 'cause not established'; publication discloses, never blocks; 'one of them is wrong' needs a written reason; a dismissal gives one fixed reason. When the other side is in a project a member cannot see, each project is told of the conflict on its own side only; a checkbox signals willingness to resolve it, and when both projects opt in their members respond through relayed notices, sharing only what each chooses; a conflict remaining at publication is highlighted without naming the hidden project (DEC-85).
ruled.title: Contradictions: how they are shown and resolved

openQuestions.question: How does a knock become part of the record: what does 'pulled' commit a member to, and does the capture name the doorbell as its provenance?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: It is the only route in for whistleblowers and outsiders, and unvetted material must never look vouched for.
openQuestions.context: The doorbell lets anyone, with no account, hand the group a file or text (a 'knock'), for example a whistleblower. The knocker gets a receipt; the material sits in a separate doorbell inbox and is not part of the record. A signed-in member reads each knock and marks it 'pulled', 'discarded' or back to 'new'.

canonSays.says: A knock 'does not enter the record by knocking'; the intake contract and the provenance-for-admission rule 'apply when a member brings its material in, not before'.

What comes through the doorbell 'has NO attributed source, and the record says so rather than supplying one'; hand-carried material must be attributed to a member, 'as distinct from anonymous material arriving through the doorbell'.
Every submission carries provenance: a locator (an address, or 'in hand' with chain-of-custody notes), who issued it, when, the capture method and the capturing actor.
Resolving records only the status (pulled, discarded, new), who and when; nothing else changes.

openQuestions.whyOpen: 'Pulled' is only a label today: it creates no capture and nothing links the knock to a later one. Two rules pull apart: the intake contract wants a named locator and issuer, while the doorbell doctrine says the source is unknown and must be stated as unknown. Also undecided: whether pulling vouches for the material (release, a weightier act) or only admits it unvetted, and whether the knocker's note and contact travel into the record.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Nothing: the old interface has no doorbell inbox or knock screen.

options.option: 'Pull' creates a capture at 'collected' whose provenance says 'received through the doorbell, source unknown' plus the knock id and digest, and commits the member to nothing more
options.tradeoffs: Honest and simple; release (vouching) stays a separate later act. Needs a doorbell provenance class in the capture module.

options.option: Pulling is itself the member vouching: they become the hand-carrying source
options.tradeoffs: One step, but it turns an anonymous source into a named one, which Membership §1.2 forbids.

options.option: Keep 'pulled' a status only; the member uploads the material separately and writes chain-of-custody notes
options.tradeoffs: No new mechanism, but the link to the knock is manual and can be lost or misstated.

openQuestions.recommendation: The first option: pulling admits the material with 'doorbell, source unknown' as its stated provenance, and vouching stays with release.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob: whether pulling vouches and how anonymous provenance is stated are intake doctrine; Design settles the inbox screens afterward.

ruled.decided: Pulling a knock admits its material as a capture at 'collected' carrying the knock's receipt, and commits the member to nothing more; vouching stays with release. The source is recorded as an unnamed knocker identified by the receipt (never 'unknown'), the pulling member is the capturing actor and never the source, a knocker may prove continuity with a secret they keep, and a source's identity is held as a dated history of disclosures, published only with consent. The note travels with the capture as the knocker's own words; the contact stays in the inbox. The inbox act is regraded reasoned once pulling admits material (DEC-88).
ruled.title: A knock: how a tip becomes part of the record

openQuestions.question: Does a project show a stage (forming, investigating, matured, closed) and a work-product readiness ladder, and how?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: The Roadmap's project workspace has phase bars; the lifecycle and readiness ladder exist in canon only and no requirement holds them.
openQuestions.context: A project is a group's line of work around a stated objective. The canon gives it a stage (forming, investigating, matured, closed) and gives its work product a readiness ladder (draft, internally checked, externally compliant, distributed), so members can see where the work stands.

canonSays.says: A project shows its stage, one of State Rules §4.3's four, 'derived and never set by hand', with its work products' readiness, computed from the questions it holds and what it has published; the redesign shows it on the project's home screen (T12).
Lifecycle: forming (scope settling) → investigating → matured (analysis supports a defensible position) → closed, with a closed_reason (resolved, superseded, abandoned), 'preserved, reversible'.

The readiness ladder advances only on recorded evaluations: internally_checked needs passing internal compliance and argument evaluations; externally_compliant passing external ones; distributed at least one distribution record.
The workproduct_state, evaluations and closed_reason checks stay in legacy code; no module requirement holds the lifecycle or ladder.

openQuestions.whyOpen: K356 settles that the stage is shown and derived. Still open: the derivation rule (what moves forming to investigating, or to matured), which BOB must word before T12 (N300). 'Closed' carries a judged reason (resolved, superseded, abandoned), which sits uneasily with 'never set by hand'. The ladder advances on compliance and argument evaluations that are not built (UC-100), and the Roadmap's 'phase bars with tooltips' are undesigned.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The workspace shows the readiness ladder read-only from the document's workproduct_state; the lifecycle is a stored state with chips and allows closed back to investigating.

options.option: Derive all four stages: forming until a question has a leg, investigating while questions are open, matured when a question has concluded, closed only by an owner's reasoned act that the display then shows
options.tradeoffs: Clear and mostly automatic; 'closed' remains an authored act, a stated exception to 'never by hand'.

options.option: Derive stage only and drop the readiness ladder until evaluations exist
options.tradeoffs: Avoids showing a ladder that never moves; loses the path-to-publication signal the Roadmap wanted.

options.option: Show both, the ladder with its unmet rungs stated as 'no evaluation recorded'
options.tradeoffs: Honest about absence; a ladder that never moves may read as failure.

openQuestions.recommendation: The first option for stage, with the ladder shown only for rungs the record can actually earn, each unearned rung stated rather than hidden.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob confirms whether 'closed' may be an authored act despite K356 (requirement); Design settles the phase-bar layout; BOB words the derivation (N300).

ruled.decided: All four stages are shown: 'forming', 'investigating' and 'matured' are computed from the record, and 'closed' is the owner's reasoned act. Only readiness rungs a case can earn are shown, and each unearned one is stated. The display is coloured bars that build up, one per stage reached, disclosing more on hover (with a focus or tap equivalent) and opening on click to what each stage needs next and when each was reached; each bar is named, and 'closed' shows its reason and never reads as a finished stack.
ruled.title: A project's stage and its cases' readiness

openQuestions.question: What are the five steps of the publication ceremony, and what does the placeholder say until it is built?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Publication is the only irreversible act and the ceremony is the safeguard; its process is deferred (DEC-33).
openQuestions.context: Publishing a case is the one act that cannot be taken back; corrections only move forward as new editions. The 'ceremony' is the deliberate screen sequence an owner goes through before signing. Bob deferred it; today the group's operator publishes and members see a placeholder page.

canonSays.says: 'The publication process is very involved. Defer anything related to the process, though create a placeholder surface.' UI-17 (the five-step ceremony) and REC-15 (its dry run) are deferred.
The ceremony reopens with Program B's member surfaces or the first self-run group, whichever first; until then a member reaches the placeholder and is told, once, what is not yet there (DEC-69).
The pre-flight is plane-sourced: op=publishpreflight runs the real refusals (uncleared hunch, below the project's strength, no signers) without writing, because the browser cannot compute them.
The top rung 'carries its own ceremony (what becomes permanent, what it does and does not claim, an explicit key act)'; 'the ceremony IS the safeguard'.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The five steps are named only in archived research, not in canon: What becomes permanent; What this rests on; What you are leaving out (the gate); The revision this creates; Sign (BUILD-ORDER UI-17, RECONCILED). They predate DEC-72, which made a case a production of a project signed by an owner, so they may need re-deriving. The placeholder's wording is also not fixed in canon beyond DEC-33's three points.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: A statement page (S8, UI-17a) says what publication is and that the operator publishes for now; it has no publish control.

options.option: Adopt the archived five steps as the design input, re-derived for DEC-72 (case as a production, owner signs), and design them now while the placeholder ships
options.tradeoffs: Uses reasoned, adversarially reviewed work; building still waits for DEC-33's trigger.

options.option: Design only the placeholder now and leave the steps for when the trigger fires
options.tradeoffs: Least work; risks the redesign's layout not leaving room for a heavy ceremony.

options.option: Ask Bob to lift DEC-33 for the redesign
options.tradeoffs: Lets members publish without the operator; brings forward REC-15 and a large body of work.

openQuestions.recommendation: The first option: design the five steps on paper so the layout carries their weight, and ship the placeholder text DEC-33 describes until the trigger fires.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob, if the steps become requirements or DEC-33 is reopened; Design for the placeholder wording within DEC-33.

ruled.decided: There is no placeholder: the ceremony and its pre-flight are designed and built in the redesign, in five steps re-derived for DEC-72 (step three discloses any unresolved record contradiction and asks consent for any source identity revealed), and an owner signs in the browser with a registered browser-held key producing the same sshsig signature. A published case may rest on a co-attested Grade B capture, each document's grade and co-attestation disclosed; one whose co-attestation failed may be published only by an attributed acknowledgement and is marked 'self-attested only' (DEC-81). Grade A and further co-witnesses are deferred, their options documented in GRADE-A-CAPTURE.md (DEC-81 item 4).
ruled.title: The publication ceremony

openQuestions.question: Does the project workspace show grades and strength, given the legacy UI hides grades there (UI-16 note) while canon says strength is shown rather than hidden?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Showing strength is the core defence against over-claiming; hiding it in the place members work may undercut that.
openQuestions.whereTheCanonStops: Case Making section 4a; legacy app.html (not canon)
openQuestions.context: Strength is how well a question's answer is supported: a pair (weakest captured document, weakest connection) with testimony beside it, never one score. The project workspace lists the questions and actions inside a project; the old interface deliberately showed no strength there.

canonSays.says: The tool should make a supported case easy and an unsupported one hard to state, visible in the surface: 'strength shown rather than hidden, exclusions named rather than dropped'.
Strength is derived, never stated: a pair of independent measurements with testimony beside them, never composed into one value.
A project declares the strength its work requires (its bar); publishing is refused when a load-bearing leg falls below it.
A project is a container and an inquiry a claim structure; the workspace 'shows NO strength, NO grade and NO conclusion', and a test asserts no grade letter appears.

openQuestions.whyOpen: Canon wants strength visible, and each project declares a bar strength is measured against, yet the screen listing a project's questions hides it. The old reason (a project is a container, a question a claim structure) is an interface choice, not a ruling; the research left open where the line falls between '3 questions live here' and 'one is at grade C'. Showing it in a list must still avoid a single summary figure (DEC-44).
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The workspace lists questions with no strength or grade; strength appears only on each question's own page.

options.option: Show each question's pair against the project's bar in the list (e.g. 'capture B, connection C; bar B/B'), unrated and undetermined stated
options.tradeoffs: Makes over-claiming visible where work happens; a busier list, and must never collapse into one badge.

options.option: Show only whether each question meets the project's bar (meets / short on connection / undetermined), with the pair one click away
options.tradeoffs: Simple and tied to what matters for publishing; a met/not-met can read like a score.

options.option: Keep the workspace grade-free
options.tradeoffs: Clean container view; contradicts Case Making §4a's 'shown rather than hidden'.

openQuestions.recommendation: The first option: show the pair per question beside the project's bar, because the bar is the project's own declaration and the canon asks strength to be seen.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design, within Case Making §4a and DEC-44; the old UI note is not canon, so no ruling is needed unless Design proposes hiding strength.

ruled.decided: The project workspace shows strength: each question shows its capture and connection badges (with testimony beside them when an account is part of the answer) and one plain phrase against the project's bar, such as 'Short on connection · bar B/B', 'Undetermined' named with its reason, never one combined score. Every scale follows the measures map Bob approved (letters grade evidence, bars show progress, weights mark acts), docs/development/ux-substrate/measures-map.html, rendered at https://claude.ai/artifact/TfqcXNaJQ86SZzUA8Xn6Ni.
ruled.title: Strength and grades in the project workspace

openQuestions.question: What is the one visual treatment and voice of UNDETERMINED, and how does it differ from 'withheld', 'unrated', 'not looked' and 'refused'?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: It appears in many unrelated places and must be identical everywhere, or members learn to ignore it.
openQuestions.context: 'Undetermined' is the system's honest 'we do not know, and here is why': an unchecked link, an unstated document date, an incomputable strength. It appears in many unrelated places. Nearby states mean different things: withheld (exists, not yours to see), unrated (nothing graded yet), never looked (nobody searched), refused (the system declined an act).

canonSays.says: A display primitive rendered 'identically everywhere', in at least six places; 'first-class and must be STATED, never invented past and never dressed as an error'; 'One visual treatment, one voice: what we do not know, and why we do not know it.'
Something out of view is stated only as an incompleteness: the member learns something is missing, never what it is (withheld).
An ungraded member is inert and named; an axis with no graded member is 'unrated' and says it rests on nothing, distinct from 'undetermined'.
Look states are looked-absent, looked-indeterminate, partial, present and never-looked; a missing look has a cause (pre-log, purged, never looked).

openQuestions.whyOpen: The canon fixes the principle (one look, one voice, with the reason) but no visual treatment or wording exists, and it does not say how the four neighbours differ visibly. The risk runs both ways: if all five look alike, members cannot tell 'nobody looked' from 'we could not tell'; if undetermined looks like an error, members learn to ignore it.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: A tinted 'undetermined' badge, but the same badge style also marks 'no grade yet', so undetermined and unrated look alike.
related: Q5, Q8 (strength and plan support status reuse it)

options.option: One component with a fixed mark and a mandatory 'because…' line, plus four distinct sibling treatments (withheld, unrated, never looked, refused), each with its own fixed sentence pattern
options.tradeoffs: Clear and teachable; needs a small, strict vocabulary and discipline in every surface.

options.option: One neutral 'gap' family with a colour-free text label for each kind
options.tradeoffs: Accessible and calm; differences rest on reading, easier to miss.

openQuestions.recommendation: The first option: one undetermined component that always carries its reason, and four visibly different neighbours with fixed wording.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design: §U already sets the principle; the treatment and wording are the designer's within it.

ruled.decided: 'Undetermined' is one component with a fixed mark and a line that always says 'because…', the same everywhere. 'Withheld', 'Unrated', 'Nobody looked' and 'Refused' each have their own visibly different treatment and one fixed sentence pattern, never shared with each other or with Undetermined. None is dressed as an error, and all are written as named terms (DEC-82). The exact marks and wording are the redesign's, within this rule.
ruled.title: “Undetermined” and its four neighbours

openQuestions.question: How does the rung ladder look and feel so a member senses weight before acting, especially the attested and irreversible rungs?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Weight flattening is named as a doctrine failure wearing a usability improvement.
openQuestions.context: Every act carries a 'rung' naming its weight: reversible, reasoned (needs a written reason), terminal, attested (signed, cannot be undone silently) and irreversible (publishing). The aim is that a member feels how heavy an act is before taking it, so dismissing a note and publishing a case never feel like the same click.

canonSays.says: 'Rung' names the weight of an act; the sequence release → … → publish is the 'path to publication'. This settles the naming conflict the substrate recorded.

'Weight flattening' is 'a doctrine failure wearing a usability improvement'; the ladder is 'a property of every act, visible and escalating, learned once and read everywhere'; the top rung carries its own ceremony: 'one thing to learn, two things to feel'.
Attestation can be corrected, but only by a further dated, signed act, never silently; publishing is irreversible and corrections move forward as editions.
The plane publishes each act's rung; 57 ops are still graded 'undetermined' and are to be reassigned by BOB.

openQuestions.whyOpen: K356 settles the word; the look and feel is undesigned. The canon wants weight felt yet also one act shape (choose, pre-flight, reason, receipt), and does not say what escalates with each rung: friction, colour, confirmation, a separate screen. 57 acts have no rung yet, so the design must handle unknown weight.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Act dialogs show a five-rung 'How heavy this act is' ladder with the act's own rung lit, worded 'at X weight', which collides with the plane's separate meaning of weight.

options.option: Escalating friction by rung: reversible acts inline; reasoned open a reason field; terminal and attested a full dialog stating what cannot be silently undone; irreversible only through the ceremony
options.tradeoffs: The hand feels the difference; heavier acts are slower, which is the point.

options.option: Same dialog for all, with the ladder shown and the current rung highlighted
options.tradeoffs: Consistent and easy to build; the difference is read rather than felt, the flattening the canon warns against.

openQuestions.recommendation: The first option, with the rung's name on the button, and an undetermined-rung act treated as reasoned until BOB assigns it.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design, within Interaction Constructs rev. 0.2 and K356; BOB assigns the 57 missing rungs (affordances R27).

ruled.decided: Friction is kept as low as possible so the tool fades and the work stays in focus, while members still feel the weight of their work and the finality of some steps; cues rich in information show state, relationships, context, progression and the acts available; everything is self-evident to newcomers and intuitive to experienced members; and a heavier act slows the member down, even for a moment. Friction follows the rung: a reversible act happens inline; a reasoned act opens a reason field in place; a terminal or attested act opens a full dialog stating what ends or cannot be silently undone, and who signs; an irreversible act goes only through the ceremony. Every act's button shows its rung's name and weight mark, and an act whose rung is not yet set is treated as reasoned. The 57 acts that had no rung have Bob's (26 reversible, 29 reasoned, 2 terminal, DEC-88). Six judgement calls carry high friction whatever their rung: choosing a person's attribution, sharing a lead, registering a subject and setting the group's strength bar open the full dialog stating their effect; approving a filing is terminal and has it already; having the assistant work an objective, the lightest of the six, opens its reason field in place with the run's budget and scope beside it. A heavy consequence is not a new rung.
ruled.title: How the weight of an act is felt

openQuestions.question: Where does a member record why something is (or is not) significant enough to escalate, given no significance field is allowed?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Significance is the point where policy preference most tempts; requirements forbid scores, so the judgment lives only in acts.
openQuestions.whereTheCanonStops: Functional Architecture Layer 2 Function 4; conformance R8
openQuestions.context: Once a group finds that a government body broke a rule, it must decide whether it is worth pursuing (escalating): a report two days late may not be; a $52.6 million unauthorised transfer is. No significance, severity or priority score may be stored, so the judgement exists only as acts on an escalation.

canonSays.says: 'Not every discrepancy is a violation'; significance is 'human judgment informed by context, scale, pattern, and consequences', the point where the temptation to let policy preferences colour compliance judgement 'is strongest'.

canonSays.source: conformance R8; escalation R19; consequences R11; K12
canonSays.says: No input or answer carries a significance, severity, priority, urgency, rank or score; 'significance is the members' judgment'.
Any joined member may open an escalation from a noncompliant determination; advancing, declining a stage and suspending each need a written reason.

openQuestions.whyOpen: Reasons are recorded once an escalation exists, but the first judgement, deciding not to escalate a noncompliant finding at all, has no act and so leaves no trace; nor does the reasoning for opening one. The ban on a significance field protects neutrality, while the doctrine that decisions are authored and kept argues for somewhere to write why. The canon does not reconcile the two.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Nothing: the old interface has no escalation surface.

options.option: Require a free-text reason when opening an escalation, and add a reasoned 'decline to escalate' act on a noncompliant determination
options.tradeoffs: Every judgement leaves an authored trace; a new act, and free text could smuggle in a severity word nobody checks.

options.option: Record the reasoning as a declined or chosen option in the action plan (S11)
options.tradeoffs: One home for 'what we chose and why'; the plan is unbuilt and never published (DEC-25).

options.option: Leave it to discussion outside the record
options.tradeoffs: No new mechanism; the most policy-sensitive judgement goes unrecorded.

openQuestions.recommendation: The first option: a required reason when opening and a reasoned decline act, both prose only, so the judgement is kept without becoming a score.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob: adding a decline act and a required reason changes the escalation and conformance requirements and touches Operational Principle 1.

ruled.decided: Whether a matter is worth pursuing is recorded only in acts and their reasons, never in a score. Opening an escalation takes a written reason. 'Decline to escalate' on a live noncompliant determination records, in the member's own words, why the group is not pursuing it now: reasoned, attributed and dated, corrected only forward (a later escalation, opened with its own reason, supersedes it and both stay readable). In an action plan, not pursuing a matter is an option declined with a short reason. No field, value or vocabulary for significance, severity, priority, urgency or rank exists anywhere. Any joined member who may open an escalation may decline one.
ruled.title: Where the judgement to pursue a matter, or not, is recorded

openQuestions.question: What does the action plan surface (S11) look like: options, dependencies, deadlines, resources, outcome branches, declined options, and support status on every element?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Impacting has no working process; a plan that hid a hypothetical premise would be the over-claiming failure.
openQuestions.context: When a group finds that an agency broke a rule, it must decide what to do: records requests, referrals, public comment, media, litigation support. The action plan (surface S11) would lay out options, order, deadlines, resources, what follows each outcome, and the options rejected. Each step taken becomes an 'action' page, which exists today.

canonSays.says: A plan is a distinct object holding candidate steps; each step has dependencies, deadlines, outcome-keyed branches, resources and a disposition (chosen, declined with reason, done, blocked); a declined step 'keeps its reason and stays visible'.

Every element carries a support status (established, short of the standard, hypothetical), displayed wherever it is 'in the same treatment everywhere, exactly as undetermined is'; a hypothetical premise is hunch debt.
The machine may suggest a plan as candidates and check it (e.g. an outcome with no next step); it never adopts a step.
The plan is working material and never published; if that changes it applies only to plans written afterwards.

openQuestions.whyOpen: No requirement or module holds a plan, so none is built. Undecided: how to draw an outcome-keyed decision tree legibly, how support status shows on every element, how a plan relates to the escalation module's built seven-stage protocol (which also sequences outward acts), and how refusing an outward act whose step is not 'established' appears.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Nothing for plans; individual action pages exist (risk tier, governing laws, correspondence).
related: Q25 (declared flows; plans must not share their machinery)
Q6 (support status reuses the undetermined treatment)

options.option: A tree/graph view with each step as a card (support status, deadline, resources list, disposition), branches labelled by outcome, declined steps greyed but present
options.tradeoffs: Matches Bob's 'dependency graphs keyed to outcomes'; graphs are hard on phones and in print.

options.option: An outline (nested list) of steps with 'if denied / if ignored' sub-steps, and a separate declined-options list
options.tradeoffs: Readable anywhere and simple to build; branching is less visible.

options.option: Fold the plan into escalation stages rather than a separate object
options.tradeoffs: Reuses built code; conflicts with Case Making §2, since an escalation is one pursued breach, not a set of options.

openQuestions.recommendation: The second option first (an outline with support status on every line), with a graph view added later; a module requirement must be written before design goes deep.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob: a plan needs requirements and a module (scope and tranche are his); Design settles the layout once he does.

elsewhere.note: Bob moved this question to a separate session on Actions, which decides it (DEC-93); BOB's action-plan rulings 1-10 there rule it in part.
elsewhere.src: DECISIONS.md DEC-93; docs/development/action-design/ACTION-PLAN.md (another session's branch, as BOB's page cites it)

rulings: D1-D6 and the closing rule of 2026-09-30 (K590)
ruled.decided: The plan page is an outline, not a graph: its subjects with their support; its options collapsed to a one-line summary, category and dates, sortable by category, date, subject or disposition, with declined options kept visible with their reasons; up to three scenarios of phases with checkpoints and branches that a member judges; and what each started option became. A strip under the title shows the checks in words. The assistant's suggestions wait in a separate tray until adopted. It holds no costs, budgets, assignees or scores and is never published. A graph view may come later. Layout detail remains Design's. The approved sketch is views/plan-page.html.
ruled.title: The action plan page

openQuestions.question: What does the assistant dialog look like on each surface, and how is 'the machine did the looking, you do the concluding' made felt?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: The assistant is one way in everywhere and must never appear to conclude; the pilot flow and wizard are unbuilt.
openQuestions.context: The assistant is a text or voice box available on every screen. A member can ask it to find something, help with a task, create something, or take an act. It may search, gather and check, but it never concludes, authors a reason or signs; for multi-step work it acts as a guide that opens the right screen and waits while the member acts.

canonSays.says: 'The machine may do the looking; the member does the concluding.'

One way in on every surface, a persistent tag expanding to a dialog (S12); the assistant may initiate an act but the act 'still runs its four beats'; it is a named non-member actor ('the assistant did this, at Anna's request').
It shows how it read the request; asks at most one clarifying question; an answer names the level searched ('I found nothing' without a level is the overclaim).
The wizard is a plan rendered as steps, 'visibly machine-made, dismissible, never blocking'; it 'never enters values into fields and never presses Submit'; an abandoned wizard is a non-event.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The rules are clear but the pilot flow and wizard are unbuilt, and nothing says how the dialog looks, where it sits on each surface, or what signals machine output versus member text. Only CHECK runs are deployed, so the dialog must explain refused modes. Showing voice transcription for correction is undesigned.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: No prompt box anywhere; only a running-session indicator for AI runs.

options.option: A side panel docked beside the owning surface; machine text in a distinct 'machine work' style with attribution; each wizard step highlights the real control but never fills it
options.tradeoffs: The member always acts on the real surface; needs space and a consistent machine style across the product.

options.option: A modal dialog that navigates away and returns
options.tradeoffs: Simple on phones; hides the surface the member is meant to act on, weakening 'you do the concluding'.

openQuestions.recommendation: The first option: a docked panel with one visible 'machine work' treatment shared with every other machine output, and acts always performed on the real surface.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design, within DEC-24, DEC-27 and ASSISTANT-PILOT; Bob only if the pilot's read-only scope or its order is to change.

ruled.decided: the assistant is a panel docked beside the surface it serves, and it never floats. Its text carries the one 'machine work' treatment every machine output shares, with attribution ('the assistant did this, at <member>'s request'); a wizard step highlights the real control and never fills or presses it, and the member performs every act on the real surface. Two refinements: the panel expands (a draggable divider and an 'expand' control let it take most of the window while some of the member's surface stays visible; it shrinks back by itself when a wizard step needs the member to act; its size is remembered, and one click restores the default), and it docks by screen shape, at the side on wide screens and at the bottom on narrow ones, with the member free to switch edges and the choice remembered.
ruled.title: The assistant panel

openQuestions.question: What does a newcomer learn first, and how do starter materials and onboarding fit a first session?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Design Requirement 11 requires usability within one session by someone with no civic experience; starter materials are not started.
openQuestions.context: A newcomer is someone just invited to a group: they open the invitation link, choose a handle (the name the record shows) and a password, and land in the product. Before they can usefully capture, weigh or publish, they need the group's values, how evidence is graded, and how to stay safe. The canon calls the learning materials the 'starter kit'.

canonSays.says: The starter kit (values and principles explained, a walkthrough of a real case, data-source and legal-tool guides, a security guide) must be 'usable within one session' by someone with no civic experience, free at believeinoakland.org.
'All starter kit materials', the explanatory paragraphs and the security guide are 'not yet started'.
Load-bearing state is 'named explicitly so a newcomer can recognize it and learn its implications'.
Informing at the act, once, is respect; 'responsibility reminders detached from any act' are the flaw.
The product must not carry Oakland-specific references that tell a group elsewhere it is not for them.

openQuestions.whyOpen: No module covers UC-148: nothing says what the first session contains, in what order, or whether the kit lives in the product or on a website. Two tensions: Requirement 11 names Oakland sources, tools and case, while the 2026-09-25 ruling bars local content from the product; and DEC-69 forbids act-detached 'responsibility' lessons, so a front-loaded tutorial risks being the nagging the canon calls a flaw.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: No onboarding or starter kit; newcomers get hover glossary definitions and short 'teach' paragraphs on each surface, and the invitation page shows cover, role and capabilities.

options.option: Teach at the act only: no tutorial; every first encounter with an act or state carries its one-time explanation, plus a public starter kit on the group's website outside the product.
options.tradeoffs: Fully consistent with DEC-69 and cheap; a newcomer never gets the big picture (values, security) unless they find the website.

options.option: A short in-product 'first session' path: values and principles, a security briefing, then a guided walkthrough of one real published case read end to end, with jurisdiction-specific guides supplied by the group's installed profile.
options.tradeoffs: Meets Requirement 11 inside the product and keeps local content in profiles; costs authoring a generic sample case and per-profile guides.

options.option: A practice sandbox: the newcomer captures, grades and drafts in a scratch space with a sample case, then enters the real record.
options.tradeoffs: Most effective learning; a second, practice world risks confusion with the real record.

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 2, with option 1's teach-at-the-act rule everywhere else: it satisfies Requirement 11 in one session while keeping local guides in jurisdiction profiles, not in the product.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob: what a newcomer must learn first, and whether the starter kit is part of the product or the group's website, is a requirement and UX principle; the layout of the path is Design's.

ruled.decided: Deferred: 'this needs to be deferred until the new UX is in place and stabilized.' Onboarding is designed against the product members will actually use. Meanwhile the measures map already rules that a newcomer meets strength against the bar and 'Undetermined' first, everything else taught at the act (DEC-82).
ruled.trigger: The redesigned member surfaces are built and have been stable in use (no major layout changes) for a period BOB judges sufficient; or Bob asks.
ruled.title: What a newcomer learns first

openQuestions.question: When your group takes on, questions or builds on another group's published work, what does each of those acts mean, who sees it, and how is it undone?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Trust signals must be ambient and travel with data; no requirement holds the indicator.
openQuestions.context: Members often use work that someone else produced, above all another group's published case. The Roadmap wants every piece of information to carry a visible trust indicator with five levels, from 'our own work' down to 'flagged concerns', so a member can tell at a glance how far to lean on it. A member meets it when reading or citing material they did not produce.

canonSays.says: 'Every piece of information carries a visible trust indicator': our work; independently verified; meets standards (compliance skill); not yet evaluated; flagged concerns. Signals are 'ambient (always visible)' (§12).

canonSays.source: Functional Architecture v3 'Trust signals throughout the stack'
canonSays.says: The signal travels with the data; 'independently verified' comes from the group re-evaluating incoming work before citing it.
Bob revised 'no transitive trust': inherited trust is accepted if disclosed; what is inherited is 'the fact of publication, never the credibility of the content'.
A leg citing a published case is 'inherited', names an edition, and cannot be stronger than that edition's frozen strength.
The five-level indicator and a group's acceptance into its own body of work are covered by no requirement.

openQuestions.whyOpen: No module produces the levels: nothing records that a group verified or accepted another group's work, and no evaluator of incoming work yields 'meets standards' or 'flagged'. The canon also shifted: the Functional Architecture says incoming work is re-evaluated before citation, while Bob's 2026-07-30 ruling and inquiry R7 let a member cite a published edition directly. Whether the levels replace, sit beside or derive from the record's own grades is undecided.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Nothing: no trust dots; a published case shows its frozen strength per finding and a stranger can verify its signature.

options.option: Derive the levels from facts the record already holds: ours (produced here); inherited (another group's published edition, signature verified); accepted (a recorded acceptance act, new); not yet evaluated; flagged only when a recorded evaluation names issues.
options.tradeoffs: Honest and ambient with little new doctrine; needs one new act (accept into our body of work) and drops or defers 'meets standards' until an evaluator exists.

options.option: Build the Roadmap's five levels as written, including a compliance evaluation of incoming work.
options.tradeoffs: Faithful to the Roadmap; requires a new evaluation module and risks a machine verdict reading as a trust grade, which the 'machine proposes, member decides' rule resists.

options.option: Drop a separate trust indicator and rely on grades, provenance chain and edition shown everywhere.
options.tradeoffs: No new construct; loses the at-a-glance signal the Roadmap requires and the idea of a group's accepted body of work.

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1: it keeps the ambient signal while grounding every level in a recorded fact, and leaves 'meets standards' for when an evaluator exists.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob: the trust hierarchy is mission doctrine (Roadmap §11) and choosing to revise it, and adding an acceptance act, are requirements; the dot's look is Design's.

ruled.decided: Information from other groups carries an origin mark in the same family as 'Machine work', answering who made this: Ours; Another group's (a published edition, signature verified); Accepted by our group; 'Not yet evaluated'; and 'Flagged'. The mark is ambient, a hover shows the fact behind it, and it is never composed with grades or strength into one trust score. Accepting another group's work is a reasoned act naming one edition (a newer edition reads 'Another group's' until accepted); it records who, when and why, changes no grade, and is withdrawn by a reasoned act that sends re-evaluation notices. A flag is a member's recorded evaluation naming the specific issue, never a machine's; it stays inside the group and is cleared by a member with a reason. 'Meets standards' stays deferred until an evaluator of incoming work exists, and if it returns it is labelled machine work. When a group's published case relies on another group's work, the case states the acceptance and discloses any open flag on it: disclosed, never blocked. A public list of acceptances and flags follows when a second group asks to see who accepted or flagged its work.
ruled.title: Where information from other groups came from (the origin mark)

brief.settledSince: Nothing since your 29 September ruling settles the four points. The rulings of 30 September to 1 October (the Action layer, removal of old code) do not touch them; the nearest says joint action with another group waits until a coalition asks.
brief.title: Accepting and flagging another group's work
brief.inOneBreath: When your group takes on, questions or builds on another group's published work, what does each of those acts mean, who sees it, and how is it undone?
brief.decision: The four points left open on 29 September: (1) what 'Accepted by our group' commits the group to, whether it is public, and how it is withdrawn; (2) how a 'Flagged' mark is raised, answered and cleared, and who sees it; (3) whether 'Meets standards' returns; (4) what a reader of your own case sees when it rests on work you accepted or flagged.
brief.alreadyDecidedPart: On 29 September you replaced the Roadmap's five trust levels with an origin mark saying who made a thing: 'Ours', 'Another group's', 'Accepted by our group', 'Not yet evaluated', 'Flagged'. It is always visible, a hover shows the fact behind it, and it is never combined with grades into a trust score. 'Flagged' comes only from a member's recorded evaluation naming specific issues, never a machine's; 'Meets standards' waits for an evaluator of incoming work.
basics: A group is the people using one copy of Civicsmith, usually one civic organisation; a member is one of them. A project is a group's line of work toward a goal. A case is a project's finished, signed argument, published and never changed: a correction is a new numbered edition, the way an errata filing sits beside the original.
Each finding in a case has two separate grades, A to D, never combined: capture (how well the documents are held) and connection (how firmly the links between them are established).

Members can cite another group's published case: part of a question then rests on, say, 'Budget Watch, edition 2'. Your ruling of 30 July sets the limit: citing carries over the fact that they published it, never the credibility of the content, and the citation can never be stronger than that edition's grades when it was signed.

The origin mark is a small label on any information saying who made it. Two of its labels, 'Accepted by our group' and 'Flagged', need acts that do not exist yet, taken by a named member with a reason.
The founding design requirements add: each group 'maintains its own accepted body of work', and 'acceptance is public and traceable'.
today: Nothing of this is built. A member can cite another group's edition, capped at its signed grades. There is no accept or flag button and no origin mark on screen.

The requirements for the acceptance act and the origin mark are owed to you under your 29 September ruling and wait on these four points. Only one group uses Civicsmith; no second group has published anything yet.
problem: Acceptance is the one place a group could take on another group's credibility, which your 30 July ruling otherwise keeps out. If it means 'we vouch for this as our own', one careless click carries another group's error into your cases. If it means nothing visible, members will not see the point.

The founding requirement says acceptance is public. But Civicsmith speaks to the outside only by publishing signed cases, so a public acceptance list would be a new kind of published object. A private acceptance falls short unless it becomes public when it matters: when your own case relies on it.

A public flag is a public criticism of an ally and needs the care of a finding, with a fair chance to answer. A private flag may never reach the group that made the error. Either way something must clear it, usually their next edition.
Too generous a choice risks your group's credibility; too strict, and members keep their doubts in email, outside the record. The owed requirements wait on it.

story.title: Dana, Luis, Priya and the Budget Watch sewer case
steps: The Alameda Budget Watch publishes edition 2 of a case: over three budget cycles the city moved $4.1 million from the sewer fund into general operations. Your group, Oakland Ratepayers, is investigating the same fund.
Dana cites it. It shows 'Another group's · Budget Watch, edition 2 · signature verified', capped at that edition's grades: capture B, connection C.

Luis fetches the three adopted budgets himself, checks the transfers, clicks 'Accept into our work' and writes: 'Re-captured the FY23–FY25 budgets; transfers match.' The mark becomes 'Accepted by our group'.
Priya then finds that $600,000 of the total is a one-time 2023 loan repayment, not a transfer, and flags it with the page and line.
Your group publishes a case relying on Dana's question. What does a reporter learn about the Budget Watch work, the acceptance and the flag? Does Budget Watch ever hear of the flag?
Budget Watch publishes edition 3 at $3.5 million. Who clears the flag, and does Luis's acceptance carry over?

fixed.point: Five labels, always visible, the fact on hover, never one trust score; 'Flagged' only from a member's named evaluation.
fixed.why: Your ruling of 29 September on the origin mark.

fixed.point: Citing carries over the fact of publication, never credibility, and is capped at the cited edition's signed grades.
fixed.why: Your ruling of 30 July on delegated trust.
fixed.src: AUTHORITY-AND-TRUST.md 'RULED: transitive trust is accepted'; inquiry R7

fixed.point: A reasoned act is corrected only forward; both acts stay readable.
fixed.why: Your rulings of 29 September on the weight of acts.

fixed.point: Each group keeps its own accepted body of work; acceptance is public and traceable.
fixed.why: Founding design requirement.

fixed.point: A newer edition of cited work sends a re-evaluation notice to findings resting on it; nothing changes by itself.
fixed.why: The built re-evaluation rules.

options.label: A
options.name: A reasoned stance, made public when your case relies on it
options.howItWorks: 'Accept into our work' asks what was checked and records who, when and why; no grade changes. An acceptance names one edition; a newer edition reads 'Another group's' until someone accepts it. Withdrawing is a reasoned act and sends re-evaluation notices. A flag names the issue and stays inside the group, and a member clears it with a reason. When your published case relies on the work, the case states the acceptance and must disclose any open flag, as it must disclose an open contradiction.
options.inTheStory: Your case reads: 'Relies on Budget Watch, edition 2 · accepted by Oakland Ratepayers on 3 Nov: re-captured the FY23–FY25 budgets; transfers match · Our member flagged one figure: $600,000 is a 2023 loan repayment, not a transfer.' Budget Watch learns of it by reading your case. After edition 3, Dana gets a re-evaluation notice and Priya clears the flag: 'Corrected in edition 3.'
gains: Every label rests on a named act with a reason.
Keeps your 30 July boundary.
No new public object; reuses correction forward, notices and disclosure at publication.
costs: Acceptance is not public until used, a looser reading of the founding requirement.
The other group may learn of a problem late.
options.commitsYouTo: Two reasoned acts (accept or withdraw; flag or clear), a citation line in the case, and a publication check that open flags are disclosed.

options.label: B
options.name: A public accepted body of work
options.howItWorks: Acceptances, withdrawals and flags are published at once, as a signed list beside the group's cases, each naming the edition, date, member (or 'a member') and reason. Flags appear as concerns the other group can answer in its next edition. Grades still do not change.
options.inTheStory: The day Priya flags, Budget Watch can read: 'Concern: $600,000 counted as a transfer is a 2023 loan repayment (FY23 budget, p. 214).' Its edition 3 answers it, and the clearing is published too.
gains: Literal to the founding requirement.
An early-warning channel between groups.
costs: A second kind of signed public object, with its own rules.
A public accusation against an ally.
Reveals what you are examining before any case exists.
options.commitsYouTo: A new published object; the directory (question 29) would likely read it.

options.label: C
options.name: Acceptance as full vouching
options.howItWorks: Accepted work is treated as your own (the Roadmap's original 'independently verified'): your members grade it afresh, above the cited edition's grades if they choose, and the mark reads close to 'Ours'.
options.inTheStory: Dana's question rests on the Budget Watch work at whatever grade your members give it; Priya's flag becomes a flaw in your own work.
gains: Accepted work becomes fully usable.
costs: Reverses your 30 July boundary.
A careless acceptance carries errors in at full weight; re-capturing the documents already makes them honestly 'Ours'.
options.commitsYouTo: Revisiting the 30 July ruling.

options.label: D
options.name: Defer until a second group publishes
options.howItWorks: Only 'Ours', 'Another group's' and 'Not yet evaluated' appear; no accept or flag button.
options.inTheStory: Luis's check and Priya's doubt stay in a chat thread; your case cites edition 2 silently.
gains: Nothing designed before it is needed.
costs: The owed requirements wait; a doubt about cited work has no recorded home and cannot be disclosed.
options.commitsYouTo: Nothing now.

brief.tradeoff: How far acceptance and flags reach: inside the group until a published case relies on them, using the channel Civicsmith already has, or public at once, literal to the founding requirement but a new public object and a public criticism of allies.

why: A is the smallest set of acts that makes every label an attributed fact, and it reuses rules you already set: correction forward, re-evaluation notices, disclosure rather than refusal at publication. It keeps your 30 July boundary.

It meets the founding requirement where a reader needs it: in the published case that relies on the work. B can be added later without undoing anything, since A's recorded acts become B's entries. If 'Meets standards' returns, it should carry the 'Machine work' label, never act as a trust level (my judgement).
recommendation.risk: Read literally, the founding requirement wants acceptance public at once. Contained by naming B as the next step, triggered when a second group asks to see who accepted or flagged its work.

howToAnswer: 12: as recommended.
12: A now, B when a second group asks.
12: B: acceptance and flags are public at once.
12: question: who may accept or flag, any member or only a project owner?
brief.ifLeftOpen: The origin mark can ship with 'Ours', 'Another group's' and 'Not yet evaluated' only, and citing keeps working as today. The acceptance and flag requirements owed under your 29 September ruling wait. Nothing else is blocked.

related.how: Both decide what readers see beyond the findings; they should sit together on the case.
Accepted work stays capped at its own grades, so it is measured against your bar like any support.
B's public list is what a directory could read; the directory's community flags are a different thing.
How the acceptance and an open flag read on the public page and in print.

glossary.plain: A project's signed, published argument; a correction is a new numbered edition.
One concluded question and its answer; a case rests on findings.
The two grades, A to D: how well documents are held; how firmly links are established.
Resting part of your question on another group's published edition.
The label saying who made a piece of information.
The case's digital signature checks out: it is exactly what that group published.
An act under a member's name with a written reason, corrected only by a later act.
An automatic note that something a finding rests on has changed.
The label on anything the machine produced.

DEC-87; DEC-88 (2); DEC-84 (11), (13) (disclose at publication, never block)
K600 (c); K628–K859 checked: none touch acceptance or flags
Correction: the earlier brief tied 'no outside channel' to DEC-94 (3), which concerns email or push to members, not other groups.

openQuestions.question: Should members get one place that lists every document the group has collected but nobody has yet vouched for or set aside, and be allowed to vouch for many of them in one act?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: The belief about what a capture is worth forms at capture; the note is currently discarded before the member sees it.
openQuestions.context: When a member captures a document from a web address, the record fetches it, fingerprints the bytes and gives the capture a grade: how strong it is as evidence of what that address served and when (a direct fetch earns at most B; A needs a chain-of-custody archive). 'Co-attestation' is a separate act that asks an independent timestamp service to record when those bytes existed. The question is what the member is told about the grade at the moment they capture. Since DEC-81, co-attestation also decides what a published case says about the document: a co-attested Grade B can be published as it is, and one whose co-attestation failed only by the owner's acknowledgement, marked 'self-attested only'.

canonSays.says: 'RENDER IT, WHOLE, AT THE MOMENT OF CAPTURE': the plane's grade note is shown when the capture completes, including the co-attestation clause, never split.

The fence wording is the record's and must state the question co-attestation answers: 'when did these bytes exist?'; not whether the document is true; it strengthens a Grade B capture toward evidentiary weight and 'never reaches Grade A'.
The grade note at capture is named as the model of 'informing at the act, once'.
A capture earns a grade (at most B for a direct fetch); an attestation is recorded and never reaches A.

A co-attested Grade B (a trusted timestamp over the digest and a third-party co-archive of the locator) is sufficient to publish; the case discloses each document's grade and whether it is co-attested; a failed co-attestation is retried at the pre-flight, then acknowledged and marked 'self-attested only'; Grade A is the ceiling for adversarial or legal use and is deferred.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The substance is already settled: DEC-51 overturned the discard this question describes, and DEC-39 states what co-attestation is worth, so the question's premise is out of date. What remains open is presentation only: where and how long the note sits after capture, how a bulk or machine-requested capture (which completes later, unattended) carries it, and how the grade looks when the member returns to the document. One real tension: the pre-capture explanation deliberately predicts no grade (the capture does not exist yet), so the member sees nothing about strength until the capture lands.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The Add surface renders the plane's full grade note, co-attestation clause included, right after a capture completes (UI-54), and states no grade beforehand.

options.option: Carry the old interface's treatment forward: the whole note shown once at completion, then the grade chip on the document page from then on.
options.tradeoffs: Already ruled and built; nothing is decided anew. A member capturing many documents sees the same long note repeatedly.

options.option: Show the whole note in full on a member's first capture, and afterwards a one-line grade statement that expands to the whole note.
options.tradeoffs: Less repetition, consistent with 'once'; but DEC-51 said 'whole', so a collapsed default needs Bob to confirm that collapsed-but-present still counts as whole.

options.option: For captures that complete later (bulk or machine-requested), attach the note to the completed-capture status on the document and in the queue's condition item.
options.tradeoffs: Fills the unattended gap; adds nothing new to the record.

options.option: Show at capture whether co-attestation succeeded, since it now decides whether the document can be published without an acknowledgement (DEC-81).
options.tradeoffs: Makes the consequence visible early; adds one more fact to a note DEC-51 requires to stay whole.

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1 plus option 3 for unattended captures; ask Bob only if Design wants option 2's collapsed form.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design: DEC-51, DEC-39 and DEC-81 settle the substance; only presentation remains. Bob only if the note is to be shortened or collapsed.

ruled.decided: The whole grade note is shown once, when a capture completes; a capture that completes later and unattended carries the note on the completed capture and on its queue item. Captures still held (collected, not yet released or set aside) are listed in a 'Held captures' view, per member and per project, showing only what the viewer may see, sortable by age, source and project, each row with its age, and never notified. A member ticks several (nothing pre-ticked) and may vouch for them together as one batch release (each document its own entry, with the member's recorded statement of how uniform the batch is and what was sampled), set them aside together with one reason (each stays held, never deleted), or link them to a question. Crucial documents, and documents caught in an unresolved contradiction, are shown as not eligible, with the reason, before the member acts. The system may also suggest that a held capture bears on a member's work, under six guards: it appears where the member already works, never as a notification; it is labelled machine work with its reason; a dismissal is remembered; it never appears during a heavy act; a member may switch it off; and its acceptance rate is measured.
ruled.title: Telling a member a capture's grade

brief.title: A list of held captures, and dealing with several at once
brief.inOneBreath: Should members get one place that lists every document the group has collected but nobody has yet vouched for or set aside, and be allowed to vouch for many of them in one act?
brief.decision: (1) Whether there is a 'held captures' list at all, per member and per project, showing each one's age. (2) If there is, whether a member may act on several at once from it: vouch for a uniform batch in one act (with the recorded statement of what they checked), set several aside with one reason, or link several to a question. (3) Whether anything other than 'crucial' material is barred from a batch, for example a document caught in an unresolved conflict.
basics: A capture is a document the group's copy of Civicsmith fetched from a public web address (or received) and stored byte for byte, with where and when it came from. Every capture lands 'held': stored and traced, but not yet part of the group's working evidence.

Vouching for a held capture (the record calls it 'release') is a named member's statement that the document appears to be what it claims to be: a real council agenda, not spam or a phishing page. It does not say the contents are true. Only a person may vouch; the machine never may.
Setting aside is the other way out: under the intake doctrine, a document the group will not proceed with stays held with its reason written down, never silently parked or deleted.

Held captures pile up: a member's own captures, captures the assistant requests (which arrive hours later), material pulled in from the public doorbell, bulk captures, and later standing 'sweeps' (searches the group approves in advance) bringing dozens per run.

Batch vouching is already doctrine. Your ruling of 27 July: a large, uniform collection (a hundred postings from a public jobs board) is 'one judgment made honestly once'. Each document still gets its own entry, the member's statement of why the batch is uniform and what they sampled is recorded, and crucial or contested material is never batch-released. That recorded statement is the only guard against a poisoned document hiding in the batch. It is like stipulating to the authenticity of a large set of routine data-request responses after a documented spot-check, while anything disputed is authenticated item by item.
today: The batch vouching act is built, and moved into its own module in the last build round. It is all or nothing: every document is checked first, and if even one is not held, is marked crucial, or lacks a required piece, the whole batch is refused, nothing moves, and each offender is named. The member writes two one-line statements (why these are alike; what they sampled), each at most 500 characters, and each document's log gets its own 'batch release' entry carrying them.
No screen reaches it. There is no list of held captures, no way to sort or tick them, and no batch vouching in the old interface.

On 29 September you ruled the neighbouring parts of this question: the grade note shown once when a capture completes (and attached to captures that complete unattended), and quiet machine suggestions that a held capture bears on a question, under six guards (shown where the member works, never notified; labelled machine work with its reason; dismissals remembered; never during a heavy act; switchable off; acceptance measured). The same day you corrected the entry: the list with bulk handling 'was proposed but not approved; it stays open'.
Two gaps I found: the built check refuses crucial documents but has no test for 'contested'; and I found no dedicated act for setting a held capture aside with a reason. Sweeps are not built yet.
problem: Without a list, held captures that bear on no live question are never seen again: your 29 September suggestions only point to captures that relate to current work. The doctrine names the danger of a growing pile ('flooding collected until review becomes rubber-stamping is an attack') and sets a ceiling on it, which members cannot manage if they cannot see it.
With a list, the risk runs the other way: a visible backlog can feel like a chore list, brushing against your 10 August ruling against nagging, and a 'tick all, vouch' button invites rubber-stamping.

It needs deciding now because the redesign is laying out the project page, the document page and the queue, and each needs to know whether a held list sits beside it. Affected: members doing intake, and the group's credibility if a wrong document is vouched for in bulk.

story.title: Rosa and the 120 job postings
steps: Rosa's project asks whether Oakland is leaving budgeted police-oversight positions unfilled. Over a week the assistant captures 120 postings from the city's jobs site, and she adds the budget memo and an amendment memo. 122 captures are held.
Her question's page shows: '2 held captures may bear on this question (Machine work: names the same position code)'. Those are the memos. Nothing points to the 120 postings.
Without a list, the postings sit unseen; next month a colleague cites the jobs board from memory, not from the record.
With a list, Rosa opens 'Held captures' for the project, sorts by source, and sees 120 rows, each with its age ('held 6 days'). Nothing is pre-ticked.

She ticks the 120, opens three at random, and chooses 'Vouch for these together', writing 'All 120 are postings from the city's official jobs site, same template.' and 'Opened 3 at random; each matched the live posting.'
The amendment memo is marked crucial, so the list shows it greyed out: 'Crucial documents are vouched for one at a time.' She vouches for it alone.

fixed.point: Batch vouching is allowed for large, uniform collections; each document gets its own entry; the uniformity and sampling statement is recorded; crucial or contested material is never batched.
fixed.why: Your ruling of 27 July on what vouching asserts.

fixed.point: Vouching is a named member's act, never a machine's.
fixed.why: The intake doctrine's release rule.

fixed.point: The built batch act is all or nothing: one ineligible document refuses the whole set, naming each offender.
fixed.why: Built in the last build round.

fixed.point: A document set aside stays held with its reason, never deleted.
fixed.why: The intake doctrine's disposition pattern.

fixed.point: Acting on many items: the member chooses, nothing is pre-selected, and nothing half-runs without saying so.
fixed.why: The rules for acting on a selection, and your ruling against unseen defaults.

fixed.point: Age may be shown; nothing about held captures is pushed as a notification.
fixed.why: Your rulings of 10 August and 29 September.

options.label: A
options.name: Held list with bulk handling
options.howItWorks: A 'Held captures' view, per member and per project, showing only what the viewer may see. Sortable by age, source and project; each row shows its age; nothing is notified. Ticking several (nothing pre-ticked) offers three acts: vouch for these together (with the two recorded sentences; crucial and conflicted documents shown as not eligible, with the reason, before the member acts), set aside with one reason, or link to a question.
options.inTheStory: Rosa releases the 120 postings in one act with her two sentences; the amendment memo is greyed out with 'Crucial documents are vouched for one at a time'.
gains: Makes the backlog visible and manageable.
Puts the batch release the doctrine already allows within reach.
Matches how assistant requests and future sweeps actually fill the record.
costs: A visible count can feel like a to-do list.
Bulk vouching invites rubber-stamping; the recorded statements are the only guard.
Needs a set-aside act that does not yet exist.
options.commitsYouTo: A new screen and a bulk set-aside act; a rule for what 'contested' means in the eligibility check.

options.label: B
options.name: List for seeing, one at a time for acting
options.howItWorks: The same list, sorted and aged, but every vouch or set-aside is done per document.
options.inTheStory: Rosa sees the 120 postings, and must open and vouch for each one separately.
gains: Maximum care per document.
No bulk-vouching risk.
costs: In practice the 120 stay held.
Withholds a batch release your own ruling allows; the built act goes unused.
options.commitsYouTo: A list screen only; batch release reachable later if you change your mind.

options.label: C
options.name: No list; held captures appear only where they bear
options.howItWorks: Held captures appear in search and through your 29 September quiet suggestions on a question's page. There is no backlog view.
options.inTheStory: Rosa sees the two memos suggested; the 120 postings are never shown to anyone again unless searched for.
gains: Nothing that feels like a chore list.
costs: Unrelated held captures are never seen.
The doctrine's ceiling on the held backlog becomes invisible to members.
options.commitsYouTo: Nothing new; the question can be reopened when backlogs grow.

brief.tradeoff: Seeing and clearing the backlog (and using the batch release you already allowed) against the risk that a visible pile and a bulk button turn careful vouching into rubber-stamping.

why: It is the only option that makes the batch release you ruled for in July usable, and the act behind it is already built and all-or-nothing, so a mistake cannot half-run.

The guards come from rules you have already set: nothing pre-ticked, age shown but never notified, crucial documents shown as not eligible before the member acts, and the two recorded sentences as the honest account of what was checked. I would add documents caught in an unresolved conflict to the not-eligible list, which fills the doctrine's word 'contested'. That addition is my judgement, not existing canon.

Showing ineligible documents greyed out with the reason, rather than letting the act refuse the whole batch, follows the interaction rule that a member should see what an act will refuse before it runs.
recommendation.risk: Rubber-stamping. It is contained by the recorded sentences (which members and readers can inspect later), the per-document entries, and the exclusion of crucial and conflicted material; your 29 September measurement rule could also be applied to batch sizes if you want a signal.

howToAnswer: 13: as recommended.
13: A, but per project only, not per member.
13: C for now; revisit when a group's backlog becomes a problem.
13: question first: can a member set aside a batch with one reason, or must each have its own?
brief.ifLeftOpen: Members vouch for captures one by one wherever they meet them; the built batch act stays unreachable from any screen; Design leaves room on the project page but builds no list. Nothing else in the build waits.

related.how: An empty held list, and a capture still on its way, need the shared 'nothing here' and 'waiting' wording that question 15 asks for.
Material pulled in from the doorbell lands held, so it would appear on this list.
If held captures ever produced a queue item, it would be one of the queue's three kinds; the recommendation keeps them out of the queue entirely.
The list's rows need the everyday word that replaces 'bundle' (here, 'document').

glossary.plain: A document the system fetched or received and stored byte for byte, with where and when.
Stored and traced, not yet vouched for (the record's word is 'collected').
A named member's statement that a document appears to be what it claims; not that it is true.
Not proceeding with a held document; it stays held with a written reason.
Vouching for many uniform documents in one act, with a recorded statement of what was sampled.
The criticality level for documents central to the group's work; always vouched for singly.
A standing search the group approves in advance; not built yet.
The label every machine output carries.
