openQuestions.question: How does the queue avoid nagging (DEC-69) while making sure obligations with clocks are not missed?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Respect for members is a requirement; so are deadlines (Operational Principle 3).
openQuestions.context: The queue is the member's one list of 'things that want me', grouped by case (a question or project). It holds obligations (a named person must act, sometimes against a legal deadline), items the record noticed (shown as 'Noticed', K356), and conditions about the product's own machinery. Some obligations carry clocks, such as a records-request response due in so many days.

canonSays.says: 'The workflow must not nag or second-guess members'; repeating, re-confirming and act-detached reminders are the flaw; informing at the act, once, is respect.
'The clock runs. Deadlines are deadlines.'
One standing entry per (member, case), no digest cadence; it 're-notifies only on a snooze increment or when something new lands'. Obligations can never be muted (queue R19, R31).
A passed clock is marked overdue and the action's members are told; the next escalation stage is proposed, never advanced.
Transport (for example email) is undecided; the in-app queue is the only channel.
An undetermined candidate is a lead, never a duty; a record duty is an unmutable obligation for the joined members of every project drawing on either side, leaving only by resolution.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The canon says obligations cannot be muted and overdue clocks are marked, but not how a clock's approach is shown: whether an item's position, colour or wording changes as a deadline nears, and whether anything reaches a member who has not opened the product. DEC-69 forbids repeated reminders, while Operational Principle 3 and monitoring R34 require members to be told; the only sanctioned re-notify triggers are 'snooze ended' and 'something new', and it is undecided whether 'a deadline is now N days away' counts as something new.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The queue lists items by class and case with mute; an overdue clock is shown as an overdue mark on the action's own page; nothing warns of an approaching deadline and nothing leaves the app.

options.option: Treat a clock crossing a stated threshold (for example 'due within 3 days', 'overdue') as a new event: the standing entry rises and says so once per threshold, never repeated.
options.tradeoffs: Uses DEC-10's 'something new' rule without inventing a reminder cadence; needs the thresholds defined (per action kind or profile).

options.option: No escalation of display: sort obligations by due date and show the date; the member judges.
options.tradeoffs: Maximally respectful; a deadline can be missed by a member who does not open the product.

options.option: Add an outside channel (email or push) for clock obligations only, opted into by the member.
options.tradeoffs: Reaches absent members; reopens the transport decision and its security concerns (D-98).

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1 inside the product, with option 3 left as a member's opt-in later: a threshold is a real change, so it is not nagging.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob: where respect ends and a deadline duty begins is doctrine (DEC-69 is his); the threshold values and look are Design's.

update.note: Not settled. One fixed point is added: a record contradiction is a duty that cannot be muted and leaves the queue only by resolution, while a world one is a lead (DEC-76 item 3; DEC-84 (1)-(2)). Where respect ends and a deadline duty begins remains Bob's.

ruled.decided: A deadline reminder is the member's own request, never the system's nagging: it is set up when the option is chosen in the action plan, from defaults the member sees and can change there, and any further reminder is one the member accepts, perhaps at the system's suggestion. As a deadline nears, the item's position, colour or wording may change; that is display, not a notification. Nothing reaches a member who has not opened the product: no email, push or other outside channel. An overdue deadline notifies once; 'due within N days' is not new unless the member asked for that reminder. An overdue condition's response offers another reminder at a further time, or none (DEC-10). A pushed notice tells once, is dispositionable and ages (DEC-70); the workflow never second-guesses (DEC-69). Threshold looks and wording are Design's.
ruled.title: Reminders without nagging

openQuestions.question: Should every screen use one shared set of plain statements for 'nothing here', 'still loading', 'could not read' and 'waiting on someone until a date', and may an empty screen suggest a next step?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Canon names waits but no treatment; an empty state can be mistaken for 'nothing to do' or 'could not read'.
openQuestions.context: Many things in the product take time: a capture may take minutes, a page render may be held back ('deferred') with a code, a capture the assistant requested may run hours later when the host allows, and a legal response clock runs for days. Every list can also be empty. What a surface shows while waiting, or when there is nothing, tells the member whether to act, wait or worry.

canonSays.says: 'undetermined' is first-class and must be STATED, 'never invented past and never dressed as an error'; one treatment everywhere: 'what we do not know, and why we do not know it.'
A condition is recorded (no surface), noticed (status where the thing lives) or actionable (a queue item); losing 'noticed' means 'either drowning the member or hiding what is happening'.
A deferred render is held with its code and translation, content 'undetermined'; past its expiry it is released as expired, 'nothing was filed'.
A page that cannot read the group says so, 'never that none is recorded'.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The canon distinguishes 'none' from 'could not read' in one place (the setup page) and defines 'undetermined', but gives no general treatment for empty, loading or long-wait states; the UX substrate marks them 'not specified' on almost every surface. The gap matters because three different truths look alike on screen: nothing exists, the record has not answered yet, and the record answered that it cannot know; plus waits measured in days need a visible 'what happens next and when'.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Mostly a plain 'Loading…' line and a few empty sentences (for example 'Nothing is waiting for review'); the group name distinguishes none-recorded from could-not-read.

options.option: One product-wide state vocabulary with four named states (nothing here; still reading; could not read, and why; not known, and why) plus a 'waiting on' pattern that names what is awaited, by whom, and the expected or legal date.
options.tradeoffs: Consistent and teachable, matching §U's 'one voice'; needs every surface's reads to tell the four apart, which some plane answers may not yet do.

options.option: Per-surface treatment designed case by case.
options.tradeoffs: Fits each context; drifts, which §U warns teaches members to ignore the signal.

options.option: Option 1 plus an empty state that offers the natural next step for that surface (for example a new project's first step).
options.tradeoffs: Helps newcomers; must not become a prompt that nags (DEC-69).

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1, adding option 3's next step only where the member has just created the empty thing.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design: the canon already sets the principle (state it, never dress it as an error); the vocabulary and treatments are detail within it.

brief.title: What screens say while waiting, loading or empty
brief.inOneBreath: Should every screen use one shared set of plain statements for 'nothing here', 'still loading', 'could not read' and 'waiting on someone until a date', and may an empty screen suggest a next step?
brief.decision: (1) Whether empty, loading and waiting states use one shared vocabulary across the product, or are designed screen by screen. (2) Whether every wait must say what is awaited, from whom, and by when (where a date is known). (3) Whether an empty screen may offer a next step, and if so only on something the member has just created.
brief.alreadyDecidedPart: On 29 September you fixed how the product states what it does not know: 'Undetermined' always carries a 'because…' line, and its four neighbours ('Withheld', 'Unrated', 'Nobody looked', 'Refused') each look and read differently, none dressed as an error. The same day you ruled that as a deadline nears, an item's position, colour or wording may change, and that this is display, not a notification. What remains is the ordinary cases those rulings do not cover: an empty list, a screen still loading, a screen that failed to load, and a long wait.
basics: Much in Civicsmith takes time. A capture (fetching a public document and storing its exact bytes) can take minutes, and the system paces itself per website so it never hammers a city's server. A capture the assistant asks for is queued and may run hours later; if it cannot be made within 24 hours, the request expires and the record says nothing was filed. A site may refuse to let a page be rendered fully, and the request is held with the site's reason. Outside the system, legal clocks run for days, such as a public-records request's response deadline.
Every list can be empty, and every screen depends on asking the record a question, which can fail (a dropped connection, a timeout).

So four different truths can look identical, as a blank or a spinner: there is nothing here; the answer has not arrived; the screen could not get an answer; and the record answered that it does not know. A fifth is a wait with a known end: waiting on someone, until a date.

The product already sorts signals three ways: recorded (never shown), noticed (shown as status where the thing lives, such as 'the system is pacing this capture'), and actionable (a queue item). Losing the middle one means 'either drowning the member or hiding what is happening'.
An analogy: a docket that shows 'no filings' must mean no filings, not 'the docket server is down'.
today: Decided and partly built: the record states 'undetermined' with its reason; a held or expired page render says so and, once expired, that 'nothing was filed'; the group setup page tells 'no group recorded' apart from 'could not read the group'. The action design approved on 30 September says queue items state whose deadline it is: the group's own checkpoint or the other party's.
Not decided: any general treatment. The inventory of screens marks empty, loading and waiting as 'not specified' almost everywhere.

The old interface has 18 plain 'Loading…' lines and empty sentences written one by one ('Nothing is waiting for review.', 'Nothing is in this project yet'). A failed load often looks like an empty list.
problem: If a failed read looks like an empty list, a member concludes there is nothing and acts on it: drops a line of inquiry, or tells a reporter the city has not responded. In a record whose value rests on stating gaps honestly, that is a credibility problem.
If waits are blank, members cannot tell 'wait' from 'worry': a records request ten days from its deadline and one ten days overdue look alike.

If each screen is designed alone, wording drifts, and the canon's own warning applies: when a gap looks like a failure in one place and a shrug in another, members learn to ignore it. The opposite risk is nagging: an empty screen that keeps telling members what to do next brushes against your 10 August ruling.
It matters now because the redesign is starting screen by screen; a shared vocabulary is cheap before the screens exist and costly to retrofit.

story.title: Darnell, the council agenda and the Clerk's deadline
steps: Darnell is tracking a proposed sale of city land. He asks the assistant to capture the Oakland City Council's agenda page for 7 October.
The city's site refuses a full render for now. Today he sees 'Loading…' for a while, then an empty documents list, and assumes the agenda was not posted.

Under a shared vocabulary he would see on the request: 'Waiting: the city's site asked us to wait before rendering this page. We will try again after 3:10 pm. Nothing has been filed yet.' If 24 hours pass: 'Expired: the site never allowed the render. Nothing was filed.'

He has also sent a public-records request to the City Clerk. Its action page reads: 'Waiting on the City Clerk's reply, due 14 October (10 days under the state public-records law).' As the date nears, the item moves up and changes colour, which you ruled is display, not a notification.
His project's 'Held captures' panel loses its connection. Instead of an empty list it says: 'Could not read this list just now. This is not the same as having none. Try again.'
Later the panel loads and genuinely has nothing: 'Nothing held for this project.'

fixed.point: 'Undetermined' always states its reason; 'Withheld', 'Unrated', 'Nobody looked' and 'Refused' each have their own look and sentence; none is shown as an error.
fixed.why: Your ruling of 29 September on the five ways of stating a gap.

fixed.point: A nearing deadline may change an item's position, colour or wording; that is display, not a notification. Overdue notifies once. There is no outside channel.
fixed.why: Your ruling of 29 September on deadlines without nagging.

fixed.point: A held page render states the site's reason and that its content is undetermined; once expired, that nothing was filed. Requests expire after 24 hours.
fixed.why: Requirements for assistant-requested captures.

fixed.point: A screen that cannot read something says so, never that none is recorded.
fixed.why: The setup page rule and the publication doctrine.

fixed.point: Signals are recorded, noticed (status where the thing lives) or actionable (a queue item).
fixed.why: Your three dispositions, 1 August.

fixed.point: Queue items say whose deadline it is: the group's own checkpoint or the other party's.
fixed.why: The action design approved on 30 September.

fixed.point: No nagging or second-guessing; informing at the act, once, is respect.
fixed.why: Your ruling of 10 August.

options.label: A
options.name: One shared vocabulary, waits always say what and when
options.howItWorks: Four plain states used everywhere, each with its own fixed look: 'Nothing here' (truly empty), 'Still loading', 'Could not read this, because…' (the screen's own request failed), and the record's own 'Undetermined, because…'. Every wait carries one line naming what is awaited, from whom, and the expected or legal date where one exists ('Waiting on the City Clerk's reply, due 14 October'). No next-step prompts.
options.inTheStory: Darnell sees each of the lines in steps 3 to 6, worded the same way on every screen.
gains: Learned once, trusted everywhere.
Empty and failed can never be confused.
Matches the 'one voice' rule you already set for gaps.
costs: Every screen's data must tell the four apart; a few answers from the record may not yet do so cleanly.
Brand-new members on an empty project get no hint of where to start.
options.commitsYouTo: Design writes the four patterns once; the build checks each screen's reads distinguish them.

options.label: B
options.name: Each screen designed on its own
options.howItWorks: Wording and look chosen per screen as the redesign reaches it.
options.inTheStory: The request page might say 'Pending', the project panel 'No items', the action page 'Awaiting reply'; a failed load may still look empty on some screens.
gains: Fits each context closely.
No up-front design work.
costs: Drift; members learn to ignore the signal.
The failed-versus-empty confusion survives wherever a designer misses it.
options.commitsYouTo: Nothing now; harder to unify later.

options.label: C
options.name: A, plus a next step on something just created
options.howItWorks: As A. In addition, an empty screen for something the member has just created (a new project, a new plan) shows one plain next step, for example 'Add the first question'. Nowhere else.
options.inTheStory: When Darnell's colleague creates a new project, its empty page says 'Nothing here yet. Add the first question.' Darnell's older, emptied panel just says 'Nothing held for this project.'
gains: Helps newcomers at the moment they act.
Fits 'informing at the act, once'.
costs: A line to hold: the step must never spread to older or emptied screens, where it would become a nudge.
options.commitsYouTo: A rule for which screens count as 'just created'.

brief.tradeoff: Consistency and honesty about gaps, at the cost of making every screen tell its states apart, against the freedom (and drift) of designing each screen as it comes.

why: A shared vocabulary is the natural extension of what you already ruled for 'Undetermined': the same principle (state it, never dress it as an error, one voice) applied to the ordinary empty, loading and failed cases. The most damaging confusion, a failed load read as 'none', is only reliably prevented if every screen is built to the same pattern.
Requiring every wait to say what, from whom and by when costs little and turns long waits from worry into information. Where no date is known, the line says so ('no date is set').

The next-step line on newly created things is informing at the act, once, which your 10 August ruling names as respect; limiting it to that moment keeps it from becoming a nudge. The exact wording and look can then go to Design.
recommendation.risk: Some screens may not yet be able to tell 'could not read' from 'none' because the record's answer does not distinguish them. Contained by making that a check in each screen's build: a screen that cannot tell them apart says 'could not read' rather than 'none'.

howToAnswer: 15: as recommended, and leave the wording to Design.
15: A only; no next-step prompts anywhere.
15: delegate the whole question to Design.
15: question first: what does a wait say when nobody knows the date?
brief.ifLeftOpen: Design treats each screen as it comes; 'Loading…' and blank lists persist in the old interface. Nothing in the build waits on this.

related.how: An empty or unreadable held-captures list is a direct case of these states.
The doorbell's refusal to a sender is a wait message to the public ('try again later'), and should follow the same pattern.
Question 28 names the queue's 'noticed' kind of item (status where the thing lives), which is where many waits are shown.
'Withheld' (something exists you may not see) is one of the neighbouring states; question 23 asks whether it also applies to work that depends on what you see.

glossary.plain: Fetching a public document and keeping its exact bytes, with where and when.
Loading a web page fully, as a browser would, before capturing it; a site may refuse or delay this.
The assistant's request that the system fetch an address later; it expires after 24 hours.
The record's own answer that it does not know something, always with 'because…'.
The four neighbours of Undetermined: something exists you may not see; nothing graded yet; nobody has searched there; the system declined an act.
A signal worth seeing but not acting on, shown as status where the thing lives.
The list of everything that wants a member's attention.
A date the group set for itself in an action plan, as opposed to another party's legal deadline.

sources: civicos-ui/app.html (18 'Loading…' lines; 'Nothing is waiting for review.')
California Gov. Code §7922.535 (10-day determination), for the story only

ruled.title: What screens say while empty, loading or waiting
ruled.decided: Empty, loading, failed and waiting states share one vocabulary across every screen, each with its own fixed look and none dressed as an error: 'Nothing here' (truly empty); 'Still loading'; 'Could not read this, because…' (the screen's own request failed); and the record's 'Undetermined, because…'. A screen that cannot tell 'could not read' from 'none' says 'could not read'. Every wait carries one line naming what is awaited, from whom, and the expected or legal date where one exists ('Waiting on the City Clerk's reply, due 14 October'), or that no date is set. An empty screen offers one plain next step only on something the member has just created (a new project, a new plan: 'Nothing here yet. Add the first question.'), nowhere else. As a deadline nears, an item's position, colour or wording may change; that is display, not a notification. Exact wording and looks are the redesign's.

openQuestions.question: What accessibility standard must Civicsmith's member screens and public case pages meet, and should anything in Civicsmith appear in languages other than English?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Canon names phones and print only; a civic product's public output may need to reach non-English readers and assistive technology users.
openQuestions.context: The member surfaces are the screens members work in; the published output is the public case page, its print version and its downloadable file, read by residents, journalists, officials and other groups. Accessibility means people using screen readers, keyboards only, magnification or with low vision can use them; language means whether anything appears in languages other than English.

canonSays.says: Devices: phones supported, 'acceptably as a viewing MVP'; the printed publication is 'first-class and must carry the full narrative'.

brief.title: Accessibility standard and languages
brief.inOneBreath: What accessibility standard must Civicsmith's member screens and public case pages meet, and should anything in Civicsmith appear in languages other than English?
brief.decision: (1) Whether to adopt a named accessibility standard now, as a requirement every screen of the redesign is built to; the candidate is WCAG 2.2 at level AA, for both the member screens and the published case. (2) Which languages: English only for now but built so its words can be translated later, or the interface also offered in the languages a place needs. (3) Whether a group may issue a translated version of a published case, and if so whether it carries the group's signature or is marked as an unofficial translation of the signed original.
basics: Civicsmith has two kinds of screens. The member screens are where a group's members do their work: the queue of things that want their attention, projects, captured documents, the publishing steps. The published output is what the public sees: the case page on the web, its printed version and its downloadable file. Its readers are residents, journalists, officials and other groups, and most of them have never used Civicsmith.

Accessibility here means access for people with disabilities: someone who is blind and uses a screen reader (software that reads the page aloud and lets them jump between headings, links and table cells), someone who cannot use a mouse and works by keyboard alone, someone who zooms the page to 200 per cent or more, or someone who cannot tell red from green. A page built without them in mind is often unusable to them, not merely awkward.

The usual yardstick is WCAG, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. Each rule has a level: A (minimum), AA (the level most laws and public bodies point to) and AAA (rarely required in full). Version 2.2 (2023) is current. As general background, not from the project's files: the US Justice Department's 2024 rule for state and local government websites uses WCAG 2.1 AA. My reading (not legal advice) is that it does not bind Civicsmith groups directly, but the officials who receive or cite a case are held to it.

Language is a separate question. Offering the interface (buttons, explanations) in several languages is mostly engineering if planned early. The published case is different: it is signed, meaning members attest it and its file carries a fingerprint that lets anyone check that not one character changed. A translation is new text and cannot carry that signature unless someone signs it too. A familiar parallel: agencies post translated decisions marked 'unofficial translation; the English version controls'.
today: No canon document, requirement or ruling names an accessibility standard or a supported language. The one 'accessibility' item in the technical architecture's open questions means ease of use for newcomers, not disability access.

Several of your rulings already lean toward accessibility without naming a standard (see 'fixed' below): colour is never the only signal, every hover explanation also opens on keyboard focus or a tap, and the assistant panel does not float, partly because floating panels trap or lose keyboard focus.

The current member app (left as it is until the redesign replaces it, by your ruling of 30 September) is one file of about 26,500 lines with almost no accessibility markup: two of the standard accessibility attributes and seven role labels. No keyboard or screen-reader check has ever been run; the old plan's 'hardening pass' was never built. It has a phone viewing layout and a full print layout.

Everything is in English. Each place's local facts live in a 'jurisdiction profile', a data file (the first covers Oakland and Alameda County). A profile records a 'locale', but that is the language of the government's own documents, used when capturing them, not the language Civicsmith speaks. If languages were chosen per place, the profile is where that choice would live.
problem: The redesign is being designed now. Accessibility designed in costs modestly: headings marked as headings, every grade badge given a spoken name, tables given header cells, contrast chosen once in the palette. Retrofitting means revisiting every built screen. Without a named target, each screen built meanwhile is a guess and may need rework. That is the reason to decide now.

Public readers are most affected. They know least about Civicsmith, cannot ask a member what a badge means, and include the residents a civic group exists to serve. A case a blind resident cannot read undercuts the mission and, in a dispute, the group's credibility. Members with disabilities are affected too. Civicsmith has particular traps: grades are small coloured badges explained on hover, stages are coloured bars, evidence tables are dense, and an accessible downloadable PDF is extra work of its own.

Languages raise doctrine as well as engineering. If a member translates a case and the group posts it, is it part of the published record? Who stands behind it? How is it corrected when the English case is? Machine translation would carry your 'machine work' marking. Decided badly one way, a careless translation misstates a finding under the group's signature. Decided badly the other way, the communities most affected (in Oakland, for example, Spanish and Chinese speakers, whom the city itself serves in their languages; general knowledge, not from the project's files) are left out.

story.title: Dolores, Minh and the sewer-fee case
steps: East Oakland Water Watch publishes a case: 'Sewer fee increase approved without the required public notice.' It cites the notice requirement, the council agenda, and a captured web page showing the notice went up two days late.

Dolores, a retired teacher who is blind, opens the case with her screen reader. Without a standard, the reader announces 'B' next to each piece of evidence, or nothing at all, the stage bars are silent, and the evidence table reads as one long run of words. Its explanations open only on mouse hover, which she cannot use.

Built to AA, the same page reads: 'Capture grade B: someone else could check this copy with some effort. Press Enter for what this grade means.' She jumps heading to heading, and each table cell is announced with its column name.
Minh, a member, asks whether his mother, who reads Vietnamese, can read the case. Ana, another member, offers to translate the summary.

Under the recommended option, the published case stays in English, and the group posts Ana's summary on its own website, unconnected to the case. Under the fuller option (B), Civicsmith publishes it beside the case marked: 'Unofficial Vietnamese translation by a member of East Oakland Water Watch. The signed English case is the record: [link].' When the English case is corrected a month later, the translation is marked 'out of date: the English case was corrected on 14 November'.
A council aide prints the case for a committee packet. Because the grades carry their names and icons and not just colours, the black-and-white printout still says what each grade is.

fixed.point: Colour is never the only signal: each evidence scale has its own icon, and each stage bar carries its name.

fixed.why: Your ruling of 29 September on the assistant panel.

fixed.point: Phones are supported, acceptably as viewing-first at the start; the printed case is first-class and carries the full narrative.
fixed.why: Your refinements for the interface design of 28 July.

fixed.point: Machine output always carries the one 'machine work' marking and is attributed.

options.label: A
options.name: AA now for everything; English first, built for translation
options.howItWorks: WCAG 2.2 AA becomes a requirement for member screens and the published case page, print and file. Each new screen is checked against it before it is accepted. The interface stays in English but keeps all its words in one place, so another language can be added without rebuilding screens. Published cases appear in whatever language the group wrote them in.
options.inTheStory: Dolores reads the case fully. Minh's mother gets nothing from Civicsmith itself; Ana's Vietnamese summary lives on the group's website, unlinked, and can silently go out of date.
gains: A recognised bar that officials, funders and journalists understand.
Modest cost when designed in, not retrofitted.
Protects the public page, where readers know the least.

Checking each screen adds some time to every design and build step.

options.label: B
options.name: A, plus local languages and translated versions
options.howItWorks: As A. In addition, the interface is offered in the languages a jurisdiction profile names (for Oakland, for example, Spanish, Chinese and Vietnamese), and a group may publish a translated version of a case through Civicsmith, marked as an unofficial translation, linked to the signed original, and flagged out of date when the original is corrected.
options.inTheStory: Ana's Vietnamese summary is published beside the case with the unofficial-translation marking and the link, and is flagged when the English case is corrected.
gains: Reaches the communities most affected.
Keeps translations tied to the signed record instead of drifting on other websites.
costs: Translating the interface is real recurring work, multiplied by every new screen.
A translated case is a new kind of publication needing its own doctrine: who may issue it, whether anyone attests it, how it is corrected, how machine translation is marked.
options.commitsYouTo: Designing a new publication act now, alongside the ceremony and corrections work.

options.label: C
options.name: Defer both
options.howItWorks: No standard and no language decision now; a later hardening pass handles both. The redesign follows only the points already ruled.
options.inTheStory: Dolores hears unlabelled badges and silent bars; nothing changes for Minh's mother.
gains: Cheapest today.
costs: Retrofitting costs far more than designing in.
Public output that excludes readers undercuts the mission and can embarrass a group in front of officials.
options.commitsYouTo: Rework of the redesign's screens once a standard is chosen.

brief.tradeoff: A named standard now costs a little on every screen but avoids rebuilding them later; offering other languages reaches more residents but turns translation into a new kind of publication that needs its own doctrine.

why: AA is the recognised bar, and the redesign is the cheapest moment there will ever be to meet it. Your earlier rulings (no colour-only signals, focus and tap equivalents, no focus traps) already point the same way; naming the standard turns them from three rules into a complete one.

Building the interface so its words can be translated costs little now and keeps option B open. A translated case, however, is a doctrine question about who signs what, and deserves its own decision with the corrections work rather than being bundled in here. My suggestion is to record now one principle for whenever it comes: a translation is never presented as the signed case; it is marked unofficial and names the original.
recommendation.risk: Meeting AA adds checking to every screen, and some displays (dense evidence tables, stage bars) will take design care. It is contained by making the check part of accepting each screen rather than a separate project at the end.

ruled.title: Accessibility standard and languages
ruled.decided: Every member screen of the redesign, and the published case page, print and file, is built to WCAG 2.2 at level AA, and each new screen is checked against it before it is accepted; the rules already set (colour never the only signal, focus and tap equivalents to hover, a docked assistant panel) are part of meeting it. The interface is in English for now, built so its words live in one place and another language can be added without rebuilding screens; a published case appears in the language its group wrote it in. A translation of a published case is never presented as the signed case: it is marked as an unofficial translation and names the signed original. Whether and how a group issues translations, and the interface in a place's languages, are decided later.

openQuestions.question: When a published case names a government office or an official in their role, how prominently and in what words should it say whether the group put its findings to them and what came back, and what should happen when their reply arrives after publication?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Right of reply is a declaration, not a gate (DEC-13); a response returns as captured evidence, not a channel.
openQuestions.context: A published case often names a subject: a government office, or an official acting in their role. Good practice is to put the findings to the subject before publishing and report what came back. The subject meets the product only as any reader does, on the public case page; the publishing group records whether it sought the subject's comment and why.

canonSays.says: 'The subject's right of reply is a declaration, not a gate': the publisher's determination and justification are an element of the group's recorded bias.
Pre-publication contact with the subject is the required workflow in practice literature, overturning its earlier listing as a hazard.
Every case must state a subject position, one of 'sought_and_answered', 'sought_no_answer', 'not_sought', and a subject justification.
A 'request_for_comment' action must name an inquiry and a clock entry; a reply is captured bytes or a member's account, and 'a non-response is recorded with its date'.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The record side is built; the experience is not. Undecided: how a reader and the subject see the three-valued position and its justification (prominence, wording, whether a reply is linked to where it is quoted); whether a subject can find cases naming them; and how a reply that arrives after publication shows up (it can only enter as captured evidence and appear in a later edition). The tension is between the practice literature calling contact 'required' and the canon refusing to make it a gate.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The published case prints 'Position on putting this case to its subject' with the justification; the review copy shows it; a reply box for subjects was considered and refused.
related: 17 (a reply leads to a new edition)
19 (position is part of the recorded bias)

options.option: Show the subject position prominently near the top of every published case in plain words ('We asked the Office of X on date; they replied / did not reply by date / we did not ask, because…'), each linked to the captured correspondence where public.
options.tradeoffs: Fair and self-evident; linking correspondence needs a rule on which correspondence is published as evidence.

options.option: Add a public 'cases naming this subject' index keyed on the subject registry.
options.tradeoffs: Lets offices find and answer cases; it also creates a listing of targets, which may read as adversarial.

options.option: Keep it where it is (a line among the completeness details).
options.tradeoffs: No new work; a reader may miss it, weakening the fairness it records.

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1: it makes the declaration legible without making it a gate; revisit option 2 when there is a directory.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob for prominence and any subject-facing index (effects on people outside the project); Design for wording and layout.

brief.title: How an office named in a case sees it and replies
brief.inOneBreath: When a published case names a government office or an official in their role, how prominently and in what words should it say whether the group put its findings to them and what came back, and what should happen when their reply arrives after publication?
brief.decision: (1) Where and in what words a published case shows the group's declared position on putting the case to its subject: asked and answered, asked with no answer, or not asked, with the reason. (2) Whether that statement links to the actual correspondence. (3) Whether a reply that arrives after publication puts a notice in front of the publishing project. (4) Whether to build a public list of the cases that name a given office. I recommend not building it yet.
brief.alreadyDecidedPart: You ruled that the subject's right of reply is a declaration, not a gate: every case must say whether the group asked the subject and why, but publication is never blocked for want of asking or of an answer. A request for comment names the questions put and a response window nobody enforces. A reply enters the record only as captured evidence or a member's signed account, and silence is recorded with its date. On 30 September you ruled that actions go to offices and roles, never to a private individual.
basics: A case is what a project publishes: a set of findings (questions the group has answered) and the evidence beneath them. The project's owner signs it, and anyone can read and check it without the group's help. Once published, a case can never be changed or withdrawn. A correction is a new edition, a separate document.

A case's subject is the office, or the official acting in their role, whose conduct the case examines: for example, the Director of Public Works or the City Administrator's office. (Civicsmith also uses the word 'subject' for any named person, office or thing in the record. Question 34 deals with that clash.)

Right of reply is the journalistic practice of putting findings to the people they concern before publishing, and reporting what came back. It resembles a party's chance to comment on a proposed decision before it becomes final, though here it is fairness, not law. The August case-making research found that practice treats it as the expected workflow.

'A declaration, not a gate' means this. Every case must declare one of three positions: 'we asked and they answered', 'we asked and got no answer', or 'we did not ask'. It must also give a written reason. Civicsmith never checks that contact happened or that the answer was favourable. 'We did not ask' is legitimate when justified, for example where warning an office could lead to records being altered. The declaration counts as part of the group's declared bias: it is the group's own judgement, shown so that readers can weigh it.

A request for comment is one kind of action in Civicsmith. A member records that the group put specific questions to an office and gave it a window to answer, much like a data request with a response date. Replies are logged against that action, either as the captured email or letter (its exact bytes, dated and fingerprinted) or as a member's signed account of a phone call. Silence is logged as a fact with its date.
today: Built on the server: every case must carry the three-way position and its reason. Both must be freshly written for each new edition, and copying the last edition's wording is refused. The request-for-comment action and its reply log are also built.

What a reader sees on the old public page: one line on the page headed 'What this case excludes', below the exclusion statement. It reads 'Position on putting this case to its subject: sought_no_answer.' followed by the reason. The position is printed as an internal code word, not in plain words, and it sits where a reader looking for fairness is unlikely to look. A review copy shows the same line.

Not connected, as far as I can find: nothing links the request-for-comment action to the case's declared position. The member types the position by hand, the case does not point at the correspondence, and a reply logged after publication tells nobody. The case has no structured 'who the subject is' field either; the subject is named only in the reason's words. And a captured reply crosses into the published case only if a finding rests on it, so a reply nobody cites stays private.

A reply box for subjects on the public page was considered by the earlier interface design and refused, because a typed comment is neither dated nor fingerprinted evidence. That was the designers' call, consistent with your ruling, not a ruling of yours. Before publication, an owner could already send the subject a review copy (a draft shown through a revocable private link) to read and comment on. The canon neither suggests nor forbids this.
problem: The fairness the group exercised is invisible. A reporter or council aide reading a critical case wants to know early whether the group asked the department, as they would in a news story. Today the answer is a code word on the exclusions page.

Late replies fall through. Offices often answer after the deadline. When the director's reply arrives after publication, the published edition says 'no answer' forever. That remains true of that edition, but it looks increasingly unfair, and nothing prompts the group to issue a new edition. The group's credibility is at stake, along with its exposure if a case is read as having ignored a response.

Linking the correspondence is a real choice. Publishing an office's reply in full makes the case self-evidently fair. But correspondence can name junior staff or include material the office asked to keep out of public view, and today a reply crosses into the published record only if a finding rests on it. Not linking keeps cases lean but asks readers to trust the group's summary.
A public list of 'cases naming this office' would help offices find and answer cases about them. But it reads like a target list, and the record has no structured subject field to build it from.
Why now: the publishing ceremony is being designed, and its step 'what you are leaving out' is where the position is written.

story.title: Lena, the Director of Public Works and the sewer overflow case
steps: Lena owns the project 'Sewer overflows in West Oakland'. Its key finding is that the department logged 14 overflows in 2025 but reported 6 to the regional water board.
On 1 October Lena records a request for comment to the Director of Public Works. It names the two questions put and gives 10 days to reply. The letter is captured.
No reply comes by 15 October. Lena publishes edition 1 and declares 'we asked and got no answer', with the reason 'Sent to the Director's office on 1 October with 10 days to respond.'
A reporter reads the case. Today she meets 'sought_no_answer' on the exclusions page, misses its meaning, and writes that the group 'did not seek comment'.
On 20 October the director emails that the other 8 events were below the reporting threshold. A member captures the email against the request.
Nothing tells Lena that her published case still says 'no answer' when an answer exists. Edition 1 will say so forever, and only a new edition can carry the reply. This is where the decision bites.

fixed.point: The right of reply is declared, never enforced, and is part of the group's recorded bias.
fixed.why: Your ruling following the August case-making research.

fixed.point: Every case states one of three positions plus a reason, written fresh for each edition.
fixed.why: Your ruling on the right of reply, built into the case rules.

fixed.point: A request for comment names the questions put and a response window; the window's length is never enforced.
fixed.why: Your ruling on requests for comment, worded on 30 September.

fixed.point: A reply is captured bytes or a member's signed account; silence is recorded with its date.
fixed.why: Your ruling: a reply is evidence, never a summary.

fixed.point: Actions are addressed to offices and roles, never to a private individual.
fixed.why: Your Action rulings of 30 September.

fixed.point: Something found after publication leaves the signed edition as it is; the owning project gets a notice, and a later edition discloses or resolves it.
fixed.why: Your 29 September ruling on tensions found after publication, the nearest pattern to a late reply.

options.label: A
options.name: A plain 'Did we ask them?' box near the top, with links and a late-reply notice
options.howItWorks: Every published case opens with a short box stating the position in words, the date asked, the window given and, where it applies, the date of the reply. Where the group chooses to publish the correspondence, the box links to it. That needs a small new rule allowing correspondence to cross into the published case even when no finding rests on it. Separately, when a reply is logged against a request for comment after its case was published, the owning project gets one notice in its queue.
options.inTheStory: Edition 1 opens with: 'Did we put this case to the people it concerns? We asked the Director of Public Works on 1 October 2026, giving 10 days to reply. No reply had arrived when this edition was published on 15 October. [Read our request]'. On 20 October Lena's queue shows: 'The Director of Public Works replied to your request for comment on 20 October, after edition 1 of "Sewer overflows" was published. Edition 1 still says no reply was received.' She issues edition 2, whose box reads: 'The Director replied on 20 October. [Read the reply in full]'.
gains: Fairness is visible where readers look for it.
Late replies lead to corrections instead of being lost.
It stays a declaration: nothing is blocked.
costs: A rule is needed on which correspondence may be published, and on removing staff names from it.
One more kind of notice in the queue.
options.commitsYouTo: A published reply becomes permanent in that edition. Groups will need guidance on what they may publish from an office's letter.

options.label: B
options.name: The same box, the group's summary only
options.howItWorks: As A, but the correspondence is never linked. The box states the facts and the group's one-line summary of any reply. The late-reply notice is kept.
options.inTheStory: Edition 2 says: 'The Director replied on 20 October that the other 8 events were below the reporting threshold.' Readers must take the group's word for it.
gains: No new rule on publishing correspondence.
No risk of exposing staff names.
costs: Readers cannot check the summary, which is weaker than the rest of a case built to be checkable.
An office may dispute the summary.
options.commitsYouTo: Correspondence stays private. Linking it could be added later.

options.label: C
options.name: Keep it where it is, in words
options.howItWorks: The line stays on the exclusions page, with the code word replaced by plain words. No links and no late-reply notice.
options.inTheStory: The reporter must still find the line, and the 20 October reply is noticed only if someone opens the action.
gains: Almost no work.
costs: Readers miss it, and late replies stay invisible to the group.
options.commitsYouTo: Nothing new.

brief.tradeoff: Making the group's fairness visible and self-correcting (A) costs a rule on publishing correspondence. Keeping things lean (B or C) asks readers to trust the group's word on exactly the point where trust matters most.

why: A makes the declaration readable without turning it into a gate, and the late-reply notice follows the pattern you already approved for problems found after publication: the signed edition stands, and the group is prompted to issue a new one. Publishing the reply itself is the fairest thing a group can do and matches your view that a reply is evidence, not a summary.

I would not build the public list of cases per office yet. It needs a structured subject field and a directory that do not exist, and it is the most likely of the options to be read as adversarial. Mentioning a review copy as an optional way to put a draft to the subject before publishing is my own suggestion. The canon does not say it.
recommendation.risk: A group may publish a reply that names a junior employee. This is contained by making publication of the correspondence the owner's deliberate choice in the ceremony, with a reminder to remove names of people who are not the subject.

howToAnswer: 17: as recommended.
17: A, but never link the correspondence; the group's summary is enough.
17: A, and build the list of cases per office as well.
17: question first: if an office asks us to publish its reply in full, must we?

brief.title: How a correction reaches people who relied on an earlier edition
brief.inOneBreath: When a group corrects a published case by issuing a new edition, how do people who read or cited the old edition learn what changed and why, given that Civicsmith never sends anyone a message?
brief.decision: (1) Should every edition after the first carry a required, written statement, 'What changed in this edition, and why', shown at the top of the new edition and quoted in the old edition's banner? (2) Should a computed list of differences appear beneath it, labelled as machine work? (How readers and citing groups learn that a newer edition exists is now part of question 36.)
basics: A case is what a project publishes: a set of findings and the evidence beneath them, signed by the project's owner. Each published edition has a fingerprint (a hash), a short code computed from its exact bytes. Anyone holding the fingerprint can check that what they are reading is exactly what was signed.

Publication cannot be undone. A correction is never an edit. It is a new edition with its own number, a separate document, and the old edition keeps answering at the same address forever. A citation names a particular edition. This is like an errata filing in a regulatory proceeding: the original filing stays in the docket, and the errata is a separate dated document.

'Pull, never push' means readers learn of changes by coming back to look. Civicsmith does not email, text or push notifications to anyone. Your ruling of 29 September says so for members, and the same holds for outside readers. A 'notify me' button for readers was considered by the earlier interface design and refused, because it would turn readers into a mailing list the group has to hold.

The freshness rule: four parts of a case must be newly written for each edition. They are the statement of what the case does not cover, the reason for its position on contacting the subject, the list of exclusions, and the bias acknowledgement. Copying last edition's wording is refused. None of these is a note about what was corrected.

A re-evaluation notice is how Civicsmith tells members that something their work rests on has changed. Inside one group's copy, if a question cites edition 1 of a case and edition 2 appears, that question's members get such a notice.
Each group runs its own copy of Civicsmith in its own hosting account. There is no central server and no central directory of groups.
today: Built: every edition page carries a banner. An old edition says: 'A newer edition of this case exists. You are reading edition 1; edition 2 was published later. Edition 1 has not been withdrawn and still answers: an edition is a separate document and every published one stands.' It then explains that the strengths shown are edition 1's own, and gives a link, 'Read edition 2'. The newest edition says 'You are reading edition 2, which is the newest edition of this case.' A published list shows every edition.
Not required anywhere: a statement of what changed and why. A group can satisfy the freshness rule by rewriting the four fields without ever saying what it corrected.
Inside one group: the re-evaluation notice for work citing an older edition is built.

Across groups: as far as I can find, nothing lets one group's copy notice that another group has published a newer edition of a case it cites. A group that built its own finding on another group's edition 1 learns of edition 2 only if a member happens to look.
problem: A reporter, council aide or another group that quoted edition 1 comes back and sees 'A newer edition exists'. They must then compare two long documents to learn what moved and why. If the change was material, such as a dollar figure falling by a quarter, they may miss it and keep repeating the wrong number. A correction that readers cannot find fails to correct.
Credibility: groups that correct themselves openly earn trust. A correction that readers have to dig for looks like quiet revision, even though nothing was hidden.

The cost is one more required field at signing. A field nobody wants to write turns into boilerplate ('minor updates'), which is worse than nothing because it looks like disclosure. A computed list of differences is honest about what changed, but it cannot say why. It can also make trivial changes look large (a reworded paragraph) or large ones look small (one changed number).
Other groups are the most exposed readers. A group whose own published case rests on edition 1 carries forward a figure the originating group has corrected, and its readers inherit the error.
Why now: the publishing ceremony's step 'the edition this creates' is being designed. Adding a required statement later means reworking that step and its pre-flight checks.

story.title: Marcus, the $4.2M transfer and the tenants' union
steps: Edition 1 of the Budget Watch project's case 'Sewer fund transfers' reports that $4.2M moved from the sewer fund to the general fund in fiscal 2025.

The decision is about what the banner and edition 2 say about the $1.1M, and whether the tenants' union ever finds out.

ruled.title: What changed in a new edition, and following other groups' editions
ruled.decided: Every edition after the first carries a required statement, 'What changed in this edition, and why', shown at the top of the new edition and quoted where the older edition points to it; a new edition cannot be signed without it. The assistant may draft it: an initial, perhaps partial, detailed high-level description of the changes and, as far as the system can tell, the motivation for the revision, never a diff. The draft is labelled machine work until a member adopts or rewrites it, and the record keeps that it began as a machine draft. A group's copy can be configured to watch the published cases of other groups it cites or follows, as it watches documents for updates, and to respond to a new edition by telling the members whose work rests on the cited edition; nothing is pushed between groups.

brief.title: How members choose how they are credited
brief.inOneBreath: When a published case uses a member's own firsthand observation, where is the member asked to choose how they are credited, and do you confirm the two rules already built around that choice?
brief.decision: (1) Confirm that a case edition cannot be signed while any member whose observation it uses has not chosen a credit level, and that the owner's way forward is to drop the finding that rests on it. (2) Confirm that 'by name' publishes the member's handle, the name they chose for the record, and never a legal name. (3) Approve where the member is asked (a to-do in their own queue, with the state shown on the case draft) and that every level appears to the public in one neutral style.
brief.alreadyDecidedPart: On 14 September you ruled that a member's material contribution to a published case is credited at one of four levels the member chooses: the group, the project, their cover, or by name. You also ruled that a source who spoke off the record is valid. On 29 September you ruled that choosing a credit is a heavy act, with a full dialog stating that the name becomes permanent at publication, and that the group is never the first to make a source more public. A case says 'an unnamed source' unless the source consented.
basics: An observation is something a member saw or heard themselves, written in their own words and signed. For example: 'On 3 March at 7 a.m. I saw sewage overflowing the manhole at 10th and Mandela for 40 minutes.' It is evidence, but it stands on that member's trustworthiness, like a witness declaration rather than a document from the agency's files.

Every piece of evidence carries a letter grade from A to D for how easily an outsider could check it for themselves. A firsthand observation is always graded D as testimony, whatever credit level the member chooses. The credit level changes only what the public reads about who said it, never how strong the evidence is.

The four levels: 'the group' (the publishing group, no person named); 'the project' (the project that produced the case); 'cover'; and 'by name'. A cover is a label an administrator gives a member when inviting them, to tell members apart, such as 'volunteer-7' or 'the CPA from the Tuesday meeting'. It is deliberately not a legal identity. A handle is the name a member picks for themselves on joining. It already appears in the record as the author of their acts, and the public sees it on what they sign. Civicsmith stores no legal names at all, so a seized membership list unmasks no one.

The observation's own signed files never name its author; only the group's private register links it to the member. So the published files are the same at every level, and the level changes only the sentence the case prints. A member may also record what an unnamed source told them; there is no place at all to store that source's identity, so it cannot leak.
Only the project's owner signs a case edition. The member whose words are used is often someone else, which is why the choice has to come from them and cannot be part of the owner's signing.
today: Built on the server: the choice itself, recorded and dated for each case edition and observation. Only the author can make it, only while active, only before the edition is signed, and 'by name' only if they have a handle. A later edition keeps the earlier choice until the member changes it. The signed case carries a section headed 'Whose Words These Are', where a chosen entry reads, for example, '… attributed to the cover the group knows its author by: volunteer-7 … chosen at edition 1', and an unchosen one reads 'NO LEVEL IS CHOSEN … This edition cannot be signed until its author chooses one, or the finding resting on it leaves the case.'

Built: signing is refused while any observation the edition reaches is unchosen, and also when the stated level is no longer the author's latest choice. The review copy's list of what is missing shows the same before anyone tries to sign, and the draft lists every observation it reaches with whether each is chosen.

These two rules (blocking, and 'name' meaning handle) are inside the requirements you approved as recommended 'for now' on 26 September. Neither was put to you as a question of its own, and the design document still marks both as yours to confirm.

Not built: any screen where a member makes the choice. The old member app has no such control, and as far as I can find no to-do reaches the author's queue. Through the member app today, a case resting on an observation cannot be signed at all.
problem: The blocking rule gives each member a veto over the use of their own words, and over nothing else. Without it, either the owner would decide how a colleague is credited or a default would, and your 14 September ruling forbids both. With it, one silent or absent member can hold up one finding; the owner can publish without it but loses the evidence. A member who has left cannot choose: their words stay usable in later editions of a case where they already chose, and in no new case.

Your phrase was 'the member by name', and Civicsmith deliberately holds no legal names. Reading 'name' as the handle keeps it that way. A member who wants their legal name printed would make their handle their legal name. Storing a typed legal name would put real names into a database that can be subpoenaed or breached.

Display: if 'Credited to the group' looks like a missing name, readers will treat anonymous testimony as weaker, and your ruling says the grade, not the name, measures strength. In proceedings, keeping a declarant's identity confidential under a protective order does not change the weight of the testimony, and the page should reflect that.
Why now: the ceremony is being designed, and until a choice screen exists no case resting on an observation can be signed.

story.title: Maria's observation at 10th and Mandela

ruled.title: How members are credited, and what anonymity does to testimony
ruled.decided: A member chooses how a published case credits their observation, at one of four levels: the group, the project, their cover, or by name ('by name' publishes their handle, never a legal name). An edition is not signed while a member whose observation it uses has not chosen; the owner's way forward is to drop the finding that rests on it. The member is asked by a to-do in their own queue, and the state shows on the case draft. Every level appears publicly in one neutral style with the grade beside it. The level also sets the testimony's weight: testimony credited at the group or project level is anonymous and is treated like an anonymous tip, potentially weaker because a member may have a vested interest, and must be corroborated to journalistic and legal standards before a finding rests on it; identified at cover or name, it may carry greater strength. A change of level reaches the findings resting on it as re-evaluation notices.

brief.title: How a group's declared bias appears to the public
brief.inOneBreath: When the public reads a published case, how should it see the lens the group worked under, so that a reader can weigh it and an opponent cannot easily quote it out of context?
brief.decision: (1) Should public readers see the lens's actual statements, each with its justification and evidence attached, or only the publisher's acknowledgement and a reference to the lens? (2) If the statements are shown, are they printed into the signed case itself, so that every downloaded or printed copy carries them? (3) Is the full form required on the public page, or may it open as a short summary?
basics: Declared bias makes a group's lens part of the record instead of pretending it has none. The group writes a short set of statements about how it treats certain sources, each with a justification. Courts do the same in judicial dress: an adverse-inference rule is a declared lens.

There are three kinds. Scrutiny: 'claims from this source must be cross-checked before they bear weight'. Inference: 'the city attorney's silence on a media request is not agreement'. Pattern: an evidenced claim about how an institution behaves, which must cite evidence in the group's record. A verdict ('X lies') is refused, whoever writes it.

A published case is a project's signed argument, released in numbered editions and never changed. Two things about the lens travel with it. The manifest, computed by the system: which statement sets were in force, at which revision, and a fingerprint (hash) of the exact statements. The acknowledgement, written by the publishing member at publication and fresh each edition: what the lens did to this edition's findings.

The doctrine's 'two-audience choice' accepts that opponents will quote the lens, betting that a declared, justified rule is more respectable than the undeclared lens every institution has, and that the no-verdict rule keeps each statement defensible when read aloud by an adversary.
today: Built: the signed case carries the acknowledgement and the manifest. I checked the manifest's actual text: it names the statement sets, their revisions and the fingerprint, but does not print the statements, justifications or evidence. A stranger holding the case can read the publisher's account and prove which lens was meant, but cannot read the lens. The earlier brief assumed the statements were published; they are not.

The old public page has a line 'Declared bias' listing only open hunches (a member's declared, unproven guess), or 'none declared'. It shows neither acknowledgement nor manifest; the acknowledgement appears only on the private review copy. So a case made under three statements reads 'Declared bias: none declared'.
problem: The two-audience bet depends on presentation. Quoted alone, 'this group says the Auditor controls the narrative' is an accusation. Shown with its kind, justification and cited audit reports, it is a reasoned, checkable position. A summary or a list of named subjects hands opponents the quotable version.

Second gap: the statements are not in the signed case. A page that reads them live leaves printed or downloaded copies with only a fingerprint, and nothing at all once the group's system is gone, although the doctrine wants a stranger to read the lens without the group's help.

Full display has its own risk (my judgement; the sources are silent). A pattern statement cites evidence in the record, some of it perhaps unpublished; printing the citation could reveal material or an interest the group kept private.
It affects readers, officials named as subjects, the group's credibility and the publishing member. Without a decision the redesign inherits the misleading label.

story.title: The Auditor statement read aloud at committee
steps: Oakland Ratepayers has three statements in force. One is a pattern statement: 'The City Auditor uses its discretion over report scope to limit the remediation options identified.' Its justification: three audit reports (2019, 2021, 2023) each left out fund transfers that were later found in the adopted budgets. It cites all three.

Ana publishes the group's sewer-fund case, edition 1, and writes the acknowledgement: 'Our pattern statement on the Auditor led us to search beyond the audit's scope. Finding 2 rests on budget records the audit did not examine.'
Marcus, a council staffer, opens the public page before a committee hearing, looking for a way to discredit the group.
At the hearing he says: 'This group's own rules say the Auditor controls the narrative.' Whether the room hears a slur or a reasoned position depends on what Marcus could copy from the page.
Keisha, a reporter, prints the case to read on the train. What does her paper copy say about the lens?

brief.title: What a hunch's grade does, and clearing hunches before publishing
brief.inOneBreath: Now that a hunch counts for nothing in a question's strength, what is its temporary grade for, does the doctrine sentence saying it 'composes normally' get corrected, and how do members see the hunches they must clear before publishing?
brief.decision: (1) Confirm that a hunch never counts in any strength reading, and that the doctrine sentence saying a hunch 'composes normally' while a question is open is corrected to match. (2) Decide what the hunch's letter is for once strength ignores it: shown on the link as the member's stated confidence, or dropped. (3) Approve a standing 'hunches to clear' list on the question and project pages, in addition to the check before publishing.
brief.alreadyDecidedPart: Your ruling of 1 August: a hunch is temporary declared bias, carries a temporary grade, is visible as a hunch everywhere from the moment it is made, and must be cleared before publication. Your ruling of 2 August: it is the one kind of bias that blocks publishing. On 26 September you approved, 'for now', the requirement that a hunch counts for nothing in strength and is always named. On 29 September you ruled that the check before publishing runs before the ceremony's first screen and names every hunch.
basics: A question is something a project is trying to answer, such as 'Did the city split the paving contract to avoid council approval?'. Its evidence is a list of links (the record calls each a 'leg') from the question to documents or to other answered questions. Each link can carry a letter grade, A to D, for how easily someone else could check that the link holds. A grade never says whether something is true.

Strength is the question's summary: two letters shown side by side, the weakest capture grade and the weakest connection grade among what the answer depends on, never added into one score. Since your ruling of 29 September, every question in the project workspace shows its strength against the project's bar.

A hunch is a member's declared guess that a link holds before the record can show it. In your words of 1 August: hunches 'can also be dead wrong', but they 'help bring an investigation together', so 'hunch-based connections must be given a temporary high enough grade that otherwise disconnected evidence can be brought together'. A hunch carries its author's name and date, and it is the only grade a member may assert above D on their own say-so.

Clearing a hunch means showing the case still holds without it: either the link earns a real grade from the record, or the hunch is removed and the answer still stands. A case cannot publish while any hunch stands.
An analogy: a hunch is like a working hypothesis in a staff analysis. Useful for deciding what to look at, but nothing in the filed testimony may rest on it.
today: Built in the new code, by my reading: strength treats a hunch link as counting for nothing, lists it separately, and explains: 'this leg is marked as a hunch, so it is visible here and does not count as evidence'. The requirement file still marks this 'not yet met'; that mark appears out of date.

Built: publishing refuses any case with a standing hunch, naming each: 'A finding in this case rests on a hunch. … Give each leg a grade the record earns, or take the hunch out of the basis, and publish again. Nothing was written.' Under your 29 September ruling this check moves before the publication ceremony's first screen.
Not decided: any member screen for hunches in the new interface. The old interface marks a hunch link 'HUNCH' with author and date and warns that the case cannot publish.

The contradiction: the bias doctrine still says that while a question is open a hunch 'composes normally — that is what makes it useful', and that treating it as ungraded 'would destroy exactly the traversability this ruling exists to preserve'. The investigative-session design and the strength requirement you approved say it 'does not count as evidence'.
Separately, the Action canon you approved on 30 September says a plan resting on unproven premises is 'shown as hunch debt': a disclosure on a plan, not a publishing block.
problem: Two canon texts disagree while the workspace strength badges are being designed. Read literally, 'composes normally' would let a hunch lift a question's strength, and a member could quote that strength to a reporter or an official: the failure the doctrine names, 'a case published over an uncleared hunch states a strength that is not true', only earlier.

If strength ignores the hunch, the sources do not say what its letter still does. I found nothing that reads the letter except to display it. What works without it: the link still ties the two items together on the question's evidence list, and a member can search for every hunch in a project. Whether that is the 'bringing together' you meant on 1 August is your call.
Clearing is only met at the end: a member who learns of five standing hunches at the publication check, after weeks of work, is surprised. A standing list avoids that, but must not nag.

story.title: Maria and the two paving contractors
steps: Maria's project asks whether the city split a street-resurfacing contract into pieces small enough to avoid council approval. Two invoices, from 'Bayside Paving LLC' and 'BSP Contracting', look like the same firm.
She cannot prove it yet, so she links the BSP invoice to the question as a hunch, graded B. The link shows in a distinct hunch style: 'Hunch (B) · Maria · 2 Oct'.
The question's strength badges read 'Capture B · Connection C · 1 hunch not counted'. The hunch does not lift the C.
On the project page, a small 'Hunches to clear (1)' list shows the link, with its two ways out: earn a real grade from evidence, or show the answer holds without it.
Two weeks later she captures the state's business registry entries: both firms list the same agent and address. She regrades the link from the record; the hunch is cleared and the list empties.
Had she not, the check before the publication ceremony's first screen would have listed the hunch by name and stopped there, writing nothing.

brief.title: Standards of proof by audience: guidance for the project's bar
brief.inOneBreath: When a group sets the standard of evidence a project's published case must meet, should Civicsmith tell it what a newsroom, a city administrator or a court actually expects, and if so, how?
brief.decision: (1) Ship the bar setting now, with plain meanings for each letter and an honest note that no audience guidance exists yet, or hold it until guidance exists? (2) When guidance comes, does it take the form you approved for legal venues on 30 September: sourced facts in the jurisdiction profile, shown beside the choice, reading 'undetermined' where nobody has researched them, and never a default? (3) Is the research commissioned now, or when a named trigger occurs?
brief.alreadyDecidedPart: The bar belongs to a project and never combines across projects: one finding may clear a journalist project's bar and miss a lawyer project's, 'and both facts stand' (10 August). Co-attested Grade B suffices to publish (29 September). For actions, each venue's standard is a sourced fact beside each exhibit's grade, never refusing (30 September).
basics: A project is a group's line of work toward a goal; a case is the argument it publishes, made of findings. A load-bearing finding is one the case relies on; a supporting one is included but not relied on.

Each finding has two separate grades, A to D, never combined. Capture: how well the documents are held (B: the group fetched and fingerprinted the document itself; 'co-attested' adds a trusted timestamp and an independent archive copy). Connection: how firmly links are established (C: the same name appears in both; plausible, not established). A grade says how easily someone else could check the work, never whether it is true.

The bar is the project's declared minimum letter on each axis for every load-bearing finding; publishing is refused if one falls short on a declared axis. An undeclared axis or absent bar is stated in words: 'an absent bar is not a bar of zero'. Think of the evidentiary standard in a CPUC proceeding versus a court: the same evidence can clear one and not the other.
A group default bar seeds new projects, binds nothing, and is a heavy act reserved for an active administrator.

Audiences are the professional roles reading cases: reporters, activists, government administrators, lawyers and others. Differences between them belong to what is done with a case (who certifies it, whether it persists, to whom it goes), never to a field on the case.
A jurisdiction profile is a data file of a place's rules and offices (Oakland and Alameda County first), each fact sourced or marked 'undetermined'.
today: The bar works in the record: a project carries it, publishing checks it, the case states it in words. The old interface shows it on a published case but has no screen to set one. Any signed-in member can still set the group default; the administrator-only rule is approved, not built.

The catalogue of standards by audience 'is owed and does not exist'; without it, says the publication design, the bar is 'a number a project picks'. Venue standards for actions are a requirement written on 30 September, not yet built.
A leftover: the publication design's glossary still says the bar is 'strictest wins', a rule your 10 August ruling removed. A wording fix for the architecture session; nothing for you.
problem: Without guidance a group is guessing. It may set B on both axes when a newsroom would run on named sources at connection C, or set D/D, and then 'this case was held to D/D' tells readers almost nothing.

Your 30 September ruling reshapes the gap: legal use runs mostly through actions, where a venue's own standard is shown. What remains is newsrooms, administrators, other groups and the public, whose standards are mostly unwritten practice. A precise-looking entry nobody can source would be worse than none (my judgement).
It is needed now because the redesign is drawing the screen where a bar is set.
