brief.title: Saying 'there is more you cannot see' about work that depends on this
brief.inOneBreath: When work a member cannot see rests on, or cites, the item they are looking at, should the screen say the list is incomplete, as it already must for hidden things the item itself rests on?
brief.decision: (1) Does your 4 August rule (something hidden is never named or counted, but the fact that something is missing is stated) also apply 'downstream', to lists of the work that rests on or cites what a member is looking at? (2) If yes, should the incompleteness line appear only when something was actually withheld, or as a standing caveat on every such list? (3) Confirm that the one-for-one placeholders still used in four places ('an object you may not see') are removed, since they let a reader count hidden items.
brief.alreadyDecidedPart: On 4 August you ruled that when something a member's item rests on is out of their sight, the screen states that the picture is incomplete, with no name, title, state or count, and that a later session must not 'fix' this toward silence. On 29 September you ruled that 'Withheld' has its own distinct look and one fixed sentence. You also ruled that in a conflict with a hidden project, each side is told only on its own side, without naming the other.
basics: A group's copy of Civicsmith holds many projects. A project is a shared workspace, and most projects are hidden from members who have not joined them. 'Sight' means what a given member is allowed to see. A confidential project might be an inquiry into a council office that only three members know exists.

Items in the record link to each other. Upstream of an item is what it rests on: the documents, observations and earlier findings beneath it. Downstream is what rests on it or cites it: the questions and findings that use it. One budget PDF can sit beneath questions in five projects.

A re-evaluation notice is how Civicsmith tells members that something their work rests on has changed (a document superseded by a newer version, a finding reopened) and asks for a second look. The member who makes the change also sees a list of what rests on the item, so they can judge how far the change reaches. A 'cited by' list shows everything that cites an item.

Even the sentence 'something you cannot see uses this' reveals one fact: hidden work touches this item. A count reveals more, and repeated looks at counts could let a determined member map a hidden project. That is why your rule forbids counts.
An analogy: a docket under a protective order notes that a filing was made under seal, without its title or contents. It does not silently omit the filing.
'Withheld' is one of five named states you ruled must each have their own look: Undetermined, Withheld, Unrated, Nobody looked and Refused. Withheld means something exists that is not yours to see.
today: Upstream, built as ruled: the queue and strength panels say, for example, 'Part of what this is filed under is not visible to you, so this list is incomplete rather than settled', with no count. The strength panel was corrected on 29 September to stop counting hidden items.

Downstream, built as silence: the re-evaluation list and the 'cited by' list show only what the member can see and say nothing about the rest. The written requirements say a hidden dependent is 'withheld whole, with no count' and, for 'cited by', 'no count of what was withheld'. Neither adds a marker. Members of the hidden project still get their own notices, so their work is not silently broken.

Placeholders in four places: the parts of Civicsmith that judge whether a government act meets a standard, its consequences, escalations and filings still replace each hidden item one-for-one with a placeholder such as 'an object you may not see'. That lets a reader count hidden items, which your rule forbids. Fixing it was deliberately held until you rule on this question.
problem: Silence misleads. A member superseding a document sees '2 questions rest on this' and judges the change minor, when three more in a confidential project rest on it. Your rule forbids exactly this silence upstream, but downstream it is current behaviour.

How real is the harm? The hidden project's members still get their notices. The harm is to the acting member's judgement (how careful to be, whether to raise it with the group) and to the record's honesty, because a list that looks complete is not.

Saying 'others you cannot see may also rest on this' tells the member that hidden work uses this document. In a small group that may be enough to guess that a confidential project exists. Your 29 September ruling on hidden conflicts already accepted this much disclosure on each project's own side.
A standing caveat on every list reveals nothing, but a line that is always there soon goes unread, and it does not truly state that this particular list is incomplete.
Why now: the redesign is fixing the Withheld look and sentence, and the four placeholder fixes are waiting. If this waits, the redesign applies Withheld upstream only and must be revisited.

story.title: Maya and the superseded budget PDF
steps: Maya, in the Budget Watch project, captured the city's FY2026 Adopted Budget PDF in July.

Unknown to her, 3 questions in a confidential project, 'Police overtime', also rest on it.

brief.tradeoff: Telling the member 'there is more' gives honest lists and costs one fact about hidden work. Silence or a standing caveat protects that fact at the cost of lists that look complete when they are not.

why: It applies your own rule consistently in both directions, and your 29 September ruling on hidden conflicts already accepted the one fact it reveals. The point of the rule was that a truncated list must not pass for a complete one, and that matters as much for 'what rests on this' as for 'what this rests on'.

Whatever you choose on (1) and (2), I recommend confirming (3): the countable placeholders go. I also recommend against adding 'ask a member of the project that holds it', since that would hint that a project exists and who is in it. This is my recommendation, not canon.
recommendation.risk: A member could probe repeatedly to infer that a confidential project uses certain documents. This is contained by giving no count, position or title, so the most anyone learns is 'some hidden work uses this', the same as on the upstream side.

ruled.decided: The rule for hidden things applies in both directions: a hidden item is never named or counted, and no id, title or state of it is shown, whether it is something the member's work rests on or something that rests on or cites what the member is looking at. Lists of dependents and 'cited by' lists withhold a hidden item whole, and say only that something was withheld, in the 'Withheld' style. openQuestions.question: How many 'spaces' should members be taught (private working and public published, or a third 'shared for review'), so that they always know whether what they are looking at is private or public?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: The privacy fence is architectural; working and published material must never share surface ambiguity.
openQuestions.context: Civicsmith holds two kinds of material: the working record (private material the group is still judging) and the published record (cases the group has signed and released, which anyone can read and verify). This 'privacy fence' is built into the system, not just the look of the screens. Members cross between the two constantly.

canonSays.says: 'Working-corpus material and published material never share a surface ambiguity. A member always knows which side of the fence they are looking at.'
A review copy 'never leaves the instance', is mutable and marked as what it is; an outside recipient reads it through a revocable grant, and it can be exported with an in-band notice on every page.

canonSays.source: DEC-19; Interaction Constructs rung ladder; K356
canonSays.says: Publishing is the only irreversible act; K356 names the sequence release to publish the 'path to publication'.
Working material 'answers an outsider exactly as something that does not exist'.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The principle is stated but no design says how the two sides look. The review copy blurs the fence: it is working material, yet a person without an account can read it and a member can export it, while the old semantics table defines the working record as 'never served to anyone without a credential'. The canon does not say whether there are two spaces or three (working, review copy, published), or how the path to publication is shown as crossing.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The old interface uses two separate spaces: the member app has a persistent footer 'Working record · not public', and the published space has its own masthead, with the semantics table defining 'working record' and 'published record'.

options.option: Two spaces with distinct frames (colour, masthead, wording), and the review copy shown in the working frame with a 'review copy, not published' band.
options.tradeoffs: Simple and matches the architecture; the recipient's view of a review copy needs its own careful marking.

options.option: Three named spaces: working, shared for review, published.
options.tradeoffs: Most accurate to what a member can do; adds a concept to learn.

options.option: Two spaces plus a fence marker on every object showing which side it is on and where it sits on the path to publication.
options.tradeoffs: Strong signal at object level; busier screens.

openQuestions.recommendation: Use two spaces with distinct frames plus a per-object path-to-publication marker, and treat the review copy as a working-side object with its own band; correct the semantics table's 'never served without a credential' wording.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design, within Bob's stated principle; Bob only if the designer proposes a third space, since that changes how members are taught the fence.

brief.title: Always knowing which side of the privacy fence you are on
brief.inOneBreath: How many 'spaces' should members be taught (private working and public published, or a third 'shared for review'), so that they always know whether what they are looking at is private or public?
brief.decision: (1) Teach members two spaces, the private working record and the public published record, with review copies and outgoing drafts shown as clearly marked items inside the working side; or three spaces, with 'shared for review' as its own. (2) Whether each document and case also carries a small 'path to publication' marker showing how far along it is. Colours, mastheads and exact markers are then for Design.
brief.alreadyDecidedPart: Your July principle is law for the interface: working material and published material never share an ambiguous screen, and a member always knows which side of the fence they are looking at. On 3 August you ruled that publishing is the only irreversible act. On 17 September you ruled that a review copy never leaves the group's copy, can be edited, and is marked as what it is. On 29 September you ruled that publishing goes through a five-step ceremony and that the steps toward it are called the path to publication.
basics: The working record is the group's private material: captured documents, observations, questions, findings and drafts that the group is still judging. To an outsider it answers exactly as if it did not exist.
The published record is the set of signed cases the group has released. Anyone can read and check them without the group's help or permission.

The privacy fence between them is built into how Civicsmith stores things, not just how screens look. The two records live in separate stores, and only the publishing act writes to the public one. It is like the confidential and public versions of a regulatory filing: two documents, each clearly stamped, so a reader never wonders which one they hold.

The path to publication is the series of steps a piece of work goes through, from a captured document being released for use to a finding concluded and a case signed. The ceremony is its last step and the only one that cannot be undone.

Some things sit in between. A review copy is a draft case shown, through a private link that can be revoked, to people the owner names, such as a reporter or a committee chair. It never leaves the group's copy, it can still change, and it may never be published. A member may export a review copy to a file. Every page is then stamped with its fingerprint, date, author and the strength bar the case would be held to, and the member is told the file cannot be recalled. Since the Action design, members also prepare letters, filings and statements, which a member approves, stamps and sends by their own hand. Nothing private leaves by the system's own doing.
Your interface brief also says the public never sees that a fence exists. Public pages show the group's face, not fence markers.
today: The old interface uses two spaces. The member app has a footer, 'Working record · not public'. The public pages have their own masthead and, for a signed-in member, a link 'Back to the working record'. Its definitions table says the working record is 'Behind the fence. Material under the group's judgment; never public, never served to anyone without a credential', and the published record is 'Across the fence. Ratified material anyone can read, and verify…'.

The review copy is built. Its page opens with 'REVIEW COPY — NOT A PUBLICATION. This is a draft of a case, shown inside this instance to the people it was addressed to. It is not signed, it is not published, it may still change, and it may never be published at all.' The recipient reads it in a browser without an account.

A correction to the last brief: it said the review copy contradicts 'never served to anyone without a credential'. The canon calls the review link's secret a read-only credential, so the sentence holds as written. A member may still read 'credential' as 'account', and plainer wording would help.
The Action screens for preparing and sending letters are sketched but not built (question 35). There is no design yet for how the redesigned app shows the two sides.
problem: Mistakes here do the most damage. A member may think a draft is private when a reporter can read it through a review link, think a published case can still be edited, or paste working notes into a public statement.

Confusion lives in the in-between things. A review copy is working material that an outsider can read. An exported copy, or a letter that has been sent, has left the system entirely. A two-space model has to mark these without implying that they are public. A three-space model names them but adds a concept to learn, and letters that have left the system still do not fit it.
Who is affected: members (confidentiality, sources), recipients (a reporter must not quote a review copy as a published finding) and the group's credibility (a draft mistaken for a publication).
Honestly, most of this is Design's. Your part is how many spaces members learn, because that is how the fence is taught. Deciding it now lets Design start on the frames.

story.title: Luis, the review link and the reporter
steps: Luis owns the project 'Measure Q spending'. He drafts a case and issues review links to a local reporter and to the chair of the Measure Q oversight committee.
The reporter opens her link without an account. The page opens with 'REVIEW COPY — NOT A PUBLICATION … it may never be published at all.'
Back in the member app, Luis sees his draft among his working items. Under option A it carries a band: 'Review copy · shared with 2 people · not published'.
The chair prefers paper, so Luis exports a file. Every page is stamped, and he is told that the file cannot be recalled, although the link can be withdrawn.
Two weeks later Luis signs edition 1 through the ceremony. It appears in the public space under the group's masthead.
The decision bites at step 3: is the draft simply 'working, with a band', or does it sit in a third place called 'shared for review'?

brief.tradeoff: Two spaces keep the fence simple and true to how Civicsmith is built but rely on strong bands for the in-between items. Three spaces name those items but add a concept that still does not cover everything.

why: Two spaces with distinct frames, plus a path marker on each item, and review copies and outgoing drafts shown as working-side items with their own band. The fence in Civicsmith really is two stores, and a review copy really is working material that a named outsider can see. Teaching it as anything else would mislead.

You need only confirm 'two spaces'. The rest goes to Design. BOB would also make the definitions table plainer ('never shown to anyone outside the group except through a review link you issue'). This is my recommendation, not canon.

ruled.title: Always knowing which side of the privacy fence you are on
ruled.decided: Members are taught two spaces, each with its own distinct frame: the group's private working record and the public published record. Review copies and outgoing drafts appear inside the working frame with a band saying what they are and who can see them (for example 'Shared for review: 2 people outside the group can read this'). Each document and case carries a small path-to-publication marker showing where it stands ('working → shared for review → published'). Publishing, through the ceremony, is the only crossing. Frames, colours, bands and the marker's look are Design's.

openQuestions.question: Should the queue's class of 'things a named member must do', now labelled 'Obligation', be shown to members as 'To do', so that the word 'obligation' in Civicsmith means only a public body's duty?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: The delta is the product; conflating plans with progressions converts a management fact into evidence.
openQuestions.whereTheCanonStops: NOTIFICATIONS.md (D-128); Case Making action plan section 3
openQuestions.context: A 'progression' is a declared model of how a public body is supposed to act, for example minutes follow a meeting, an award follows a solicitation. Members thread real documents into it, and the system shows where reality departed: a missing earlier step, a late later step, or too many documents at one stage. Separately, an 'action plan' is the group's own steps and deadlines.

canonSays.says: 'The analytic product is the DELTA. Declared flow versus observed flow'; a civic obligation (the body's duty) is not a member task, and 'naming them one thing would have modelled our inbox and called it the institution.'
Plans and progressions 'MUST NOT SHARE AN OBJECT': otherwise 'our own missed deadline would surface as a finding about the record — converting a management fact into evidence.'
Progression divergences reach the queue as FINDING items (shown to members as 'Noticed'); the queue's OBLIGATION class holds member tasks and bias debt.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The data exists but no design draws it. D-128's 'flow model' home is still open, and there is no module for the action plan (S11), so nothing yet keeps the two visibly apart. The queue's OBLIGATION class holds member tasks while Bob's ruling says OBLIGATION means the body's own duty, so the labels invite the conflation the canon warns against.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The old interface has a Progressions screen that lists declared stages with threaded documents and text findings; it draws no timeline or declared-versus-observed chart and has no action-plan surface.

options.option: A swim-lane timeline per instance: declared stages as a ghost track, observed documents placed on it, gaps and late steps marked in the record's words.
options.tradeoffs: Makes the delta the picture; needs care with undetermined dates and grades.

options.option: A table of instances by stage with divergence counts, drilling into a single instance's timeline.
options.tradeoffs: Scales to many instances; the story is less immediate.

options.option: Keep our own plans on a separate surface with a different visual language (a checklist or task board, never the timeline style).
options.tradeoffs: Guards the doctrine structurally; needs the S11 design to exist.

openQuestions.recommendation: Use the timeline with a summary table above it for the world, and a visibly different surface for our own plans. Ask Bob whether to relabel the queue's member-task class so it no longer carries the word 'obligation'.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design for the drawing; Bob for any relabelling of the OBLIGATION class, since it is his ruled vocabulary.

ruled.title: Our own missed deadlines are never findings, and the queue's 'To do'
ruled.decided: A plan's checkpoints are the group's own intentions: a missed or not-met checkpoint is never a finding, a condition of the record or a fact about the government, and its reminder reaches the queue as the group's own item. The other side's missed deadline is a signal on the action, raised once when it passes. Members see the queue's to-do class as 'To do' (its internal code unchanged, as with 'Noticed'); on members' and readers' screens 'obligation' means only a public body's duty. Each item's sentence names whose step it is where that matters ('our plan', 'the city's deadline'). How declared flows and their deltas are drawn is Design's.

brief.settledSince: Nothing since 30 September changes this question. The part already decided (below) was settled on 30 September; only the word for the to-do class remains, and it is still yours.
brief.title: What members call the queue's to-do items
brief.inOneBreath: Should the queue's class of 'things a named member must do', now labelled 'Obligation', be shown to members as 'To do', so that the word 'obligation' in Civicsmith means only a public body's duty?
brief.decision: (1) The word members see on the queue's to-do class: 'To do' (recommended), 'Obligation' with the owner named ('Obligation · ours'), or 'Obligation' as now. (2) Whether, beyond the queue, 'obligation' is kept in everything members and readers see for a public body's duty only. Renaming the internal code is a technical matter the architecture session can handle without you, and is not asked here.
brief.alreadyDecidedPart: On 30 September you approved the Action design's answers: a plan's checkpoints are the group's own intentions, and a missed or not-met checkpoint is never a finding, a condition of the record or a fact about the government; its reminder reaches the queue as the group's own item. The other side's missed deadline is a different kind of item, a signal about the action, raised once when it passes. On 29 September you ruled that the queue's class of things the record noticed is shown to members as 'Noticed'. Only the word for the to-do class was left to you, by name.
basics: The queue is each member's list of things that want their attention, grouped by the case they belong to (a case is an inquiry or a project). Every item belongs to one of three classes. To-dos: something a named member must do for the work to proceed; it can be forwarded to someone else, cannot be muted, and leaves everyone's list once done. Noticed items: something the record noticed about the world or about the record that nobody has judged yet; a member takes it up or sets it aside with a reason. Signals: mostly facts about the system's own machinery, such as a capture paused because a city website is limiting requests; a member can mute them.

Inside the system the to-do class is named 'obligation', and members see the label 'Obligation'. That is the problem. On 1 August you said what obligations are: 'the flows (edges) that go on in a living civic system', meaning a public body's duties, such as posting a meeting's minutes within ten days or following a solicitation with an award. Civicsmith models these duties as declared sequences of steps and shows where the real documents depart from them; you called that difference 'the analytic product'. The note that day added that giving a member's task the same name 'would have modelled our inbox and called it the institution'. The class kept its name anyway.

An analogy from your world: a utility's compliance obligation (file an advice letter within 30 days of a decision) and an intervenor's internal to-do (draft our comments by Friday). If the intervenor's tracker labelled both 'obligations', a missed internal date could be read in a summary as the utility's non-compliance.

The word also appears in its civic sense on screens members and readers see. When two records conflict because a rule required one thing and the body did another, the conflict is classed 'obligation against act', and its published form follows the government auditor's elements of a finding (criteria, condition, cause, effect, recommendation), as you ruled on 29 September.
today: The system publishes three labels for the queue's classes: 'Obligation', 'Noticed' and 'Condition'. The current app shows them as small chips on each item, to-dos first, then noticed items, then signals.

Every kind of item in the to-do class is the group's own work, and the list is growing with the Action work being built now: a checkpoint in the group's action plan has come and a member must judge it met or not met; a proposed next stage of an escalation to advance or decline; a deadline reminder a member asked for; a conflict in the record that the project must resolve; a conflict in a record the member cannot see; a 'bias debt' (an AI run whose declared outlook has since changed, to be re-run or settled with a reason); a member who registered their own signing key, which an administrator may revoke; membership requests, endorsements and expertise confirmations owed. None of them is a public body's duty.

The approved Action answers themselves say the checkpoint's reminder is 'an obligation of the group's own'. One Action screen sketch (not separately approved) labels it 'obligation · ours' and labels the city's missed reply 'condition · the counterparty's deadline, not ours'. So the Action design solved the ownership problem by adding a qualifier, and left the word.
Nothing of the redesigned queue is built yet.
problem: The same word now names opposite owners, on the same screen, in the same case. A member, a journalist shown a screen, or a lawyer in a later dispute can read 'Obligation · overdue' as the city's failure when it is the group's own, or read a real civic duty as just one more item on the group's list. Your 30 September ruling keeps a missed checkpoint out of the record's findings; the words on the screen do not yet keep it out of people's heads.

This matters more for Civicsmith than for an ordinary task tool. Its groups make claims about public bodies, and in a records or legal setting 'obligation' carries the weight of a duty. Using it for the group's internal chores invites careless or hostile quoting. That is my judgement, not a canon statement.

Why now: the redesigned queue is being designed, the three class labels (question 28) depend on this one, and the Action work is adding more of the group's own to-dos right now. Labels are cheap to change before members learn them and costly after.

The risk of changing it carelessly is the other way round: if 'To do' replaced the word but items lost the Action design's 'ours' versus 'theirs' wording, a reader could no longer tell the group's checkpoint from the city's deadline. Whatever label is chosen, each item's own sentence should still say whose step it is where that matters.

story.title: Rosa's Monday queue and the Measure U checkpoint
steps: Rosa coordinates her group's project on Measure U bond spending. The group's action plan says: if the city shows earnest commitment by 15 October, hold off on the formal demand (scenario A).

On Monday her queue, under 'Measure U', shows: 'Obligation · Checkpoint due: the city shows earnest commitment [Met] [Not met]'. Directly below: 'Noticed · Minutes of the 9 September oversight committee meeting have not appeared (the committee's rules expect them within 10 days)'.
Rosa is away for a week, and the checkpoint passes unjudged.
Jamal, a reporter working with the group, sees a screenshot of the list and writes that 'the city has missed several obligations on Measure U', counting the group's own checkpoint among them.

Under the recommended label the same queue reads: 'To do · Checkpoint due (our plan): the city shows earnest commitment [Met] [Not met]', above 'Noticed · Minutes of the 9 September meeting have not appeared'. The word 'obligation' appears only in the case itself, about the committee's duty to post minutes.

When the city's reply to the group's formal demand is late, a third row appears once: 'Signal · The city's reply to “Demand to rescind” was due 9 October; no reply recorded'. Nothing about it reads as the group's own failing.

fixed.point: 'Obligation' means a public body's duty, the civic system's own flows; a member's task is downstream of it.

openQuestions.question: When the public doorbell turns senders away because a limit is reached, should the group's members be able to learn that it happened, as a bare count with nothing about who, or should refused knocks stay entirely unrecorded?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: A refusal must teach; a 429 is a claim that needs a count behind it.
openQuestions.context: The 'doorbell' lets anyone, with no account, hand a group a document (a 'knock'). To stop one sender or a flood filling the group's inbox, the instance limits knocks: 12 per sender and 300 in total in any 10 minutes. The person knocking (the knocker) meets the limit when they are refused; members meet the doorbell when they review the inbox.

canonSays.says: 'A 429 tells a member of the public they knocked too often, which is a claim that needs a count behind it'; the bound is published with its method ('at most 12 knocks from one source in any 10 minutes, estimated by a sliding window').
RATE_IP and RATE_GLOBAL 'have no member-facing translation yet'.

The refusal carries the catalogue row's translation plus the stated bound; nothing is stored or counted. A code without a translation 'never reaches a knocker as a bare code: the doorbell fails as an internal error instead.'

openQuestions.whyOpen: The canon is behind the code: the plane's catalogue now has plain-language translations for both refusals, yet the doctrine still says none exist, so what the knocker sees has been drafted by a builder and never reviewed. Nothing on the member side exists: refusals are not stored, so members cannot learn their doorbell is saturated, although the RATE_GLOBAL wording tells the knocker 'the group's members can be told'. There is also no public knock page, only the programme call.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Nothing for the knocker (no public knock form); members see the inbox list on the setup page with 'Mark as taken up' and 'Set aside', and nothing about refused knocks.
related: Q2 how a knock becomes part of the record

options.option: Adopt the plane's existing translations with the stated bound and a 'try again after' hint for the knocker; members see nothing.
options.tradeoffs: Cheap and consistent with 'nothing is counted'; the RATE_GLOBAL wording's promise to members becomes false and should be removed.

options.option: Record a count-only saturation signal (no fingerprints, no content) and show members a condition 'the doorbell turned people away N times today'.

brief.title: When the doorbell is full: what the sender and the group are told
brief.inOneBreath: Now that the doorbell's inbox, limits, gatekeeper and discard archive are set, should the group be able to see how often its doorbell turned people away?
brief.decision: Whether the system keeps a count-only tally of knocks it turned away (a daily total for the whole doorbell, how often the whole-doorbell limit was reached, and when last; no addresses, fingerprints or content), shown as status on the inbox page, or records nothing. With the limits now 5 and 10, a busy day will reach the whole-doorbell limit far more often, which makes the tally more useful.
brief.alreadyDecidedPart: On 1 October you ruled: the doorbell's inbox reads like an email inbox: unhandled knocks highlighted, handled ones still visible, sortable by time, status, whether the knocker presented a secret, the project affected, and so on. The limits are at most 5 knocks from one source and 10 in total in any 10 minutes, and a would-be knocker is made aware whenever a limit is in effect, so nobody believes they knocked when they did not. A group may enable a gatekeeper (machine work) that identifies and dismisses obvious spam and denial-of-service submissions. Discarded knocks go to an archive, in case a gem is buried in the flood, cleared automatically a week after receipt.
basics: The doorbell is the one way into a group's copy of Civicsmith that needs no account: anyone may hand the group a document. Each hand-over is a 'knock', and the person is the 'knocker'. It exists because a group whose purpose is accountability must be reachable by people who will not or cannot join it, whistleblowers above all.

A knock writes one row in the group's inbox: the bytes, their fingerprint, the time, an optional note and an optional contact. Nothing enters the record until a signed-in member reads it and pulls it in, or discards it.

To stop one sender or a flood filling the inbox, the doorbell limits knocks: at most 12 from one sender and 300 in total in any 10 minutes. 'One sender' means one connecting internet address, kept only as a keyed fingerprint that cannot be turned back into the address. Over a limit, the sender gets a refusal (the web's standard 'too many requests' answer) with a plain explanation and the published limit. Nothing about a refused knock is stored, and it does not count toward the limits.

Since 29 September, a source who gave a knocker secret can also use it, with no account, to consent to (or withdraw consent from) publishing a detail about themselves, such as their job title. Each such attempt counts against the same limits as a knock.

An analogy: a public comment portal that goes down on the last day of a comment period. The commission wants to know it happened, even without knowing who was turned away, so it can extend the deadline or open another channel.
today: Built: both limits, the published statement of each ('at most 12 knocks from one source in any 10 minutes, estimated by a sliding window', and 300 for the whole doorbell), and a plain explanation for each refusal. Those explanations were drafted by a builder and never reviewed by you or Design. The doctrine's status line still says they do not exist yet; that line is out of date.

The explanation for the whole-doorbell limit ends: 'If it keeps happening, the group's members can be told the doorbell is saturated.' Nothing records refusals, so nobody can tell them. The sentence promises something the system does not do.
Neither explanation tells the sender when to try again; both say the limit 'lifts on its own shortly'.
What members see: on the old setup page, a list of knocks with 'Mark as taken up' and 'Set aside'. Nothing about refused knocks. There is no designed public page for knocking yet.

A correction to the previous brief: it argued for counting refusals because the doctrine says a refusal is 'a claim that needs a count behind it'. That sentence means something narrower: the system may only tell someone they knocked too often when a real count shows it, and a storage failure must never be reported as a rate refusal. It does not by itself argue for keeping a tally.
problem: A flood is the case that matters. A hostile party who wants to stop a whistleblower reaching the group can send 300 knocks every 10 minutes from many addresses and keep the doorbell full for hours. The whistleblower is turned away, and so is a source trying to consent to publication. The members see a quiet inbox and conclude nothing is coming. They have no reason to post another way in, such as a lawyer's address or a drop box.

Recording anything about refused knocks changes what the record holds about members of the public. Even a bare total is a fact about public activity, and a record can be subpoenaed. That is why it is your call under the intake doctrine and not Design's.
Whatever you choose, the current refusal text should match it. A sentence that promises members will be told, when they cannot be, is a small but real breach of the record's honesty to the public.
Your rulings against nagging (10 August) and on reminders (29 September) bear on how members are told, if at all: status where the thing lives is fine; a pushed message is not.

story.title: The flooded doorbell during the port contract hearing
steps: A group is investigating a disputed port maintenance contract. The week of the council hearing, a hostile party floods its doorbell from dozens of addresses.

Lena, a port employee, tries to send a second internal memo. She sees: 'This group's inbox is not taking any more material from anyone just now… it lifts on its own shortly.' She tries twice more over three hours and gives up.
Under the current text, her refusal adds: 'If it keeps happening, the group's members can be told the doorbell is saturated.' They cannot be.
With no tally, Andre, who handles the inbox, sees a normal day's three knocks and nothing else.
With a tally, the inbox page shows him: 'Turned away 4,180 knocks today (whole doorbell full 9 times; last at 14:05). Nothing is known about who sent them.'
Andre posts on the group's public site that sources can also reach them through their lawyer, and Lena does.

fixed.point: Limits: 12 per sender and 300 in total in any 10 minutes, published with how they are estimated; the statement travels with each refusal.
fixed.why: The doorbell's limit rule, 24 September.
fixed.src: Intake Doctrine §2a; capture R31, R47, R48

fixed.point: A refused knock stores nothing and counts toward neither limit; a refusal explanation never reaches a sender as a bare code.
fixed.why: As built.

fixed.point: A storage failure is reported as silence, never as a rate refusal.
fixed.why: The doctrine's rule that a 'too many' claim needs a real count behind it.

fixed.point: A knock's source is an unnamed knocker; the contact stays in the inbox and never enters the record.
fixed.why: Your ruling of 29 September.

fixed.point: Consent by knocker secret counts against the same limits.
fixed.why: The sources requirements folded on 30 September.

fixed.point: Signals are recorded, noticed (status where the thing lives) or actionable (a queue item); there is no outside channel such as email.
fixed.why: Your three dispositions (1 August) and your ruling of 29 September.

options.howItWorks: No tally. The sender's explanation loses its promise to members, and gains an estimated retry time where one can be computed ('try again after about 14:20').
options.inTheStory: Lena sees an accurate refusal and a retry time; Andre sees nothing unusual all day.
gains: Nothing about the public is stored.
No new requirement.
costs: The group never learns of floods or of the sources it lost.
An attacker can silence the doorbell unnoticed.
options.commitsYouTo: Striking one sentence; Design reviews the two explanations.

options.label: B
options.name: A count-only status on the inbox page
options.howItWorks: The system keeps a daily total of refusals for the whole doorbell, how many times the whole-doorbell limit was reached, and when last. No addresses, fingerprints, times of individual knocks or content. Members see it as status on the inbox page. The sender's text says, truthfully, that the group can see how often its doorbell turns people away.
options.inTheStory: Step 5: Andre sees the total and posts another way in.
gains: The group learns of floods and can respond.
Reveals nothing about any single sender.
costs: 'Nothing is counted' becomes 'only a daily total', which needs a requirement change and a privacy check.
A small new fact about public activity is kept and could be requested in litigation.
options.commitsYouTo: A requirement for the tally and its privacy limits; Design for the status line and the two explanations.

options.label: C
options.name: B, plus one queue item when it lasts
options.howItWorks: As B. In addition, when the whole-doorbell limit holds for, say, an hour, administrators get one queue item: 'The doorbell has been full for an hour.'
options.inTheStory: Andre's administrator sees the item without opening the inbox page.
gains: Reaches administrators who never open the inbox page.
costs: Closer to nagging, though a single item for something a member can act on fits the 'actionable' kind.
More to design.

brief.tradeoff: Storing nothing at all about the public, against giving the group the one fact it needs to notice that someone is silencing its doorbell.

why: The doorbell exists so that people who cannot join can still reach the group. A flood that silently defeats that purpose is the one failure the group must be able to see, and a whole-doorbell daily total tells them without saying anything about any sender.
Showing it as status on the inbox page, not a queue item, keeps to your rulings against nagging. C can be added later if groups miss it.

Whatever you choose, the promise in today's refusal text should be made true (B or C) or struck (A). This is my recommendation, not canon; the privacy check of the tally is BOB's to do before it is built.

openQuestions.question: When someone installs and claims a group's copy of Civicsmith, what should they be told about the fact that whoever controls the hosting account can take over the whole copy, and should that stay visible to administrators afterwards?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Losing or leaking it has costs the group should understand at claim time.
openQuestions.context: When a group installs Civicsmith, the installer produces a one-time password (technically the ADMIN_TOKEN) and the founder uses it to 'claim' the copy and set their own password. Whoever controls the group's hosting account can reset that token and take the instance back, which makes the hosting account the real 'root of trust'.

canonSays.says: What a root of trust should be is deferred until 'a BIO instance running with MULTIPLE MEMBERS' shows what a real group can hold; the alternative is to 'document the limit honestly, which is what is happening by default.'
'Whoever can set ADMIN_TOKEN can take the group over... The holders of ADMIN_TOKEN are the root of trust.'
Hosting access should be separated from administrator status; 'no interface may imply otherwise' than that governance cannot decide who runs the machine.
The token has no custody model, no audit trail and no rotation short of returning the instance to unclaimed; until designed, root of trust means 'whoever controls the hosting account'.

openQuestions.whyOpen: Bob has deferred the policy, so the design can only explain the current arrangement, but no text decides how much to say or when. The current claim page frames the hosting sign-in only as a reassuring way back in ('you are not locked out'), while §4.6 says the same power lets anyone holding it take the group over, and §4.8 forbids an interface that implies governance controls the machine. What the founder must be told, and whether to acknowledge it, is unwritten.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The setup page tells the founder that losing the password is recoverable by replacing ADMIN_TOKEN in Cloudflare ('Your Cloudflare sign-in is the way back in'), and says nothing about takeover risk or who should hold hosting access.
related: UC-030 verified export gated on the token

options.option: A short plain explainer at claim: who holds the hosting account holds the group; keep it separate from administrators; what losing or leaking it costs.
options.tradeoffs: Honest and cheap; adds reading at a moment founders want to get started.

options.option: A standing 'custody' card in administrator settings that restates the risk and shows when the token last changed (the plane can detect a change).
options.tradeoffs: Keeps the fact visible beyond day one; the detected change is only partial evidence.

openQuestions.recommendation: Adopt the explainer at claim plus the standing custody card, and correct the claim page's one-sided reassurance; leave any acknowledgement act until DEC-2's trigger fires.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob for what the group is told about a policy he deferred (a doctrine-adjacent disclosure); Design for placement and wording once he agrees.

brief.title: What the founder is told about who really controls the group's copy
brief.inOneBreath: When someone installs and claims a group's copy of Civicsmith, what should they be told about the fact that whoever controls the hosting account can take over the whole copy, and should that stay visible to administrators afterwards?
brief.decision: (1) Whether the claim page tells the founder the whole truth about the hosting account's power, not only that it is a way back in. (2) Whether the same explanation stays visible in administrator settings, with who the group recorded as holding hosting access. (3) Whether anyone must record that they read it. This is only about what the group is told; it does not reopen how custody should work, which you deferred.
basics: Each group runs its own copy of Civicsmith in a hosting account at Cloudflare, a cloud provider. The Civicsmith project does not host it; the group's own account does.

Installing and claiming: a setup wizard creates the copy and shows a one-time password. The founder, the person installing, opens the new copy, types the one-time password and chooses a real password, becoming its first administrator. The one-time password is stored as a setting inside the hosting account.

The power that follows: anyone who can sign in to the hosting account can replace that setting. That returns the copy to 'unclaimed', and whoever claims it next becomes its administrator, able to read everything in the working record (confidential sources included), make the full export of the group's working material, which is gated on exactly this credential, and shut everyone else out. The membership design says it plainly: whoever can set the one-time password 'can take the group over', its holders 'are the root of trust for that group', and 'membership does not and cannot constrain them'.

'Root of trust' means the one power everything else rests on and nothing inside the system can overrule. An analogy: a board can vote an officer out, but whoever holds the signature card on the bank account can still move the money until the bank is told. Administrator votes inside Civicsmith are the board; the hosting account is the bank.

'Custody' means how a group holds that power: how many people, who, how it is changed, and how changes are logged. On 31 July you deferred designing custody until a real group with several members shows what it can manage, and said meanwhile to document the limit honestly. That record also notes the question had been re-raised more than once. This brief does not re-raise it; it asks only what the founder and administrators are told.
today: Under the password fields, the claim page shows this card: “If you ever lose the password you choose here, you are not locked out. Sign in to Cloudflare, replace the [one-time password's technical name] value in this worker's settings, and this claim step starts over. Your Cloudflare sign-in is the way back in.” The wizard's final screen says the same. Nothing mentions takeover, using a personal login, or sharing the account with a second person.

The canon already asks more than the screen says: holding the power must be a deliberate, named arrangement shared by at least two people and transferable; the hosting account must never be one person's personal login; hosting access and administrator status should be held by different people where a group can manage it; and no screen may imply that the administrators' rules bound this power.

Some of this is built. When a second administrator is added, the group is asked to record who holds hosting access, and the record keeps the answer. Removing the founder as administrator is refused, naming the hosting account as the remedy. When any administrator is removed, the answer says that the other half is replacing the one-time password and reviewing who can sign in to hosting.
The copy can tell that its one-time password has changed (it then offers re-claiming, under a 'Recovery mode' notice) but keeps no history of who changed it or when.
The claim page belongs to the system itself, not to the old member app you ruled on 30 September should be left alone, so changing its wording does not touch that app.
problem: The current wording is true but one-sided. It tells the founder the account is a safety net, and not that it is also the master key. The founder is the one person who chooses whose login hosts the copy, and they choose at claim time, usually alone and in a hurry. A personal login chosen then is hard to undo later.

What goes wrong: a founder uses a personal account and later leaves after a dispute, or becomes unreachable, or has the personal login phished. In each case one person, or a stranger, holds the whole group's record, including the identities of confidential sources. The group's administrators cannot fix it from inside Civicsmith.
Who is affected: confidential sources first, then members, then the group's credibility. A leaked full export is the worst event the system can suffer, and it runs through this account.

Why decide now: the redesign's setup and administrator screens are being designed, and the claim page is used on every install today. Onboarding as a whole is deferred until the redesign settles, but this is one paragraph on an existing page, not onboarding.
Decided badly the other way: a wall of warnings at setup frightens a founder who just wants to start, or wording implies a safeguard that does not exist, which the canon forbids.

story.title: Keisha, the Fruitvale tenants' group and a personal login
steps: Keisha installs her tenants' group's copy using the Cloudflare login she already has for her personal blog. The claim page says, 'Your Cloudflare sign-in is the way back in,' and she feels reassured.
The group grows to eight members. A city housing inspector becomes a confidential source; his name is in the working record, restricted to two members.
When Marcus is added as second administrator, the copy asks who holds hosting access. Keisha types 'Keisha'.
A year later, after a dispute, Keisha leaves. The administrators vote to remove her, and the copy refuses: she is the founder, and the remedy is the hosting account. It is her personal account.
She could replace the one-time password, claim the copy afresh and read or export everything. Even if she never would, her blog login could be phished.

Under the recommended option, the claim page told Keisha at the start to use an account belonging to the group and add a second trusted person. She set one up with Marcus as a second account member. At step 4, the group simply removes her from that account, and the record shows who held it all along.

fixed.point: Custody design is deferred until a real group with several members shows what it can hold; meanwhile the limit is documented honestly.
fixed.why: Your ruling of 31 July.

fixed.point: Whoever can set the one-time password is the root of trust; membership cannot constrain them; holding it should be deliberate, named, shared by at least two and transferable.
fixed.why: The membership design confirmed in July.

fixed.point: Hosting access is separate from administrator status; never one person's personal login; no screen may imply governance controls the machine.
fixed.why: The same design, §4.8.

fixed.point: When a second administrator is added, the group records who holds hosting access.
fixed.why: Built from §4.8's 'when this is enforced'.

fixed.point: Removing the founder is refused, naming the hosting account; an ejection's answer names the other half (replace the password, review hosting access).
fixed.why: Built from §4.6 and §4.8.

fixed.point: The full export of the working material requires this credential, not administrator status.
fixed.why: The membership and publication designs: an export any administrator could run would be the easiest attack.

openQuestions.question: Should the queue's three kinds of item each get a plain name, its own look and its own buttons, and a link to where that kind of work lives, while staying one list?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Bob ruled they deserve different treatment; each has its own home beyond the queue.
openQuestions.context: The queue is the member's daily list of 'things that want me', grouped by the case they belong to. It holds three classes of item: obligations (work assigned to someone), findings (something the system noticed, like a missing step in a declared flow) and conditions (signals about the system's own work, such as a capture waiting). Bob ruled they are one list but deserve different treatment, and each also has a home of its own elsewhere in the product.

canonSays.says: 'The QUEUE stays ONE surface'; findings compose into a case, obligations populate a flow model of the institution, conditions accumulate into a signal history 'mostly read as status on the thing'.
Recorded (never surfaces), noticed (surfaces as status where the thing lives), actionable (earns a queue item).
The queue class FINDING is shown to members as 'Noticed', its code unchanged.

Order is obligations, findings, conditions; obligations are member tasks and bias debt; a finding 'never reads as an obligation' and leaves only by a recorded disposition; conditions can only be muted.

openQuestions.whyOpen: K356 settles the finding class's label but not the treatment of the three. brief.title: The queue's three kinds of item: names, look and where each leads
brief.inOneBreath: Should the queue's three kinds of item each get a plain name, its own look and its own buttons, and a link to where that kind of work lives, while staying one list?
brief.decision: (1) The three names members see: 'To do' (settled by question 25), 'Noticed' (already ruled), and for the third kind 'Signal' (recommended) or 'Status', replacing today's 'Condition'. (2) That each kind is shown differently, with its own icon and wording, its own buttons and a link to its home, while the queue stays one list in its present order. The detailed look then goes to Design.
brief.alreadyDecidedPart: On 1 August you ruled that the queue stays one list ('things that want me, grouped by case') but that its three kinds are presented and treated differently, each with a home beyond the queue. On 29 September you ruled that the record-noticed kind is shown as 'Noticed'. Other rulings fix how particular items behave: a conflict inside the record is a to-do that cannot be muted, while a possible conflict not yet determined is a lead; reminders are only those a member asked for; a nearing deadline changes only the display; an overdue deadline notifies once.
basics: The queue is each member's list of things that want their attention, grouped by the case (inquiry or project) they belong to. Every item is one of three kinds, and the kinds differ in who acts and how an item leaves the list.

To-dos (labelled 'Obligation' today): something a named member must do for the work to proceed, such as judging a plan checkpoint or resolving a conflict in the record. The assignee acts or forwards it. It cannot be muted, and once done it leaves everyone's list.

Noticed items (internally 'findings'): something the record noticed about the world or about the record that nobody has judged yet, such as minutes that never appeared after a meeting, or a source document that changed. Anyone able to judge it takes it up as a question, defers it, or sets it aside with a reason; that decision is recorded with its author. A member may also mute it for themselves only.

Signals (labelled 'Condition' today): mostly facts about the system's own machinery, such as a capture paused because a city website is limiting requests, plus, since the Action work, the other side's passed deadline. Usually nobody must act; a member can acknowledge or mute it for themselves. Most signals never reach the queue at all: on 1 August you set three dispositions, recorded only, shown as status where the thing lives, or worth a queue item because a member's action can change it.

Each kind's 'home' beyond the queue, as you ruled on 1 August: noticed items build into a case; obligations into a model of how the institution is supposed to work, declared against observed; signals into a history read mostly as status on the thing itself. You also accepted that the kinds are sorted by meaning, not by loudness, with no warning and error colour ladder.
today: The current app shows one list grouped by case, to-dos first, then noticed items, then signals, each with a small chip reading 'Obligation', 'Noticed' or 'Condition' (labels the system itself publishes). Buttons differ by kind: to-dos offer 'Resolve' and 'Forward…' or the kind's own act (judge a checkpoint, revoke a key); noticed items offer 'Adopt as a question', defer, 'Dismiss…' with a reason, and a personal mute; signals offer 'Mute'. A member can select several items and act on them at once.

About fifty kinds of item are defined: twelve to-do kinds, twenty-six noticed kinds and thirteen signal kinds. Many have no producer yet; the Action work being built now adds new ones in all three kinds.

Of the three homes, the case exists. The institution's flow model is designed in outline but not built. The signal history has no design and no requirement. So today the queue cannot point into two of its three homes.
problem: Three word clashes sit in the current labels. First, 'Obligation' names the group's own to-dos while you ruled it means a public body's duty (question 25). Second, 'Condition' is also one of the auditor's elements of a finding (criteria, condition, cause, effect) that you adopted on 29 September for published findings of the 'rule required X, body did Y' kind; there 'condition' means what the body actually did, the opposite of a note about our machinery. Third, 'Noticed' in the queue is not the same as 'noticed' in the 1 August note, where it names signals shown only as status and never in the queue. The third clash is internal vocabulary the architecture session can fix itself; the first two are on members' screens.

The homes need one correction, in my reading. The 1 August note says to-dos populate the institution's flow model. But by your correction the same day, that model is the body's duties, and its gaps (a missing step, a late step) reach the queue as noticed items, not to-dos. A to-do's natural home is the thing it acts on: the plan for a checkpoint, the action for a reminder, the member list for a key. This is my judgement from the sources; it does not change any ruling, but it decides where each 'open' link goes.

Why now: the redesigned queue is being designed, and members learn these names once. If the kinds look alike, members either treat everything as a to-do (and feel nagged, against your no-nagging ruling) or treat everything as ignorable (and miss real duties); and the system's own plumbing dilutes the record's findings, the reason the 1 August note gave for never merging noticed items and signals.

brief.title: Does Civicsmith connect to the network's directory, forum and 'working on' signals?
brief.inOneBreath: Should Civicsmith itself talk to the Believe in Oakland network's shared directory, forum and 'working on' signals, or leave them to the network's own websites?
brief.decision: (1) Do the directory of published work, the cross-group forum and 'working on' signals stay outside Civicsmith, with at most links out, or does Civicsmith submit to them and show what they say? (2) If 'working on' signals ever come inside Civicsmith, what does 'anonymous-compatible' mean for a group whose only public identity is its name?
basics: Believe in Oakland is the wider network of independent civic groups, with no headquarters. Civicsmith is the software one group uses to investigate and publish; each group's copy is its own and speaks outward only by publishing signed cases.

The network's platform plan names three shared functions, each on its own platform so none is essential. A forum: a self-hosted Discourse discussion site (Discourse is open-source forum software) where groups find each other and debate methods. Hosting: each group publishes wherever it likes, with a stable public link. A directory at believeinoakland.org: a searchable index of all published work, open to submissions without pre-approval, showing an automated metadata check and community flags (flagged entries stay visible), downloadable so anyone can mirror it.

'Working on' signals, per the Roadmap: 'lightweight directory entries. Optional, anonymous-compatible, no ownership implied.' They help groups avoid duplication and hand off leads; 'no group owns an issue'.

Civicsmith already serves a public, login-free index of each group's published cases that anyone can read and verify. A group's only public identity is its short name, the slug. And by the 'tell discipline', any act visible outside the group says so at the moment it is taken.
today: Nothing in Civicsmith connects to the three. The publication design records that nothing built serves the directory; when last checked the directory's domain was not serving, and whether it or the forum runs today is not recorded.

The canon pulls two ways: the Roadmap's early interface sketch put forum threads and 'working on' signals inside the app; the later platform plan and design requirements put them on network sites. Nothing reconciles the two.

Nearby: other groups' work carries an origin mark (29 September); an action may be addressed to another civic group, and joint action waits until a coalition asks (30 September); your 29 September design for conflicts between projects kept to notification replies, with no discussion thread or general messaging.
problem: The use cases for finding related work, listing a case and signalling interest have no requirement, so the redesign has nothing to build to; members do it by hand.

Building Civicsmith around believeinoakland.org cuts against the network's own rule that no platform is essential: a takedown of the site should not break publishing, and a group elsewhere may use another directory.

A 'working on' signal tells the public, including the officials being examined, what a group is investigating before any case exists, in a network designed for active opposition. 'Anonymous-compatible' is undefined: an anonymous signal cannot carry the group's name, and then cannot be told from astroturf.
The redesign is drawing the publishing flow and home screen now; whether a 'list in directory' step or 'related work' panel belongs there depends on this.

ruled.title: The network: believeincities.org, 'working on' notices, and keeping them honest
ruled.decided: The network's directory and forum stay outside Civicsmith: after publishing, a member gets links out and a prefilled directory submission, after the warning; nothing is sent automatically. Inside Civicsmith, a project's owner may tell the network the group is working on something, but only from a project defined as working on the issue, after a warning that the public, including anyone being examined, will see it and that stopping later won't unsay it. The notice names the group by its slug (never its members; there are no anonymous notices) and carries the owner's own wording, optionally naming the public body and the matter; 'Working on this since', a date no earlier than the project's creation and no later than today; the date posted; an activity level in five steps (Very active, Active, Some work, Quiet, Dormant) counted from the weeks in the last 13 with real work by members, never the assistant's and never by volume, by a published method and re-signed monthly; 'Interested in collaborating' with a link to knock, only if the owner chooses; and links to any case the project published. Nothing else from the project's private work. Each counted week gets an independent timestamp on a sealed summary of its work, opened when the project publishes. An owner signs the notice as a case is signed, and it is published at the group's own public address, whose page lists its owners' public keys without names. Stopping says so, with an optional handoff note; a notice Dormant for a further month lapses. As holder of the domains, Bob set the network site's policy: the directory lives at believeincities.org/<place> (believein.city for short; believeinoakland.org redirects to /oakland), reads notices where groups publish them, records when it first saw each and keeps them all, and shows each as Stated (typed by hand; lapses after 60 days), Reported (signed by a group's copy) or Proven (its seals opened at publication). A group's record is facts, never a score; notices on the same matter sit side by side, each saying others are welcome; public pages never say 'claim'; impossible combinations are flagged; a group with no published work may have at most two open notices. The screens are Design's.

openQuestions.question: Should each finding on a published case open with one plain line about the standard it met before the detailed grades, and should the printed edition carry every layer of explanation however long it gets?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Readers know least; print loses interactivity and must carry the full narrative.
openQuestions.context: Published cases are read by the public, journalists, officials and other groups, who know the least about Civicsmith. A case reports each finding's strength on two separate axes (how directly the documents are held, and how strongly the links between them are established), letter grades A-D, and 'look states' saying what was searched and what nobody looked at. Bob wants this explained in layers on screen, and the printed version must carry the whole story without interactivity.

canonSays.says: Interactive story visuals extend to the published surface, 'where readers know the least, so progressive disclosure matters most there. The PRINTED version... is first-class and must carry the full narrative, progressively explained and documented'.
No answer composes a case-level strength: every pair is per member and per axis.
The published case carries scope, completeness, bias acknowledgement, the bar with its words, each member's pair and grounds; undetermined is stated, never filled.
Absence has five states (NEVER_LOOKED, LOOKED_ABSENT, LOOKED_INDETERMINATE, PARTIAL, PRESENT); the completeness statement's search record is designed, not built.
Letters grade evidence, bars show progress, weights mark acts; every grade and bar step opens its meaning on hover, focus or tap; colour marks the scale, never the value.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The canon demands layered explanation and a full printed narrative but defines neither the layers nor the words. Readers expect one overall score, while DEC-44 forbids combining the two axes, so the explanation must teach why there is no single number. brief.alreadyDecidedPart: Your measures map (29 September) sets words and forms for every grade: each mark opens to its plain question, colour marks the scale, never the value, and no combined score appears. For members' workspaces you approved a phrase against the bar ('Meets the bar', 'Short on connection'). On 28 July you said readers need layered explanation most, and print is first-class and carries the full narrative.
basics: A published case is a project's signed argument, read by those who know least about Civicsmith: residents, reporters, officials, other groups. It is made of findings; load-bearing ones are relied on, supporting ones are included but not relied on.

Each finding has two grades, A to D, never combined: capture (how well documents are held) and connection (how firmly links are established). A finding is only as strong as its weakest document and weakest link, counted separately.

The bar is the project's declared minimum per axis. Publishing is refused if a load-bearing finding falls short on a declared axis, so on a published case every load-bearing finding meets the bar by rule; only supporting findings can be short, and the bar may be low, partial or absent. A verdict line therefore means something different here than in a member's workspace.
Layers (progressive disclosure) mean a short answer first, detail a click away. Print loses the clicks, so whatever the screen hides must be printed.

The signed case also carries 'What was searched': for the case's subjects, how many were looked at, never looked at, or undetermined. The five gap terms are fixed: Undetermined, Withheld, Unrated, Nobody looked, Refused.
today: The signed case already carries each finding's grades and grounds, the bar in words, each document's grade and co-attestation, 'What was searched' and disclosed contradictions. The earlier brief said the search record could not appear yet; that is out of date, though an older design table still lists it as not built.

The old public page opens: 'A case does not have a strength. It has two, and they are never combined, averaged or scored against each other.' It states the bar, or 'NONE WAS DECLARED … an absent bar is not a bar of zero'. Its print version puts the identifying notice first, expands everything collapsed, and adds each link's full address and fingerprint. The redesigned page is not built.
problem: Readers expect one score; your rule forbids one. A plain first line helps readers who will never compare letters to a bar. But a bare 'Meets the bar' reads like a certificate, especially for a D/D or one-axis bar, and on a published case it would appear on every load-bearing finding by rule, adding nothing unless it names the bar.
In print nothing can be clicked. A large case with every layer may run to dozens of pages; cutting it breaks your 28 July principle, keeping it needs an order a reader can stop in.
The redesign's public page and print are being designed now, and these are the two points the measures map does not cover.

ruled.title: The forms of a published case: the public page, the complete edition and the case file
ruled.decided: The test of a published case is that anybody can review it, and even recreate it, without Civicsmith. It comes in three forms. The public page: each finding opens with one line naming its role and the project's bar ('Relied on · meets this project's bar (capture B, connection C)'), never a bare 'meets', then its two grades, then the detail; the strength section opens 'a case has two strengths, never one'. The complete edition (what was called print): a self-contained file anyone can open with nothing to install, with no length limit, ordered so a reader can stop early, carrying every layer, the grading method and 'How to check this case yourself'; every page carries the identifying notice, and printing is incidental. The case file: the complete structured record in a published, versioned format rich enough that the results can be recreated, holding the complete edition, every document and observation a conclusion rests on (whole, with its extracted text), the findings' chains, attestations, signatures, and the method version inside the signed case; split into parts, never trimmed; an open specification and a standalone open checker let anyone recreate it. Everything a conclusion rests on must be presentable: publishing is refused while a relied-on finding rests on material that cannot travel whole; the warning says the case republishes these documents and that judging whether they may be is the group's. An off-the-record source's material travels whole with its attestations (member, project, group); only the identity is withheld, labelled 'Withheld' with its reason. Evidence from a member credited only at the group or project level counts as anonymous and cannot carry a relied-on finding without independent corroboration, including when that member attests an off-the-record source. Another group's copy imports a case file into a new, read-only project, and the system confirms each finding by recreating it: Recreated, Recreated in part (naming what is missing) or Did not recreate (naming what differs), shown also against the importing group's own bar. Recreating is not endorsing; the group may accept an edition only for recreated findings, and an accepted finding may support its own work, marked as another group's. The screens are Design's.
