brief.settledSince: Your answer of 1 October settled the act: 'hold in place' or 'hold released', with a reason, recorded by a member, clears the reminder. It is built. What the hold stops, how far it reaches, what members see and whether it blocks the wipe remain open.
brief.title: The litigation hold: what placing it stops, how far it reaches, and what it blocks
brief.inOneBreath: Now that a member can record 'hold in place' on a reply marked as a legal threat, should that record actually stop the scheduled deletion of assistant transcripts on members' devices, for which projects, with what shown to members, and should it block the operator's wipe of the group's record?
brief.decision: (1) Whether recording 'hold in place' itself stops both scheduled deletions of assistant transcripts on members' devices (at the time limit and at publication), once those deletions are built. (2) How far it reaches: the threatened action's project, with other projects named by the member who places it, or the whole group. (3) Who may place and release it (today any member who can see the action), and whether releasing, which would restart deletion, is heavier than placing. (4) What members see while a hold is in place. (5) Whether the operator's wipe of the real record is refused while any hold is in place.
brief.alreadyDecidedPart: You ruled on 1 October that the litigation-hold reminder is cleared by a member's own, named act on the reply marked as a legal threat: 'hold in place' or 'hold released', always with a written reason. That act is the reminder's only way out. Each statement is kept, never rewritten, and the latest one stands; no machine can make it. BOB read your 'a member's act' as any member who can see the action, with the reminder going to the administrators and to the member who marked the threat.
basics: A group (say, a neighbourhood budget watchdog) runs its own copy of Civicsmith. Members work in projects, some hidden from outsiders; a project may publish a case, the group's public account of what it found. A few members are administrators, who look after membership and settings.

An action is one outward engagement with an addressee, such as a records request to a city department; members record what was sent and what came back. Since your ruling of 30 September that Civicsmith is prepared for opposition, a member can mark a received reply as pressure: legal (a threat to sue, a subpoena, a demand to preserve records), retaliation, discrediting or other. The mark is kept as evidence.

A member's session with the AI assistant produces a transcript: the assistant's working notes and the conversation. On 6 August you ruled that transcripts are internal notes, like a reporter's notebook: kept only on the member's own device, never in the shared record; deleted after a set time; and deleted when the work is published. The reason was subpoena protection: the group's hosting company can be served directly, sometimes without the group knowing, while a member's device can only be reached through the member, who can contest the demand.

The same ruling said why that deletion is safe only until a lawsuit is in view. Deleting on a schedule fixed in advance is defensible; deleting once litigation is reasonably expected is spoliation (destruction of evidence), treated far worse than whatever the material showed. So once the group is on notice, both deletions must stop for relevant material: a litigation hold, the duty a utility has to switch off its email auto-delete once a complaint is in view.
today: Built in the engine on 1 October (the old interface shows none of it): a reply marked as a legal threat sends one reminder to every administrator and to the member who marked it: 'a legal threat was recorded on [the action] and no litigation hold is stated for it', with one button, 'Record whether a litigation hold is in place'. It is shown once and leaves only when a member records 'hold in place' or 'hold released' with a reason, even if the action has closed.

Any member who can see the action may record either statement, not only an administrator. 'Released' covers both 'we have stopped preserving' and 'no hold was needed'. Each letter marked as a legal threat needs its own statement. The statements are listed on the action; nothing else shows them.

The statement suspends nothing; the requirement says so plainly, leaving the transcript deletion as a separate matter on the devices. That matter does not exist yet: nothing writes transcripts to devices or deletes them, and no time limit is set, so nothing is being destroyed today. As far as I can find, those two transcript deletions are the only scheduled deletions in Civicsmith.

The operator's wipe of the group's whole record (used to reset it) still runs while a hold is in place, and erases the hold statements too. With no email or push, a device learns of anything only when its member next opens Civicsmith.
problem: Your August ruling requires deletion to stop once the group is on notice. Your October ruling created the moment of notice: a named member saying 'hold in place', for a reason, on a dated threat. The link between the two is missing. Left separate, the group can record 'hold in place' while devices go on deleting: a written admission of notice followed by destruction, the worst position in a dispute.

Reach is the second tension. The statement sits on one reply in one project. Too narrow, and related notes in another project keep being deleted after notice, which a court may sanction. Too broad, and unrelated notes pile up for months, reachable by exactly the demand the device-only rule resists, and a group-wide notice may reveal a hidden project's trouble.

Who may release now matters more than who may place. Placing only keeps things. Releasing would restart deletions that cannot be undone, and today it is as light as placing and anyone may do it. The wipe is the third gap: it would erase both the record and the proof that a hold was placed.
Why now: the device transcript store is not yet planned, and this decides what it must do. Nothing here is legal advice; whether California's shield law reaches a civic group is for counsel.

story.title: Sam, the towing letter and Paula's laptop
steps: Eastlake Budget Watch's project 'Towing contracts' has an action: a records request to the Oakland Department of Transportation for tow-contract invoices.

On 2 October the City Attorney's office writes, disputing the group's draft findings, asking it to 'preserve all documents, notes and communications concerning the towing contract', and hinting at a defamation claim. Paula records the letter on the action and marks it as a legal threat.

Sam, an administrator, and Paula each see the reminder. Paula presses 'Record whether a litigation hold is in place', chooses 'Hold in place' and writes 'City Attorney letter of 2 Oct demands preservation.' The reminder leaves both their lists. This much is settled and built.

Paula's laptop holds three towing transcripts; the oldest reaches the time limit next week. Dev, in the separate project 'Parking citation revenue', has transcripts about the same tow operator. The towing case is due to be published on 15 October, which would delete the towing transcripts on each device.
In March the city drops the matter. Any member could record 'Hold released'. In April, Ray, who runs the group's server, plans to wipe and reload the record after a hosting move.

The decision bites at each step: whether Paula's statement keeps her transcripts, whether it reaches Dev's laptop, what Paula and Dev are told, what the release in March restarts, and whether Ray's wipe may run while the hold stands.

ruled.title: The litigation hold: what it stops, how far it reaches, and what it blocks
ruled.decided: A hold is a member's recorded statement on a reply marked as a legal threat, 'hold in place' or 'hold released', always with a reason; the latest stands, and it is the reminder's only way out. Once devices store assistant transcripts, 'hold in place' stops both scheduled deletions (at the time limit and at publication), on every member's device, for the threatened action's project (filled in automatically) and any other projects the member names; more can be added by a further statement. A device checks for a hold before deleting and deletes nothing if it cannot check. Any member who can see the action may place a hold; releasing is heavier: its form says what will be deleted and that this cannot be undone, and the administrators and whoever placed the hold are told once. Members who can see a held project see a strip: 'Litigation hold in place since 2 Oct 2026, recorded by Paula Reyes. Assistant transcripts for this project stay on your device: they are not deleted after the usual time or at publication. Please do not clear them yourself.' openQuestions.question: Now that you have retired 'bundle', what word do members (and readers of published cases) see for a single thing the record holds when the screen cannot or should not say what kind of thing it is?

brief.title: The everyday word for one thing in the record (replacing 'bundle')
brief.inOneBreath: Now that you have retired 'bundle', what word do members (and readers of published cases) see for a single thing the record holds when the screen cannot or should not say what kind of thing it is?
brief.decision: (1) The general word used when the type is unknown or must stay hidden: 'item', 'entry', or another you prefer. (2) Confirm that wherever the type is known and visible, the specific word is used instead: document, firsthand observation, question, finding, plan, action. (3) Whether 'document' covers all evidence (captured files and members' own written observations), as the draft glossary has it.
basics: Inside the system, everything the record holds is stored the same way, as a 'bundle' with an id: a captured council PDF, a member's written account of a meeting, a question the group is investigating, a finding, an action plan. The word came from the files each one is stored as.

On 26 September you called the word 'bundle' outdated. Since then, new canon and requirement text avoid it, and older files are reworded when next touched. The code's internal names (for example the id field and the table) keep it, because renaming them means a data migration, which BOB schedules separately. Members should never see internal names.

The difficulty is that one word covered two different families. Evidence: captured documents and members' firsthand observations. Analysis: questions, findings, plans and actions. Most screens know which one they are showing and can use the specific word. A few cannot, or must not.

The 'must not' case comes from your ruling of 4 August on hidden material: something a member may not see answers exactly as if it did not exist. No id, title, state, count, and not its type either. Only the fact that something is missing may be stated. So the message for a link to a hidden thing cannot say 'This question…', because that would reveal it is a question.
today: Member-facing text still uses the word in a few places. In the old interface: 'This bundle was not found.' when a link leads nowhere; tooltips such as 'no bundle has registered them'; and, on the published-case page every reader sees, 'the signature covers the bundle's hash'. Among roughly 1,060 refusal explanations in the system's catalogue, one still says 'bundle': 'The record already holds this document, under another bundle… Cite the bundle that holds it'.
The inventory's draft glossary proposes 'Document' for evidence only (a captured page or file, or a member's own written observation). It is not approved.
The next build round's plan defers renaming one internal identifier until you answer this question, because an internal rename should follow the member word.
problem: Every screen of the redesign needs words, and the generic case appears in the most sensitive places: broken or hidden links, search results that mix types, lists of 'what depends on this', and refusal messages. If no word is chosen, designers will pick one per screen and the product will speak in several voices.

A bad choice has real costs. A word that suggests evidence ('document') used for a question confuses members about what they are looking at. A word that reveals type in a hidden-link message breaks your 4 August rule. A word that collides with an existing term ('record' already means the group's whole working record) invites misreading.
Readers of published cases are affected too, since the published page's integrity paragraph uses the word.

openQuestions.question: On the action plan page, should the list of things the plan is about be headed 'Subjects' or 'Matters', given that 'Subject' already names a person, office, place, law or thing elsewhere in Civicsmith?

brief.title: What a plan is about: 'Subjects' or 'Matters'
brief.inOneBreath: On the action plan page, should the list of things the plan is about be headed 'Subjects' or 'Matters', given that 'Subject' already names a person, office, place, law or thing elsewhere in Civicsmith?
brief.decision: Choose the word members see for the things an action plan addresses, used everywhere they appear: the plan page's heading and buttons, the preview when an action starts, queue items and the glossary. The term inside the requirements stays 'subject' whichever you pick; members never see it.
basics: The Action layer is where a group decides and records what to do with what it has learned. A project keeps an action plan, its private working notes (never published). The plan lists options: a demand letter, a records request, a grand-jury complaint, a press briefing. A member chooses some and declines others with a reason. Starting a chosen option creates an action, one outward engagement that a member sends by their own hand and records.

Each plan is about one or more things, which you ruled on 29 September may be several related ones. Each is one of two kinds. A suspected one is an open question the group is still investigating, such as 'Was the measure properly certified?'. A determined one is a member's judgement that a named government act was compliant, noncompliant or unclear against one named standard, resting on published findings: 'The city's certification of the bond measure as passed, against the two-thirds vote requirement'. Each shows its support: established, short (determined, but short of the project's evidence bar) or hypothetical (suspected, not yet shown).

Elsewhere, 'Subject' already has a meaning. The Subjects screen is the record's index of people in public roles, offices, places, laws and things it knows by name and alias, such as 'City Council (office)' or 'Office of the City Clerk'. Documents are linked when they name the same subject. And 'a subject named in a case' is the office or official a case is about, who may reply before publication.
The Action canon you approved on 30 September already says 'matters' in its own prose: 'one plan may address several related matters'.
today: The plan page sketch you approved on 30 September (views/plan-page.html) heads its first section 'Subjects', with an 'Add subject' button. Options show 'serves 1 and 2', and the list sorts by 'subject'.

The other sketches already drift between the two words. The preview for starting an action lists 'Rests on: Subject 1 … Subject 3', and its refusal says 'one of the matters it rests on (subject 3)'. The matter page sketch's breadcrumb reads 'Matters'.
Nothing is built: the plan page waits for the interface redesign. The old interface's Subjects screen exists and is in use. The glossary lists both senses, with a note that the word is your decision.
problem: A member who uses the Subjects screen will read 'Subjects' on a plan as people and offices. 'Add subject' looks like 'pick the City Council'. A plan 'about' an office reads as a campaign against a body, when the group acts on what an office did. On the start preview, 'Addressed to: Office of the City Clerk' (a subject in the first sense) sits a few lines above 'Rests on: Subject 1' (a subject in the second): two meanings on one screen.

Why now: the redesign is about to draw the plan page. The word then spreads to buttons, queue items, help text and the glossary, and changing it later touches all of them. The stakes are small, but the change is cheapest now.

Honest downsides of 'Matters': it is a small change to a sketch you approved. Lawyers use 'matter' for a case ('in the matter of …'), though the everyday sense is close. And the matter page sketch uses 'matter' for a whole government act judged against several standards, while a plan's matter is one act against one standard, or an open question. That nesting needs one sentence in the glossary, or the matter page needs another name (see question 35).

story.title: Tanya and the two kinds of subject
steps: Tanya, a new member of School Bond Watch, spent the morning on the Subjects screen tagging documents that name 'City Council (office)'.
She opens the plan 'Bond measure: certification and proceeds'. Its first section reads 'Subjects · 2'.
She wants the plan to cover the council's late release of minutes too. She presses 'Add subject' and expects a list of offices. Instead she is asked for an open question or a determination's outcome.

Later she starts 'Complaint to the county civil grand jury'. The preview reads 'Addressed to: Civil Grand Jury (an office)' and 'Rests on: Subject 1: certification against the two-thirds requirement'.

She asks the group whether the grand jury is now one of the plan's subjects. Under 'Matters', the same screens read 'Matters · 2', 'Add matter' and 'Rests on: Matter 1', and the question does not arise.

openQuestions.question: Besides the plan page you approved, should the Action design's other three screen sketches (starting and sending an action, the matter page, and the sheet of standards, filings and queue items) bind the interface redesign as the plan page does, or stay examples the designer may rework?

brief.title: The other three Action sketches: fix them as the reference, or leave them to Design
brief.inOneBreath: Besides the plan page you approved, should the Action design's other three screen sketches (starting and sending an action, the matter page, and the sheet of standards, filings and queue items) bind the interface redesign as the plan page does, or stay examples the designer may rework?
brief.decision: (1) For each of the three sketches, say whether it is fixed as the design reference or left to Design. Fixed means the redesign keeps what it shows, the order of its steps and its wording; look and layout stay Design's, as for the plan page. (2) If you wish, fix only part of a sketch, for example the filing panels of the third sheet but not its queue items.
basics: The Action layer is where a group decides what to do with what it has learned. A project's action plan, its private working notes, lists options (a demand letter, a records request, a grand-jury complaint). Starting a chosen option creates an action: one outward engagement with an addressee such as the City Clerk's office. Civicsmith sends nothing itself. The assistant may draft the text as a proposal; a member edits and approves it, sends it by the venue's own means and records the sending with the exact text sent.

One rule shapes starting. An action that asserts a breach (says the government broke a rule) must rest on a member's determination, made on published findings, that the act was noncompliant. On 30 September you ruled that such an action is refused by default when it does not; a member may still proceed, by an act signed with their name and a stated reason, and then the action and everything prepared from it say it 'rests on an unestablished premise'. Actions that seek evidence, such as a records request, are never refused this way.

In the week of 29 September the Action design session drew four sample screens as clickable web pages with made-up data. You approved one, the plan page, on 30 September, leaving its look (spacing, colour, narrow screens) to Design. The interface redesign is done separately from the build, so a sketch is how your intent reaches whoever draws the screens.

The approved plan page (views/plan-page.html), for comparison: the plan's title; a 'Checks' strip in words ('no branch answers a hostile response'); the plan's subjects with their support; options collapsed to one line, sortable, with Choose and Decline and the assistant's suggestions in a separate tray marked 'not yet in the plan'; up to three scenarios of phases with checkpoints a member judges; 'Started', each action's state; and 'Close plan…'.
today: Starting and sending (views/start-and-send.html), in two steps. Step 1, 'Start "Complaint to the county civil grand jury"', begins 'Nothing runs until you confirm.' It lists what the action will say: kind (tier 1), addressed to (Civil Grand Jury, an office), rests on (subject 1 'established'; subject 3 'hypothetical: not yet shown'), clock ('none regulated for this kind'), the plan and option it came from, the group's contact (none, or a cover name) and 'Asserts a breach: yes'. Then a box, 'Would be refused': 'This action asserts a breach, and one of the matters it rests on (subject 3) is not established… You can remove subject 3, wait for its determination, untick "asserts a breach", or proceed anyway with a reason. If you proceed, the action and everything prepared from it will say so.' A reason field, 'Proceed with this reason', then 'Start the action'. Step 2, 'What the group sends': the complaint drafted from a template, labelled 'a proposal until a member approves it', each filled blank naming its source ('[source: canvass report, capture grade B, co-attested]'); a line giving each exhibit's evidence grade and the venue's standard; 'Approve this text' ('Approving fixes the bytes and adds the stamp. The instance sends nothing.'); and 'I have sent it · record the sending' ('By the venue's own means: its web form, mail, or in person').

The matter page (views/matter-page.html): one page per government act, here 'The certification of the bond measure as passed' (a resolution of 18 July, by the City Council). It has five parts. Determination: a row per standard, giving what it requires, what the act did and the outcome, with 'A compliant outcome is recorded with the same care.' Consequences: who or what was affected (a class or programme, never a person), the measure, how it is known and whether the act caused it ('Undetermined is never read as zero'). Escalation (the group's seven-stage pursuit of a breach): 'Proposed: stage 3 … The system proposes; a member decides', with Advance and Decline. Actions attached, and the legal tools available 'as facts … Nothing here is a recommendation'. Pressure recorded: a council member's statement calling the group 'saboteurs', kept as evidence, with 'Mark a reply as pressure…' and 'Open an inquiry'. The member's path written by the Action design does not name this page. It overlaps the Standards and Escalation screens already planned, and it is about a whole act, while a plan's matter is one act against one standard.

problem: If a sketch is left open, the designer may keep the rules but lose their feel. Your override ruling could become a yellow banner with a one-click 'Continue', no reason asked. openQuestions.question: Now that you have ruled who has standing and that nothing on the docket is sealed or redacted, how should the rest of a published case's docket work: its shelves and required core, how outside responses are found, kept and placed, how entries are signed and travel, and how a case is withdrawn?

brief.settledSince: Your rulings of 1 October settled who has standing (the named subject, and others a group grants it to), that the docket holds no confidential entries, that redaction is only ever the submitter's own and a redacted submission may be declined, and that off-the-record contacts need not be disclosed. The rest stays open and is what this brief asks.
brief.title: After publication: a case's docket, outside responses, and withdrawing a case
brief.inOneBreath: Now that you have ruled who has standing and that nothing on the docket is sealed or redacted, how should the rest of a published case's docket work: its shelves and required core, how outside responses are found, kept and placed, how entries are signed and travel, and how a case is withdrawn?
brief.decision: (1) The docket's shape: three shelves (what the group stands behind, 'Reactions elsewhere', and 'In our record only', never public) and its required core, including whether the subject's public statements elsewhere, such as a press release, count as required. (2) The outside-response path you asked for: find, capture with proof, link to the edition it answers, then a member's reasoned choice of record only, public docket, or both. (3) A subject's unredacted reply that names a private person: list it whole, or list only its receipt and invite the subject to resubmit (with its own redactions, which the group may then accept or decline). (4) What a grant of standing gives (the named subject's rights, or less) and whether it can be withdrawn. (5) Who adds and takes back entries and how they are signed; how the docket travels; and withdrawal: whether, what it means, who, what readers, citing groups and the subject see, and whether it can be undone.
brief.alreadyDecidedPart: On 1 October you ruled these points. (1) The subject named in a case has party-like standing: its responses that reach the group are listed on the public docket. (2) A group may also grant standing to others besides the named subject, as the CPUC grants party status; anyone without standing may still submit, and whether their submission goes on the public docket is the group's call. (3) No confidential filings: an entry is public whole, or it is not on the public docket, though the group may still keep it in its record. (4) Redaction is the submitter's alone: whoever submits may send a redacted version of their own material, but the group never redacts what others submit. The group may decline to post any submission that contains redactions, even one from the named subject, which in practice discourages redaction. (5) The group is not required to disclose its off-the-record contacts with the subject after publication.
brief.absorbNote: Question 17 (how a case's subject sees it and replies) is wholly inside this one: its 'Did we ask them?' box, linked correspondence and late replies become part of the docket. Question 18 is settled (DEC-101): every new edition carries a 'What changed, and why' statement, which the docket's 'newer edition' entry quotes, and a copy may watch other groups' editions.
basics: A case is what a project publishes: findings (questions the group has answered) with the evidence beneath them. Load-bearing findings are those the case stands on. The project's manager, by default its owner, signs each published version, an edition, with a key registered to them; each has a fingerprint, a code computed from its exact bytes, so anyone can check it. Publication is one-way: a correction is a new edition, the old one stays readable, and a citation names one edition.

Your point of 1 October: a case is a waypoint, not an end product. After publication the world responds without changing the case: the office replies, a paper writes about it, another group cites it. The proposal is a docket beside each case: dated entries, each naming the edition it concerns, growing while the signed editions never change.

How the CPUC curates its docket, which you asked about: structurally, not editorially. Only parties file formally, and party status is ruled on. The public comments on a separate shelf, which the Commission says is not evidence and not part of the formal record. The Docket Office rejects for form only, with reasons. The decision rests on a record narrower than the docket. Corrections come as new filings or decisions. Anyone can follow through the information-only service list, by email.

What carries over. Here the publishing group keeps its own docket, a built-in conflict of interest, so neutrality is replaced by rules. The docket has shelves. The first holds what the group stands behind as accurately listed (vouching that each is what it says, not agreeing with it): the subject's responses, a newer edition, corrections, a withdrawal, outcomes. The second, 'Reactions elsewhere', is labelled 'Listed by the group. Not evidence. Not endorsed.' The third, 'In our record only', is seen by members and never published.

Checks are on form, never merit: every entry is dated, attributed, names its edition and has a captured copy with its origin. A docket entry never makes anything evidence: to affect a finding, material is captured, read, made to support it, and a new edition follows. Email push does not fit: Civicsmith sends nothing. A feed does: a page at a fixed address that a reader's own software checks, with no list of readers kept.

A capture is the group's kept copy of a document's exact bytes, with where and when they came from and a grade saying how strongly that is proven. Where it can, it also has an independent archive, such as the Internet Archive, save the same page (a co-archive), so proof survives if the original is deleted. The doorbell is the group's public submission page; each submission is a knock, limited per sender and in total. Correspondence is the letters and calls recorded against one of the group's actions, such as a request for comment.

Withdrawal (in journals, retraction) is not a correction. A correction says 'here is what we now conclude'; a withdrawal says 'we no longer stand behind this'. A retracted article stays readable, stamped and linked to a notice with the reason.
today: Built: each edition page carries a banner; an older one says a newer edition exists and that it 'has not been withdrawn and still answers'; a public list of editions, each verifiable. Inside the group: the request for comment and its reply log, a reply linked to the action it answers by a 'responds to' relationship; a received letter can be marked as pressure (threat, retaliation, discrediting, legal harassment), and a legal mark prompts a litigation hold decision; action plans with checkpoints a member judges; the doorbell; capture with co-archive.

The monitor watches named documents for change; watching a listing, such as the city's press page, for new items about a case does not exist. The assistant may suggest that a held capture bears on a question, under your six guards of 29 September, but not that something responds to a case.

Not built: any docket. Today only evidence a published finding rests on may become public outside a signed case, so your ruling's public docket widens that rule by design. Pointing an outside response at a case edition, rather than at an action, is new.

Withdrawal has no act. The design rules say reversing a signed act is a further signed act, both standing; the consistency rules say a retraction sends re-evaluation notices (to members whose work rests on it). That was never built and, since 1 October, has no trigger.
problem: Shelves answer the conflict of interest only with a core the group cannot leave out. You fixed its centre, the subject's responses. One edge is open: subjects often answer in public, by press release or at Council. If that is optional, a group can list the polite letter and skip the public rebuttal; if required, the group must list what the subject says anywhere, once it has captured it.

The group may never trim what others send, and the group is never first to make a private person more public: published work names people only in their official capacity, and actions address roles, never private individuals. So when a subject's own reply names a complainant, the group cannot cut the name out. The subject can resubmit with its own redaction, which the group may accept or decline; the open point is what the group shows in the meantime, and whether it may hold back an unredacted reply at all.

Outside responses arrive scattered, rarely to the group, and some are later deleted. Without a path to find, keep, link and place them, members lose them or post them unchecked. Placement matters: a contesting article belongs in the record, where it can prompt a re-look; a threat belongs with the group's defences; only some belong in public. Republishing others' articles whole raises copyright and fairness questions.

You confirmed that a group may grant standing to others, such as a contractor the case names. What that grant gives (the same rights as the named subject, or fewer) and whether it can later be withdrawn must be settled before the first grant.

Withdrawal is a real need: if a key document proves forged, the group must say plainly it no longer stands behind the case. Today it can only publish a new edition, leaving the old one saying it 'has not been withdrawn'. Those relying on the case must be able to discover it; an erase button would be untrue, since copies exist and the bytes still verify. The re-evaluation build and the case page redesign wait on this.

story.title: The towing case, its shelves, and a forged memo
steps: Dana Reyes manages the project 'Oakland towing contract' in the Eastlake Accountability group. Edition 1, published 3 March, has two load-bearing findings: (1) the towing contractor overcharged storage fees on 1,240 tows in 2025, from invoices obtained by records request; (2) the Department of Transportation approved them without the audits the contract requires, resting on a memo left anonymously at the doorbell. The Department, the subject, did not answer the request for comment.

5 March: the group's standing watch over the city's press page sees a release, 'Transportation stands by towing oversight'. On the case page one quiet line appears: '1 new item may respond to this case. Machine work: names the towing contract and quotes finding 2.' Luis captures it, with co-archive, and links it as responding to edition 1. It is the subject speaking in public, not to the group.

9 March: a former council aide's op-ed in a local paper calls the case 'a hit job built on an anonymous memo'. Luis pastes the link; it is captured and co-archived. Dana places it on 'Reactions elsewhere': date, paper, a link to the original and to the archived copy, and two lines in the group's words, marked as theirs.

12 March: the contractor's lawyer writes, threatening a defamation suit. A member records it and marks it as legal pressure; the queue asks about a litigation hold. It stays in the record only, and becomes a checkpoint in the group's action plan: 'If the contractor sues, brief counsel within 7 days.'

20 March: the Director's office writes to the group: the audits were done but never filed with the City Clerk, and the review began with a complaint from a named resident, Mr. Tillman of East 18th Street. This is the subject's response, so it is to be listed. But it names a private person, and the group may not cut the name out.

22 March: Marisol Ortega, a resident with no standing, knocks with her own 2025 tow receipt at the schedule rate: 'finding 1 is wrong'. Rachel brings it in; as it contests a finding, a re-evaluation notice reaches finding 1's members. Her tow ran two days; the overcharges begin on day four. Finding 1 holds; Dana keeps the knock in the record only.

2 April: the Tenants' Defense Network accepts edition 1 and cites finding 1. In August the group concludes the memo is forged: its file was created two months after its date. Finding 1 stands; finding 2 does not. Eastlake's 15 March letter to a Council committee rests on edition 1.
What does a reader of the public case page see on 20 August, and what was the group obliged to put there? The options differ on the press release, the Director's letter and the withdrawal.

options.label: A
options.name: Shelved docket with a strict core; withdrawal as a signed, final notice
options.howItWorks: Shelves as in the basics. Required on the first shelf, each a To-do (a queue item that leaves only when done) for the manager: every response the subject sends; any public statement by the subject the group has captured and linked to the case; a newer edition; a withdrawal; and anything the case would have had to disclose at signing, such as an open conflict on a load-bearing finding. Outcomes are optional. Outside responses are found by a member pasting a link, by standing watches over known sources (the city's press page, Council agendas), or by the assistant's labelled suggestion under your six guards; captured with grade and co-archive; linked as responding to a named edition; then a member chooses, with a reason, record only, public, or both. In the record, a contesting response prompts a re-evaluation notice, may become a plan checkpoint, and a threat takes a pressure mark. A public 'Reactions elsewhere' entry shows date, source, links to the original and the independent archive's copy, and a short summary marked as the group's words, never the article whole. A subject's reply naming a private person is listed as received, by date, without its text and with the reason, and the subject is asked to resend it without the name; the resent version is listed whole. A group may grant standing to others by a signed entry with its reason; their responses then join the required core. Any member files to the record; only the manager places an entry in public, signing with their registered key in a short step. An entry is taken back by a later entry with a reason. Withdrawal is the manager's signed entry naming an edition or all, with a published reason; the edition stays readable under a stamp; it is never lifted, and standing behind the case again needs a new edition. The docket travels by pull: the public page, a feed per case, citing groups' copies turning entries into notices, and the directory reading feeds if it exists.
options.inTheStory: The press release raises a To-do: '5 March 2027 · Public statement by the subject · Department of Transportation press release · [Original] [Archived copy]'. The op-ed sits under 'Reactions elsewhere'. The lawyer's letter and Ms. Ortega's knock never appear. The Director's letter shows: '20 March · Reply from the subject received. Its text is not shown because it names a private individual; we have invited the Department to resubmit it.' On 28 March the Department resubmits the letter with the resident's name marked as withheld by the Department; the group could decline a redacted submission, but accepts it, and it is listed exactly as sent. In August edition 1 opens: 'Withdrawn by Eastlake Accountability on 14 August 2027. Finding 2 rested on a memo we now believe was forged. Finding 1 is republished unchanged in edition 2.' Eastlake's queue names its Council letter; the tenants' copy tells its members finding 1 is carried unchanged.
gains: The subject's public rebuttals cannot be skipped once the group has them.
Outside responses are kept with proof, placed for a reason, and never mistaken for evidence.
Withdrawal becomes a signed, readable fact that people and software can act on.
costs: The most to build: shelves, watches, the suggestion, required To-dos, signing, the feed, citing copies' checks.
The core can be evaded by never capturing or linking a statement; the docket shows its last entry's date, and the subject can publish its own letter.
Each public entry is a publication that cannot be unseen.
options.commitsYouTo: A second signed public object beside every case, kept by the group under rules; withdrawal final; a group's grant of standing permanent for what it already brought in.

options.label: B
options.name: As A, but only what the subject sends the group is required
options.howItWorks: The subject's public statements elsewhere go to 'Reactions elsewhere', listed at the group's discretion like any outside reaction. Everything else as A.
options.inTheStory: Dana may list the press release or not. If not, the docket shows the op-ed and, from 28 March, the Director's letter; the Department's public rebuttal is missing.
gains: Lighter: no duty to watch or list what the subject says elsewhere.
Reads your ruling's 'responses that reach the group' literally.
costs: A group can show a subject's mild letter and omit its sharper public rebuttal.
Subjects learn to answer in public, where listing is optional.
options.commitsYouTo: Standing means 'what you send us', which the subject must be told.

options.label: C
options.name: As A, but a subject's reply is always listed whole
options.howItWorks: No exception for private names: the subject chose to write to a publisher, so its reply is listed in full.
options.inTheStory: On 20 March Mr. Tillman's name and street go on the public docket, signed by Eastlake, though he never chose to be named.
gains: No judgement call; the subject's words are never held back.
costs: The group becomes first to make a private person more public, against the naming rule.
A subject could use the docket to expose a complainant.

brief.tradeoff: How much of a case's after-life the group must show, given that it keeps its own docket: strict enough that rebuttals cannot be buried, without making the group the first to expose private people or republish others' work; and whether 'we no longer stand behind this' becomes a signed fact or stays words.

why: The shelves replace the CPUC's neutrality with rules: the group lists, but cannot pass a reaction off as evidence or hide what the subject said once it has it. Counting the subject's captured public statements is my judgement: a press release is the subject's answer to the world, and a docket with only the private letter would look complete while missing it. 'Link and short quotation, never whole republication' for others' articles is also my judgement: the archived copy proves what was said without the group republishing another's work.

On a subject's reply that names a private person, I recommend, as judgement, listing its receipt without the text, with the reason, and inviting the subject to resubmit. The group trims nothing: the entry shown is whole, the letter itself is simply not on the public docket, and any redaction is the subject's own, which you have ruled the group may accept or decline. It keeps 'asked, no answer' from standing falsely and exposes no private person. If you see holding back the text as redaction in disguise, C is the honest alternative.

On standing, which you confirmed a group may grant, I recommend the grant be a signed docket entry with a reason, giving exactly the named subject's rights, and permanent for what the holder has already submitted (a later withdrawal of standing would cover only future submissions). Withdrawal of a case stays as a signed, final notice, the edition readable under a stamp, supplying the missing trigger for re-evaluation notices. It never erases, so a legally compelled removal has no path; that would be a separate question.
recommendation.risk: The required core rests on the group capturing and linking what it knows. Contained in part: watches and suggestions make missing things harder, the docket shows its last entry's date, the subject can always publish its own letter and point to the group's 'asked, no answer', and a citing copy that cannot reach the docket says 'Could not read the publisher's docket', never that nothing changed.

ruled.title: After publication: a case's docket, outside responses, and withdrawing a case
ruled.decided: Each case has a docket: dated entries, each naming the edition it concerns, growing while the signed editions never change. The named subject has party-like standing, and a group may grant the same standing to others by a signed entry with a reason (permanent for what they already submitted). There are no confidential entries; only the submitter redacts, and the group may decline redacted submissions. Three shelves: what the group stands behind as accurately listed; 'Reactions elsewhere' ('Listed by the group. Not evidence. Not endorsed.'); and 'In our record only', never published. Checks are on form, never merit, and an entry never makes anything evidence. Required on the first shelf, each a To-do for the project's manager: every response the subject sends; the subject's public statements the group has captured, a press release included; a newer edition with its 'What changed' statement; a withdrawal; anything that would have had to be disclosed at signing. Outside responses are found by a pasted link, a standing watch or a labelled suggestion; captured and co-archived; linked to an edition; and a member chooses, with a reason, record only, public or both. A public reaction shows date, source, links to the original and the archived copy, and a short summary in the group's words, never the whole article. A reply naming a private person is listed as received, without its text, and the subject is asked to resend it without the name. Any member files to the record; only the manager signs an entry into public view; an entry is taken back by a later one, never deleted. Withdrawal is the manager's signed, final entry naming an edition or all, with a published reason: the edition stays readable under a stamp, re-evaluation notices go to everything resting on it, it is never lifted, and nothing is erased. The docket travels by pull: the public page, a feed per case, citing groups' copies and the directory; a copy that cannot reach it says 'Could not read the publisher's docket'.
